title: RBS-Attention: Radius-Bounded Sparse Prefill for Long-Context Large Language Models
summary: Long-context large language model inference is increasingly limited by prefill, where dense self-attention processes the entire prompt before generation begins. Sparse block selection can reduce this cost, but a block centroid may hide a highly relevant token among many irrelevant ones. We call this failure mode mean dilution and propose RBS-Attention, a training-free sparse-prefill method with two complementary selection branches. A centroid base branch captures average relevance, while a rescue branch uses the maximum key-block radius and its prompt-, layer-, and head-dependent distribution to identify blocks at risk of underestimation. Independently thresholding the two branches and combining their masks controls the contribution of rescue blocks while preserving regular block-sparse FlashAttention execution. On H100 GPUs, RBS-Attention achieves 20.65$\times$ standalone prefill-attention speedup, 11.92$\times$ vLLM prefill-attention speedup, and 5.97$\times$ end-to-end time-to-first-token speedup at 128K on Qwen3-30B-A3B-Instruct-2507-FP8. On the dense Qwen3-32B model, it obtains 88.65 overall RULER accuracy versus 89.52 for dense attention; LongBench-v2, InfiniteBench, and Video-MME provide additional quality evaluation. Supporting experiments measure actual retention, compare selectors at matched density, and characterize block-size, threshold, and memory behavior. Together, these results support radius-adaptive dual-branch selection as an effective approach to long-context prefill.

AI.tldr: RBS-Attention is a training-free sparse-prefill method that uses dual-branch (centroid + rescue) block selection to overcome mean dilution, achieving large prefill speedups with minimal quality loss.
AI.motivation: Prefill dominates long-context LLM inference cost because dense self-attention must process the entire prompt. Sparse block selection can cut this cost, but summarizing a block by its centroid may hide a highly relevant token among irrelevant ones—a failure mode the authors call mean dilution.
AI.method: RBS-Attention uses two complementary selection branches: a centroid base branch capturing average relevance, and a rescue branch using the maximum key-block radius and its prompt-, layer-, and head-dependent distribution to flag blocks at risk of underestimation. The two branches are thresholded independently and their masks combined, controlling rescue-block contribution while preserving regular block-sparse FlashAttention execution. The method is training-free.
AI.result: On H100 GPUs, RBS-Attention achieves 20.65x standalone prefill-attention speedup, 11.92x vLLM prefill-attention speedup, and 5.97x end-to-end time-to-first-token speedup at 128K on Qwen3-30B-A3B-Instruct-2507-FP8. On dense Qwen3-32B it reaches 88.65 overall RULER accuracy versus 89.52 for dense attention, with additional evaluation on LongBench-v2, InfiniteBench, and Video-MME. Supporting experiments measure retention, compare selectors at matched density, and characterize block-size, threshold, and memory behavior.
AI.conclusion: Radius-adaptive dual-branch selection is an effective approach to long-context prefill, delivering substantial speedups while closely matching dense-attention quality, as supported by both speed and quality evaluations.

title: Attention-Aware Routing: Coupling Routing and Attention in MoEs
summary: In Mixture-of-Experts language models, the router typically selects and weights experts based on the token's hidden state, utilizing limited contextual information. We propose Attention-Aware Routing (AAR), which augments the router with temporal and spectral features extracted from a sliding window of attention weights that represent a summary of the model's contextual state, disentangled from the hidden state. Keeping the base transformer entirely frozen, we train only the routing parameters, isolating routing as the sole variable. AAR improves GSM8K by +3.37 pp over a routing-only SFT baseline on OLMoE. Beyond performance, we show that routing and attention form a coupled circuit: routing changes at layer l propagate through the residual stream to amplify attention sinks at layer l+1, reshaping attention without any direct update to the attention mechanism itself. Further, AAR reduces long diverging generation, with incorrect answers getting shorter, while correct answers remain unchanged in length. Finally, AAR is strongly depth-sensitive: applying it indiscriminately across layers can degrade factual retrieval, whereas mathematical reasoning gains persist when it is introduced deeper in the network. This sensitivity exposes a retrieval--reasoning tension across depth and makes layer-selective AAR a controlled probe of the routing-relevant information carried by attention at different layers.

AI.tldr: Attention-Aware Routing (AAR) augments a Mixture-of-Experts router with temporal and spectral features from a sliding window of attention weights; with the base transformer frozen, it improves GSM8K by +3.37 pp on OLMoE and reveals a coupled routing-attention circuit that is strongly layer-dependent.
AI.motivation: Standard MoE routers select and weight experts solely from the token's hidden state, using only limited contextual information. The authors aim to enrich routing decisions with contextual signals that are disentangled from the hidden state, and to isolate routing as the single controllable variable for study.
AI.method: AAR augments the router with temporal and spectral features extracted from a sliding window of attention weights, which summarize the model's contextual state independently of the hidden state. The base transformer is kept entirely frozen; only routing parameters are trained, isolating routing as the sole variable. Layer-selective application is used to probe depth sensitivity.
AI.result: AAR improves GSM8K by +3.37 pp over a routing-only SFT baseline on OLMoE. Routing changes at layer l propagate through the residual stream to amplify attention sinks at layer l+1, changing attention without directly updating the attention mechanism. AAR reduces long diverging generations: incorrect answers shorten while correct answers keep their length. Effects are depth-sensitive: indiscriminate cross-layer application can hurt factual retrieval, whereas mathematical reasoning gains persist when AAR is introduced deeper in the network.
AI.conclusion: Routing and attention form a coupled circuit rather than operating in isolation. This depth sensitivity exposes a retrieval–reasoning tension across depth, and makes layer-selective AAR a controlled probe of the routing-relevant information carried by attention at different layers.

title: CaLR: Causal Latent Revision for Robust Diffusion Reasoning
summary: Autoregressive (AR) models suffer from local greediness, while diffusion language models (DLMs) often lack the strict causal structure required for reasoning. To combine the advantages and overcome the drawbacks of the dual, we propose Causal Latent Revision (CaLR), a framework that reformulates reasoning as constrained latent optimization. By adopting a causal topology matrix (CTM) from an expert model and implicit differentiation, CaLR performs gradient-guided ``thought revision" to enforce logical consistency, enabling dynamic self-correction of intermediate steps during parallel generation. Empirically, CaLR achieves SOTA DLM performance on complex benchmarks, surpassing strong AR baselines and demonstrating superior robustness in constrained tasks like Sudoku.

AI.tldr: CaLR reformulates reasoning as constrained latent optimization, combining AR models' causal structure with DLMs' parallel generation via a causal topology matrix and implicit differentiation for gradient-guided thought revision.
AI.motivation: Autoregressive (AR) models suffer from local greediness, while diffusion language models (DLMs) often lack the strict causal structure required for reasoning. The paper aims to combine the advantages and overcome the drawbacks of both paradigms.
AI.method: CaLR (Causal Latent Revision) adopts a causal topology matrix (CTM) from an expert model and applies implicit differentiation to perform gradient-guided "thought revision", enforcing logical consistency and enabling dynamic self-correction of intermediate steps during parallel generation.
AI.result: CaLR achieves SOTA DLM performance on complex benchmarks, surpassing strong AR baselines and demonstrating superior robustness in constrained tasks such as Sudoku.
AI.conclusion: By reformulating reasoning as constrained latent optimization, CaLR effectively integrates the causal structure of AR models with the parallel generation of DLMs, yielding stronger reasoning performance and robustness.

title: LoRA Enhanced Contrastive Learning with SAS Vision Transformers
summary: Automatic target recognition (ATR) with synthetic aperture sonar (SAS) supports advanced naval capabilities, but deep learning is constrained by scarce target imagery, background clutter, and human-in-the-loop assessment. We adapt DINOv3 Vision Transformer (ViT) models to underwater SAS ATR using a three-stage parameter-efficient framework. Stage 1 uses Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) while freezing the ViT backbone, bridging the gap between natural-image pretraining and underwater acoustic propagation. Stage 2 uses hard-negative mining to strengthen the decision boundary against acoustic mimics, including rocks and sediment formations resembling man-made targets. Stage 3 uses Supervised Contrastive Learning (SupCon) to separate target and clutter representations. We evaluate at-sea SAS data using a mission-level geographic split, compare all arms at 85 percent test recall, and repeat each comparison over three random seeds. LoRA accounts for the primary effect, increasing area under the precision-recall curve (AUPRC) from 0.300 to 0.679 +/- 0.027 using the same frozen backbone. Rank 4 achieves this result while training only 0.26 percent of weights. Neither refinement stage exceeds its matched control: hard-negative mining changes AUPRC by -0.0045 +/- 0.0119 versus an equal-size random curriculum, and SupCon changes AUPRC by +0.0002 +/- 0.0096 versus the preceding stage. These null results indicate that mining occurred on data the encoder had already fit and that supervised stages had already imposed most target-clutter geometry. One efficient adaptation stage is sufficient; stacked refinement is not.

AI.tldr: A three-stage parameter-efficient DINOv3 ViT adaptation for synthetic aperture sonar ATR shows that only the LoRA stage drives gains (AUPRC 0.300→0.679), while hard-negative mining and SupCon refinement yield null effects versus matched controls.
AI.motivation: Deep learning for SAS ATR is limited by scarce target imagery, background clutter, and human-in-the-loop assessment, motivating a parameter-efficient adaptation of large pretrained models from natural images to underwater acoustics.
AI.method: DINOv3 ViT adapted via three stages: (1) LoRA with frozen backbone; (2) hard-negative mining against acoustic mimics (rocks, sediment formations); (3) Supervised Contrastive Learning to separate target and clutter representations. Evaluation on at-sea SAS data with a mission-level geographic split, comparing arms at 85% test recall across three random seeds.
AI.result: LoRA is the primary effect: AUPRC rises from 0.300 to 0.679 +/- 0.027 with the same frozen backbone, achieved at rank 4 while training only 0.26% of weights. Hard-negative mining changes AUPRC by -0.0045 +/- 0.0119 versus an equal-size random curriculum; SupCon changes AUPRC by +0.0002 +/- 0.0096 versus the preceding stage—neither refinement exceeds its matched control.
AI.conclusion: One efficient adaptation stage is sufficient; stacked refinement is not. Null results suggest mining occurred on data the encoder had already fit, and supervised stages had already imposed most target-clutter geometry.

title: WM-VS: Progress-Aligned World Models for Closed-Loop Visual Servoing
summary: Closed-loop visual servoing requires predictions that indicate whether an action reduces task error, not only whether the action is plausible. We call this gap the prediction-control mismatch and introduce WM-VS, a target-centric progress-aligned world-model framework for closed-loop visual servoing. Offline target-region DINOv2 correspondences define a signed four-dimensional servo coordinate for translation, scale, and in-plane rotation. Stage 1 aligns action-conditioned latent transitions with this coordinate; Stage 2 freezes the world model and trains a reactive joint-velocity policy with action imitation, consequence supervision, and short imagined rollouts that favor error contraction. Deployment is RGB-only and reactive, without online trajectory optimization. On a real 7-DoF eye-to-hand system, WM-VS reaches a corner RMSE no larger than 10 percent of its initial value in 30/30 trials and retains this criterion at the final valid frame in 25/30 (83.33 percent). Removing future-error alignment reduces retention to 26.67 percent. The learned progress signal agrees with an external AprilTag corner error not used for training or control (mean Spearman rho = 0.8778). Without retraining, two unseen 3D targets achieve translation-error reductions of 86.48 percent and 90.27 percent and rotation-error reductions of 70.01 percent and 65.70 percent. These results link progress-aligned action consequences to repeated closed-loop correction and transfer. Code and data will be released as open source.

AI.tldr: WM-VS is a target-centric, progress-aligned world-model framework for closed-loop visual servoing that trains predictions to favor task-error contraction, achieving robust real-robot servo convergence and transfer to unseen targets.
AI.motivation: Closed-loop visual servoing needs predictions indicating whether an action reduces task error, not merely whether it is plausible; this prediction-control mismatch limits effective closed-loop correction.
AI.method: Offline target-region DINOv2 correspondences define a signed 4D servo coordinate (translation, scale, in-plane rotation). Stage 1 aligns action-conditioned latent transitions with this coordinate; Stage 2 freezes the world model and trains a reactive joint-velocity policy using action imitation, consequence supervision, and short imagined rollouts favoring error contraction. Deployment is RGB-only and reactive, without online trajectory optimization.
AI.result: On a real 7-DoF eye-to-hand system, WM-VS reaches corner RMSE no larger than 10 percent of its initial value in 30/30 trials and retains this criterion at the final valid frame in 25/30 (83.33 percent). Removing future-error alignment reduces retention to 26.67 percent. The learned progress signal agrees with an external AprilTag corner error not used for training or control (mean Spearman rho = 0.8778). Without retraining, two unseen 3D targets achieve translation-error reductions of 86.48 percent and 90.27 percent and rotation-error reductions of 70.01 percent and 65.70 percent.
AI.conclusion: Progress-aligned action consequences are linked to repeated closed-loop correction and transfer. Code and data will be released as open source.

title: Detecting Hallucination in LLMs: Tracing the Topological Signatures of Impaired Context Sharing
summary: In this work, we examine the topology of information flow patterns within attention graphs to effectively distinguish hallucinated from non-hallucinated responses. We analyze the Forman-Ricci curvature to identify structural patterns indicating information bottlenecks in attention graphs. We then introduce a method that captures both semi-local and global information-flow characteristics of attention heads associated with hallucinated responses. We evaluate our approach extensively across several LLMs and established benchmarks. Empirical results demonstrate that our proposed single-pass approach provides consistent improvements over existing attention-based and multi-response baselines across two hallucination-detection benchmarks, while achieving competitive performance across diverse LLM architectures. Further analysis reveals that impaired context sharing among tokens during causal generation is strongly associated with hallucination occurrences in LLMs. In particular, hallucinated responses are consistently characterized by an over-reliance on self-attention, diffused context retrieval from earlier tokens, or information over-squashing, especially in the final transformer layer.

AI.tldr: This paper detects LLM hallucinations by analyzing the topology of information flow in attention graphs, using Forman-Ricci curvature to capture semi-local and global information-flow characteristics of attention heads.
AI.motivation: To effectively distinguish hallucinated from non-hallucinated LLM responses, this work exploits the topology of information flow patterns within attention graphs, addressing the limitations of existing attention-based and multi-response detection baselines.
AI.method: The authors analyze Forman-Ricci curvature to identify structural patterns indicating information bottlenecks in attention graphs, then propose a method capturing both semi-local and global information-flow characteristics of attention heads associated with hallucinated responses. It is a single-pass approach evaluated across several LLMs and benchmarks.
AI.result: The proposed single-pass approach consistently outperforms existing attention-based and multi-response baselines on two hallucination-detection benchmarks while achieving competitive performance across diverse LLM architectures.
AI.conclusion: Impaired context sharing among tokens during causal generation is strongly associated with hallucination occurrences. Hallucinated responses are characterized by over-reliance on self-attention, diffused context retrieval from earlier tokens, or information over-squashing, especially in the final transformer layer.

title: AeRove: A Compact Bimodal Aerial-Terrestrial Drone with Rapid Bistable Reconfiguration for Close-Range Pipeline Inspection
summary: Close-proximity pipeline inspection is challenging for standard drones due to high hovering power consumption, airflow sensitivity, and propeller wash interference with gas sensing. To address this, we present AeRove, a compact bimodal aerial-terrestrial robot. AeRove uses its propeller guards as wheels to roll along pipes and employs a spring-loaded bistable mechanism to reconfigure between ground and flight modes in 200 ms without continuous actuator power to maintain either state. The converging propeller-guard geometry also improves measured thrust efficiency. By reserving flight for obstacle hopping and using ground rolling for continuous traversal, current draw is reduced 14x compared to continuous flight (0.7 A vs. 10 A), extending estimated travel distance from 144 m to 2057 m. Autonomous trials on a 51 cm diameter steel pipe demonstrated navigation on straight and curved sections, obstacle jumping, and leak detection of simulated inspection markers. Separate CO2 sensing experiments evaluated gas-detection performance under perched and aerial operating conditions. Perched inspection produced a substantially larger concentration response than hovering under the tested conditions. During flight, an underbody propeller-intake configuration produced a faster and stronger gas-detection response than an extended probe by leveraging propeller-induced airflow. Code and designs are released under the CC-BY license.

AI.tldr: AeRove is a compact bimodal aerial-terrestrial robot that rolls on pipes using propeller guards as wheels and switches between rolling and flight modes via a passively stable bistable mechanism, cutting power draw 14x and enabling autonomous pipe inspection with improved gas sensing.
AI.motivation: Close-proximity pipeline inspection is difficult for standard drones due to high hovering power consumption, airflow sensitivity, and propeller wash interfering with gas sensing. A platform is needed that can traverse pipes continuously while reserving flight only where necessary, and that improves rather than degrades gas-detection performance.
AI.method: AeRove uses its propeller guards as wheels for rolling along pipes and a spring-loaded bistable mechanism to reconfigure between ground and flight modes in 200 ms without continuous actuator power to hold either state. The converging propeller-guard geometry enhances thrust efficiency. Flight is reserved for obstacle hopping while ground rolling handles continuous traversal. Autonomous trials were run on a 51 cm diameter steel pipe (straight and curved sections, obstacle jumping, leak detection of simulated inspection markers), plus separate CO2 sensing experiments comparing perched vs. aerial conditions and an underbody propeller-intake vs. an extended probe configuration.
AI.result: Current draw dropped 14x versus continuous flight (0.7 A vs. 10 A), extending estimated travel distance from 144 m to 2057 m. Autonomous trials demonstrated navigation on straight and curved sections, obstacle jumping, and leak detection. Perched inspection produced a substantially larger CO2 concentration response than hovering, and during flight the underbody propeller-intake configuration gave a faster and stronger gas-detection response than the extended probe by leveraging propeller-induced airflow.
AI.conclusion: A passively reconfigurable bimodal rolling-flying design enables efficient, close-proximity pipeline inspection, and propeller-induced airflow can be exploited to enhance rather than hinder gas sensing. Code and designs are released under the CC-BY license.

title: Decoupling Internal Representational Changes and Causal Importance in Fine-Tuned Large Language Models
summary: Fine-tuning has emerged as a widely adopted approach for adapting LLMs to a variety of downstream tasks. However, how it reshapes their internal mechanisms remains poorly understood. To address this, we investigate how fine-tuning alters internal representations in LLMs, including attention patterns and layer-wise activations, and examine whether these changes are linked to task-relevant components identified by EAP (e.g., attention heads and logit-level activations) that drive task performance. We find that EAP-identified components are concentrated within specific layers, indicating a degree of functional localisation in how models internalise task-specific behavior. Notably, the distribution of these components across layers is largely uncorrelated with the layers undergoing the most substantial representational changes during fine-tuning. Furthermore, we observe that overlap in EAP-identified components across tasks does not translate into cross-task performance transfer if the tasks are different in nature (e.g. classification vs. generative tasks). More specifically, fine-tuning on one task can lead to a degradation of performance on another when the two tasks exhibit a high degree of overlap in their EAP-identified components.

AI.tldr: Fine-tuning localises task-relevant components in specific layers, but these layers do not coincide with those undergoing the largest representational changes; high EAP component overlap between dissimilar tasks can cause cross-task performance degradation rather than transfer.
AI.motivation: Fine-tuning is a widely adopted method for adapting LLMs to downstream tasks, yet how it reshapes their internal mechanisms remains poorly understood. This work aims to clarify how fine-tuning alters internal representations (attention patterns and layer-wise activations) and whether these changes relate to task-relevant components identified by EAP.
AI.method: The authors investigate how fine-tuning alters internal representations in LLMs, including attention patterns and layer-wise activations, and examine whether these changes are linked to task-relevant components identified by EAP (e.g., attention heads and logit-level activations) that drive task performance.
AI.result: EAP-identified components concentrate within specific layers, indicating functional localisation in how models internalise task-specific behavior. The layer distribution of these components is largely uncorrelated with the layers undergoing the most substantial representational changes during fine-tuning. Overlap in EAP-identified components across tasks does not translate into cross-task performance transfer when tasks differ in nature (e.g., classification vs. generative). Fine-tuning on one task can degrade performance on another when the two tasks show high overlap in their EAP-identified components.
AI.conclusion: Fine-tuning induces task-relevant functional localisation that is decoupled from the layers with the largest representational shifts. EAP component overlap between dissimilar tasks can lead to negative transfer, suggesting that shared circuits do not guarantee beneficial generalisation.

title: Shake to Learn: Dynamic Interrogation of Hidden Object Physics for Robotic Manipulation with Physical Reservoir Computing
summary: Many physical properties relevant to robotic manipulation are hidden from vision. A sealed object, for example, may reveal little about its center of mass (COM) or internal contents until it is lifted, shaken, or otherwise dynamically perturbed. This study shows that such interactions can enable a new modality of robotic perception and learning, in which interaction-induced dynamic responses are used to infer object physics that is inaccessible to conventional sensing. We implement this idea using an origami-inspired soft robotic arm that functions as a physical reservoir computer. After grasping an object, the arm is excited by a fixed shaking input at its base, and the resulting ringdown response is recorded through either camera tracking or embedded sensors. Because the input is held constant across trials, hidden object properties, such as the COM position, are encoded through their effect on the dynamics of the coupled robot-object system. A lightweight linear readout can then decode these dynamics to recover interpretable information about the hidden object physics. Using this framework, the soft robotic arm reservoir completed three tasks of increasing difficulty: inferring the orientation of the object's hidden COM, inferring the COM distance from the grasp point, and using the inferred COM information to guide a subsequent regrasp. We further develop a dynamic summary representation of the ringdown response that improves prediction accuracy. Together, these results establish shake-to-learn mechanical interrogation as a promising strategy for robotic systems to convert brief physical interactions into actionable cues about hidden object properties for downstream manipulation.

AI.tldr: A soft origami robotic arm functioning as a physical reservoir computer uses fixed shaking and ringdown dynamics to infer hidden object properties like center of mass, enabling downstream manipulation tasks.
AI.motivation: Many physical properties relevant to manipulation (e.g., an object's center of mass or internal contents) are invisible to vision and only become observable when the object is lifted, shaken, or dynamically perturbed. This work aims to exploit such interactions as a new perception modality for inferring physics that conventional sensing cannot access.
AI.method: An origami-inspired soft robotic arm acts as a physical reservoir computer. After grasping an object, the arm is excited by a fixed shaking input at its base, and the resulting ringdown response is recorded via camera tracking or embedded sensors. Because the input is constant across trials, hidden object properties are encoded through their effect on the coupled robot-object dynamics. A lightweight linear readout decodes these dynamics, and a dynamic summary representation of the ringdown response is developed to improve accuracy.
AI.result: The reservoir arm completed three tasks of increasing difficulty: inferring the orientation of the hidden COM, inferring the COM distance from the grasp point, and using inferred COM information to guide a subsequent regrasp. The dynamic summary representation improved prediction accuracy.
AI.conclusion: Shake-to-learn mechanical interrogation is established as a promising strategy for robotic systems to convert brief physical interactions into actionable cues about hidden object properties for downstream manipulation.

title: TinyCeNN-LM: Quality-Gated Conversion of Pretrained Attention with CeNN-Inspired Cellular-Recurrent Layers
summary: Replacing attention in a pretrained language model is a compatibility problem: a plausible substitute may alter representations expected by later layers. TinyCeNN-LM introduces a \emph{quality-gated post-training conversion} framework using CeNN-inspired cellular-recurrent layers with bounded local processing, compact recurrent memory, routing, fusion, and accept-or-rollback validation. Three implementations are studied: Integrated Memory, MemoryFusion, and PDelta3-GDN2-CLVR+Local32. Strict PDelta3 conversion accepts a layer only when representation and NLL criteria pass fixed thresholds. On SmolLM2-135M, layers 0-2 are accepted with cumulative $Δ\mathrm{NLL}=+0.01209$, while layer 3 is rejected despite acceptable NLL because representation fidelity fails. On Qwen3.5-0.8B, full-attention layers 3, 7, and 11 are accepted with final $Δ\mathrm{NLL}=+0.02073$. Integrated Memory keeps perplexity within $-0.07\%$ to $+0.93\%$ while reducing total cache by up to $6.01\%$. A sampled 200-item downstream sanity check gives $28.5\%$--$32.0\%$ overall accuracy for converted Qwen releases. The results support conservative, quality-gated structural conversion rather than universal attention replacement or speedup.

AI.tldr: TinyCeNN-LM proposes a quality-gated post-training framework that converts pretrained attention layers into CeNN-inspired cellular-recurrent layers only when representation fidelity and NLL criteria pass fixed thresholds, accepting or rolling back each layer.
AI.motivation: Replacing attention in a pretrained language model is a compatibility problem: a plausible substitute may alter representations expected by later layers, so naive attention replacement risks breaking downstream computation.
AI.method: A quality-gated post-training conversion framework using CeNN-inspired cellular-recurrent layers with bounded local processing, compact recurrent memory, routing, fusion, and accept-or-rollback validation. Three implementations are studied: Integrated Memory, MemoryFusion, and PDelta3-GDN2-CLVR+Local32. Strict PDelta3 conversion accepts a layer only when representation and NLL criteria pass fixed thresholds.
AI.result: On SmolLM2-135M, layers 0-2 are accepted with cumulative ΔNLL=+0.01209, while layer 3 is rejected despite acceptable NLL because representation fidelity fails. On Qwen3.5-0.8B, full-attention layers 3, 7, and 11 are accepted with final ΔNLL=+0.02073. Integrated Memory keeps perplexity within -0.07% to +0.93% while reducing total cache by up to 6.01%. A sampled 200-item downstream sanity check gives 28.5%–32.0% overall accuracy for converted Qwen releases.
AI.conclusion: The results support conservative, quality-gated structural conversion rather than universal attention replacement or speedup.

title: ForeTac-VLA: A Forecasting-Based Tactile-Vision-Language-Action Model for Contact-Rich Robotic Manipulation
summary: Vision-language-action (VLA) models have demonstrated strong capabilities in robotic manipulation, yet their reliance on visual perception limits robustness in contact-rich environments, where critical physical interaction states may not be visually observable. Existing tactile-enhanced VLA methods improve physical grounding using observed tactile feedback, but most remain largely reactive rather than explicitly modeling how contact may evolve. Therefore, we propose ForeTac-VLA, a forecasting-based tactile-vision-language fusion model that predicts future tactile states to guide action generation. Specifically, ForeTac-VLA encodes recent tactile observations into temporal representations and integrates them with vision-language features through bidirectional cross-attention. Further, a transformer-based forecasting module predicts multi-step future tactile states, enabling the model to reason jointly over observed and anticipated contact. Finally, the fused multimodal representations and predicted future tactile states are fed into the VLA backbone to condition action generation. To stabilize training, a ground-truth-to-prediction curriculum is employed when early forecasts are unreliable. Across four real-world contact-rich manipulation tasks, ForeTac-VLA achieves an average success rate of 95%, outperforming the fine-tuned VLA model by 36.25 percentage points and state-of-the-art tactile-enhanced VLA baselines by over 22 percentage points. ForeTac-VLA also maintains strong performance under low-illumination and visually cluttered conditions. Video demonstrations can be found on https://foretac-vla.github.io/

AI.tldr: ForeTac-VLA is a forecasting-based tactile-vision-language fusion model that predicts future tactile states to guide robotic action generation, achieving 95% average success across four real-world contact-rich tasks.
AI.motivation: Vision-language-action (VLA) models rely on visual perception, which limits robustness in contact-rich environments where critical physical interaction states are not visually observable. Existing tactile-enhanced VLA methods use observed tactile feedback but remain largely reactive, without explicitly modeling how contact may evolve.
AI.method: ForeTac-VLA encodes recent tactile observations into temporal representations and fuses them with vision-language features via bidirectional cross-attention. A transformer-based forecasting module predicts multi-step future tactile states, enabling joint reasoning over observed and anticipated contact. The fused multimodal representations and predicted future tactile states condition the VLA backbone for action generation. A ground-truth-to-prediction curriculum stabilizes training when early forecasts are unreliable.
AI.result: Across four real-world contact-rich manipulation tasks, ForeTac-VLA achieves an average success rate of 95%, outperforming the fine-tuned VLA model by 36.25 percentage points and state-of-the-art tactile-enhanced VLA baselines by over 22 percentage points. It also maintains strong performance under low-illumination and visually cluttered conditions.
AI.conclusion: Explicitly forecasting future tactile states improves physical grounding and robustness of VLA models in contact-rich manipulation, surpassing reactive tactile-enhanced baselines and remaining effective under degraded visual conditions.

title: Clinician-Grounded Quality Assurance for AI-Assisted Psychiatric Intake
summary: Before patients can use AI-assisted psychiatric intake systems, health systems need practical ways to routinely evaluate these tools against their clinical standards for quality assurance. Because clinicians may use different intake styles, evaluation for this task must (1) support comparison across interviewing approaches, (2) minimize clinician burden, and (3) measure clinically relevant performance for health systems deploying these technologies. We present a clinician-grounded evaluation platform built around a memory-augmented patient simulator for open-ended AI interviewing, InterviewPlayground. We created interactive patients using InterviewPlayground with our expert-authored vignettes, constructed a simulated intake platform for the interviews, and designed evaluation modalities relevant to intake. In a pilot of 6 clinicians in a 25-minute assessment compared to a GPT-based LLM intake interviewer, the LLM recovered more of the clinically relevant items embedded in the patient vignettes (88.0% vs. 38.9%), but made more clinical inferences not based on the interview (56.8% vs. 27.8%), and characterized identified safety concerns less often (33.3% vs. 66.7%), setting the stage for deployed quality assurance for this task.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces InterviewPlayground, a clinician-grounded evaluation platform with a memory-augmented patient simulator for open-ended AI psychiatric interviewing, and reports a pilot comparing a GPT-based LLM intake interviewer against 6 clinicians.
AI.motivation: Health systems need practical methods to routinely evaluate AI-assisted psychiatric intake tools against clinical quality standards before deployment. Existing evaluation approaches do not simultaneously support comparison across differing clinician interviewing styles, minimize clinician burden, and measure clinically relevant performance for deploying health systems.
AI.method: The authors built InterviewPlayground, a platform centered on a memory-augmented patient simulator enabling open-ended AI interviewing. They created interactive patients from expert-authored vignettes, constructed a simulated intake platform, and designed intake-relevant evaluation modalities. A pilot study with 6 clinicians (25-minute assessment) compared clinician intake to a GPT-based LLM intake interviewer.
AI.result: The LLM recovered more clinically relevant items embedded in the patient vignettes (88.0% vs. 38.9%), but made more clinical inferences not grounded in the interview (56.8% vs. 27.8%) and characterized identified safety concerns less often (33.3% vs. 66.7%).
AI.conclusion: InterviewPlayground provides a clinician-grounded, low-burden, cross-style evaluation framework that measures clinically relevant intake performance, establishing a foundation for deployed quality assurance of AI-assisted psychiatric intake systems.

title: PIVOT: Physically Informed Vision-Language Off-Road Traversability for Field Robot Navigation
summary: Terrain assessment is a critical capability for off-road mobile robots, enabling safe and reliable navigation through unstructured and geometrically complex environments. Conventional geometry-based terrain assessment is fast to compute but often overly conservative in unstructured environments. We present PIVOT: a Physically Informed Vision-Language Off-Road Traversability navigation system that augments conventional geometry-based planning with vision-language-model (VLM)-based semantic reasoning for field robots. To physically ground this assessment, we quantify how strongly the VLM's predicted traversal energy cost, robot vibration, and wheel slip correlate with real-world measurements and introduce a unified traversability score that weights each modality by its prediction-measurement correlation. For efficiency, we design a two-level navigation architecture that retains geometry-based planning as the nominal mode and invokes semantic replanning only when that mode fails to find a path. Across five repeated closed-loop trials on a mixed-terrain route totalling around $6.4$ km, the proposed system increases overall autonomy from $59.6\%$ to $97.0\%$, reduces human interventions from $11$ to $3$, and increases the mean distance between interventions (MDBI) from $69.2$ m to $412.9$ m compared with geometry-only navigation. These results demonstrate that physically grounded VLM-based terrain assessment can substantially extend autonomous navigation beyond the limitations of geometry alone, while preserving efficient geometric planning as the nominal mode.

AI.tldr: PIVOT is a physically grounded, VLM-based off-road traversability system that augments geometry-based planning; it raises autonomy from 59.6% to 97.0% and cuts interventions from 11 to 3 over ~6.4 km of mixed-terrain trials.
AI.motivation: Terrain assessment is critical for off-road robots, but conventional geometry-based methods, though fast, tend to be overly conservative in unstructured environments, limiting autonomous navigation.
AI.method: A Physically Informed Vision-Language Off-Road Traversability (PIVOT) system that augments geometry-based planning with VLM-based semantic reasoning. The VLM's predicted traversal energy cost, robot vibration, and wheel slip are correlated with real-world measurements, and a unified traversability score weights each modality by its prediction-measurement correlation. A two-level navigation architecture keeps geometry-based planning as the nominal mode and triggers semantic replanning only when it fails to find a path.
AI.result: Across five repeated closed-loop trials on a mixed-terrain route totalling about 6.4 km, overall autonomy rose from 59.6% to 97.0%, human interventions dropped from 11 to 3, and mean distance between interventions (MDBI) increased from 69.2 m to 412.9 m versus geometry-only navigation.
AI.conclusion: Physically grounded VLM-based terrain assessment can substantially extend autonomous navigation beyond the limits of geometry alone, while preserving efficient geometric planning as the nominal mode.

title: Can Agents Design Better Chips with a Higher Level Abstraction?
summary: Large Language Model (LLM) agents are increasingly being explored for chip design, but most existing approaches operate directly at RTL. We ask whether agents can design better chips by leveraging higher-level abstractions. We compare Direct RTL Design, Agent-based HLS Design, Post-Compiler HLS Refinement, and Post-HLS RTL Refinement, and combine Agent-based HLS Design with Post-HLS RTL Refinement as Agent-based HLS with RTL Refinement (AHRR). We use FPGAs as a practical, easy-to-deploy platform for end-to-end evaluation, but note that the design-flow tradeoffs we study are largely independent of the target technology. Across a diverse 11-tasks benchmark suite, AHRR achieves a 2.6$\times$ geometric-mean speedup over Direct RTL Design across our benchmark suite. Case studies show that HLS distills design knowledge into abstractions that agents can leverage, while RTL refinement recovers lower-level optimization opportunities. Together, these results make AHRR a promising workflow for agentic chip design. The code and evaluation artifacts are available at https://github.com/ZijD/AHRR.

AI.tldr: LLM agents for chip design usually work directly at RTL. This paper investigates whether higher-level abstractions help, comparing four design flows and proposing AHRR (Agent-based HLS with RTL Refinement), which achieves a 2.6× geometric-mean speedup over Direct RTL Design across an 11-task benchmark.
AI.motivation: Most existing LLM-agent chip design approaches operate directly at the RTL level, potentially missing the benefits of higher-level abstractions. The authors ask whether agents can design better chips by leveraging such abstractions.
AI.method: The paper compares four design flows: Direct RTL Design, Agent-based HLS Design, Post-Compiler HLS Refinement, and Post-HLS RTL Refinement. It then combines Agent-based HLS Design with Post-HLS RTL Refinement into AHRR (Agent-based HLS with RTL Refinement). FPGAs are used as a practical evaluation platform, though the design-flow tradeoffs studied are largely technology-independent.
AI.result: Across a diverse 11-task benchmark suite, AHRR achieves a 2.6× geometric-mean speedup over Direct RTL Design. Case studies indicate that HLS distills design knowledge into abstractions agents can leverage, while RTL refinement recovers lower-level optimization opportunities.
AI.conclusion: Combining HLS-based agent design with post-HLS RTL refinement (AHRR) is a promising workflow for agentic chip design. Code and evaluation artifacts are available at https://github.com/ZijD/AHRR.

title: Do Spinning Radar Doppler Velocity Measurements Improve Vehicle Detection and Tracking?
summary: Spinning frequency-modulated continuous-wave (FMCW) radars have been gaining popularity in autonomous vehicle perception on account of their robustness to adverse weather conditions and 360° field of view. Recently, scanning radars have also been shown capable of generating per-azimuth Doppler velocity. In this paper, we investigate whether these Doppler velocity measurements improve spinning radar vehicle detection and tracking performance. For detection, we estimate the ego motion and use it to undo the Doppler range distortion of the radar image before passing it to a network. For tracking, we propose a new way to estimate a per-vehicle velocity and use it as a prior for the tracker's motion model. Since Doppler-enabled spinning radar data is not available in any dataset with ground-truth dynamic object labels, our first contribution is an automatic labelling pipeline that uses an ensemble of fine-tuned off-the-shelf lidar detectors to label all 643 km of the Boreas Road Trip dataset. We then transfer detections to radar, and use over 250 km of vehicle-dense sequences as ground-truth training data. By training and evaluating two state-of-the-art detectors, we show that Doppler undistortion can improve detection accuracy by up to $2.37$ points on mean average precision. Furthermore, we show that the Doppler velocity prior can improve tracking accuracy by $13.68$ points on multi-object tracking accuracy (MOTA) versus the zero-velocity initialization baseline, while achieving $99.7\%$ of the MOTA obtained using ground-truth velocities as the prior.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates whether per-azimuth Doppler velocity from spinning FMCW radars improves vehicle detection and tracking. It introduces an automatic labeling pipeline (using fine-tuned lidar detectors on the Boreas Road Trip dataset) to create Doppler-enabled radar training data, then shows that Doppler undistortion boosts detection mAP by up to 2.37 points and a Doppler velocity prior improves tracking MOTA by 13.68 points over zero-velocity initialization.
AI.motivation: Spinning FMCW radars are attractive for autonomous vehicle perception due to robustness to adverse weather and 360° field of view, and they can produce per-azimuth Doppler velocity. However, it is unclear whether these Doppler measurements actually improve spinning radar vehicle detection and tracking. A key obstacle is that no existing dataset provides Doppler-enabled spinning radar data with ground-truth dynamic object labels.
AI.method: For detection, the authors estimate ego motion and use it to undo the Doppler range distortion of the radar image before feeding it to a network. For tracking, they propose a new method to estimate per-vehicle velocity and use it as a prior in the tracker's motion model. To obtain training data, they build an automatic labeling pipeline that uses an ensemble of fine-tuned off-the-shelf lidar detectors to label all 643 km of the Boreas Road Trip dataset, then transfer detections to radar, using over 250 km of vehicle-dense sequences as ground-truth training data. Two state-of-the-art detectors are trained and evaluated.
AI.result: Doppler undistortion improves detection accuracy by up to 2.37 points on mean average precision. The Doppler velocity prior improves tracking accuracy by 13.68 points on MOTA versus the zero-velocity initialization baseline, while achieving 99.7% of the MOTA obtained using ground-truth velocities as the prior.
AI.conclusion: Doppler velocity measurements from spinning radar provide meaningful improvements for both vehicle detection and tracking. The proposed automatic labeling pipeline enables Doppler-enabled radar training without manual annotation, and the use of Doppler information (undistortion for detection and velocity priors for tracking) yields substantial gains, with tracking performance nearly matching that of ground-truth velocity priors.

title: SpecOpt: Contact-Diff Reasoning for Agentic Molecule Optimization Toward Binding Specificity
summary: Off-target protein binding is a major source of adverse effects for small-molecule drugs, yet most structure-based molecular design methods focus on generating selective compounds de novo rather than improving the selectivity of existing, well- characterized drugs. We introduce specificity optimization (SpecOpt), a molecular design task that seeks constrained structural modifications to an existing compound that increase its binding preference for an intended target over known off-targets while preserving its structural identity and drug-like properties. To enable systematic evaluation, we construct a ChEMBL-derived benchmark from compound-target interaction data, identifying intended targets through curated drug-mechanism annotations and off- targets through measured activities. We then develop an agentic framework that docks each compound against its intended target and off-targets, compares the resulting poses through residue-aware atom-protein contacts, and provides these differential interactions to a large language model to propose targeted structural modifications. Candidates are retained only if they satisfy molecular similarity, ADMET, and target-off-target docking selectivity criteria. On 915 compounds, the agent improves the target- off-target binding gap for 84.8% of compounds, shifting the mean gap from -0.72 to +0.47 kcal/mol while maintaining a mean Tanimoto similarity of 0.72 to the starting compounds. Ablation studies identify residue-specific contact information as the critical optimization signal: replacing residue identities with binary contact indicators eliminates improvement on all 29 ablation compounds. These results establish SpecOpt as a distinct molecular design problem and demonstrate residue-aware differential interactions as an effective signal for improving the specificity of existing compounds.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces SpecOpt, a task for improving the target-vs-off-target binding specificity of existing drugs via minimal structural edits. An agentic pipeline using docking-derived residue-aware contact differences and an LLM improved the binding gap for 84.8% of 915 compounds while preserving similarity.
AI.motivation: Off-target protein binding causes adverse drug effects, yet most structure-based design methods focus on de novo generation of selective compounds rather than improving the selectivity of already well-characterized drugs.
AI.method: The authors define SpecOpt: constrained structural modification of an existing compound to increase binding preference for its intended target over known off-targets while preserving structural identity and drug-like properties. They build a ChEMBL-derived benchmark, identifying intended targets via curated drug-mechanism annotations and off-targets via measured activities. An agentic framework docks each compound against intended target and off-targets, compares poses through residue-aware atom-protein contacts, and feeds these differential interactions to an LLM to propose targeted modifications. Candidates are filtered by molecular similarity, ADMET, and target-off-target docking selectivity.
AI.result: On 915 compounds, the agent improved the target-off-target binding gap for 84.8% of compounds, shifting the mean gap from -0.72 to +0.47 kcal/mol while retaining a mean Tanimoto similarity of 0.72. Ablation showed residue-specific contact information is critical: replacing residue identities with binary contact indicators eliminated improvement across all 29 ablation compounds.
AI.conclusion: SpecOpt is established as a distinct molecular design problem, and residue-aware differential interactions are shown to be an effective signal for improving the specificity of existing compounds.

title: Project SCOUT: Interceptor Drone for Perimeter Defense
summary: The rapid proliferation of unauthorized unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) has created a growing need for robust, jamming-resistant counter-UAV systems for perimeter defense. This paper presents \textbf{SCOUT} (Spatial Computation for Optimized UAV Tracking), a ROS-integrated onboard perception and control framework for real-time aerial defense against incoming UAVs. SCOUT performs visual detection, target association, track filtering, and control command generation directly onboard the defender UAV, without relying on external sensing infrastructure or ground-station computation. To provide stable control inputs, the perception pipeline combines TensorRT-accelerated drone detection with ByteTrack-based association and a lightweight track-retention state machine. The state machine rejects abrupt target jumps and maintains short-term target continuity during temporary detection degradation, reducing unstable control responses caused by false detections or target switching. We evaluate the proposed architecture through an integrated hardware deployment executing a planar ``goalkeeping'' interception strategy. In this setting, the defender UAV tracks the incoming target and adjusts its motion to maintain a blocking configuration near the protected boundary. Real-world flight results show that SCOUT maintains valid target detections for 92.2\% of frames while operating at real-time onboard detection rates, demonstrating the feasibility of visual tracking and closed-loop control for UAV perimeter defense. A video demonstration of the end-to-end perimeter defense operation is available online. https://figshare.com/s/497befc033091fc0b84f

AI.tldr: SCOUT is a ROS-integrated, fully onboard perception and control framework for jamming-resistant counter-UAV perimeter defense, combining TensorRT-accelerated detection, ByteTrack association, and a track-retention state machine to enable real-time goalkeeping-style interception.
AI.motivation: The rapid proliferation of unauthorized UAVs creates a growing need for robust, jamming-resistant counter-UAV systems for perimeter defense, particularly ones that do not depend on external sensing infrastructure or ground-station computation.
AI.method: SCOUT performs visual detection, target association, track filtering, and control command generation directly onboard the defender UAV via a ROS-integrated architecture. The perception pipeline combines TensorRT-accelerated drone detection with ByteTrack-based association and a lightweight track-retention state machine that rejects abrupt target jumps and maintains short-term target continuity under temporary detection degradation. Evaluation uses an integrated hardware deployment executing a planar goalkeeping interception strategy, where the defender tracks the incoming target and adjusts motion to maintain a blocking configuration near the protected boundary.
AI.result: Real-world flight results show SCOUT maintains valid target detections for 92.2% of frames while operating at real-time onboard detection rates, demonstrating feasibility of visual tracking and closed-loop control for UAV perimeter defense. A video demonstration is available online.
AI.conclusion: SCOUT demonstrates the feasibility of a fully onboard visual tracking and closed-loop control framework for jamming-resistant UAV perimeter defense, achieving high detection validity at real-time onboard rates without external infrastructure.

title: Implicit Rule Induction with Test-Time Task Embeddings in ARC-like Tasks
summary: The Abstraction and Reasoning Corpus and related benchmarks evaluate whether AI models can solve novel reasoning tasks, but often leave unclear whether success reflects inference of the intended underlying rule or reliance on shortcuts. We address this gap by studying test-time task embeddings in Vision ARC (VARC), a model in which a pre-trained backbone is complemented by a trainable embedding representing the transformation rule. In the original VARC, test-time training (TTT) is jointly applied to the backbone and task embedding. Here we introduce a novel two-step TTT protocol: first finetune only the task embedding (Embed-TTT), then freeze it and finetune the backbone. Across ARC-AGI-1, ConceptARC, and two controlled datasets with known rules, Embed-TTT consistently yields improved task embeddings, ones that align better with underlying task rules, improve embedding-based retrieval, and enable accurate linear probing of known rules. Qualitatively, Embed-TTT identifies more semantically meaningful relations between test and train tasks on ARC-AGI-1. We also show that optimizing only task embeddings (less than 0.01% of model parameters) already solves a non-trivial fraction of ARC-AGI-1, ConceptARC, and Mini-ARC tasks, while the full two-step pipeline improves final performance. Finally, we show that Embed-TTT recovers the underlying geometric structure of parametric rules and learns compositional capabilities that enable rule-wise interpolation, but not extrapolation. These findings support a clearer separation between rule induction and rule execution in ARC-like evaluations, motivating benchmarks that better distinguish in-distribution from out-of-distribution rules.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces a two-step test-time training (TTT) protocol for VARC—first finetuning only the task embedding (Embed-TTT), then freezing it and finetuning the backbone—and shows it yields more rule-aligned task embeddings and improved ARC performance, revealing a clearer separation between rule induction and rule execution.
AI.motivation: Success on the Abstraction and Reasoning Corpus (ARC) and related benchmarks is ambiguous: it is often unclear whether models infer the intended underlying rule or rely on shortcuts. The authors aim to disambiguate rule inference from mere performance by examining test-time task embeddings in VARC.
AI.method: The authors propose a novel two-step TTT protocol for VARC, a model combining a pre-trained backbone with a trainable embedding that represents the transformation rule. First, only the task embedding is finetuned (Embed-TTT); then it is frozen and the backbone is finetuned. They evaluate across ARC-AGI-1, ConceptARC, and two controlled datasets with known rules using embedding quality, embedding-based retrieval, and linear probing of known rules.
AI.result: Embed-TTT consistently produces improved task embeddings that align better with underlying rules, enhance embedding-based retrieval, and enable accurate linear probing of known rules. It reveals more semantically meaningful test-train task relations on ARC-AGI-1. Optimizing only task embeddings (<0.01% of parameters) already solves a non-trivial fraction of ARC-AGI-1, ConceptARC, and Mini-ARC, while the full two-step pipeline improves final performance. Embed-TTT also recovers the geometric structure of parametric rules and learns compositional ability enabling rule-wise interpolation, but not extrapolation.
AI.conclusion: The findings support a clearer separation between rule induction and rule execution in ARC-like evaluations and motivate benchmarks that distinguish in-distribution from out-of-distribution rules.

title: SPARROW: Survival-POMCP for Adaptive Robot Routing, Observation, and Waiting
summary: Temporary obstacles that may block a robot's planned route create a sequential navigation problem: a robot must decide whether to wait for a blockage to clear, reroute, or acquire more information about the obstacle before acting. We formulate graph navigation among temporary obstacles as a partially observable semi-Markov decision process and introduce SPARROW, a belief-space planner built on Partially Observable Monte Carlo Planning (POMCP). SPARROW searches over traversal, observation, and finite-duration waiting actions while maintaining a particle belief over latent obstacle classes and clearance times. Class-conditioned survival models are learned online from both clearance observations and right-censored encounters where the robot reroutes before clearance is observed. A generative model simulates obstacle arrivals and clearances as each action unfolds, so the planner can account for blockages that may occur along alternative routes. We further introduce a value-of-learning criterion that trades the immediate cost of collecting labelled survival data against its expected reduction in future navigation regret. Across two simulation graphs and multiple obstacle-class settings, SPARROW reduces mean time-to-goal by 12-26% relative to OSCAR, a recent survival-based method for the same problem. On a physical mobile robot, SPARROW reduces mean time-to-goal by 20.5% relative to OSCAR while selectively observing, waiting, and rerouting as environment conditions change.

AI.tldr: SPARROW is a belief-space POMCP planner for robot navigation among temporary obstacles, searching over traversal, observation, and waiting actions with online-learned survival models and a value-of-learning criterion, outperforming OSCAR by 12-26% in simulation and 20.5% on a physical robot.
AI.motivation: Temporary obstacles blocking a robot's planned route pose a sequential decision problem: the robot must decide whether to wait for clearing, reroute, or gather more information. Prior approaches (e.g., OSCAR) do not adequately handle partial observability, alternative-route blockages, or the cost-benefit of acquiring information. This work aims to formalize the problem and improve navigation efficiency.
AI.method: The problem is formulated as a partially observable semi-Markov decision process. SPARROW, a belief-space planner built on POMCP, searches over traversal, observation, and finite-duration waiting actions. It maintains a particle belief over latent obstacle classes and clearance times, learns class-conditioned survival models online from clearance observations and right-censored encounters (reroutes before clearance), and uses a generative model simulating obstacle arrivals/clearances as actions unfold. A value-of-learning criterion trades immediate labelling cost against expected reduction in future navigation regret.
AI.result: Across two simulation graphs and multiple obstacle-class settings, SPARROW reduces mean time-to-goal by 12-26% relative to OSCAR. On a physical mobile robot, SPARROW reduces mean time-to-goal by 20.5% relative to OSCAR while adaptively observing, waiting, and rerouting as conditions change.
AI.conclusion: SPARROW effectively addresses sequential navigation among temporary obstacles under partial observability, and its online survival learning plus value-of-learning reasoning yield consistent gains over the state-of-the-art survival-based method in both simulation and real-world deployment.

title: AI-GRACE: A Use-Case Operationalization Framework for Agentic AI: From Organizational Objectives and Obligations to Deployment Capabilities and Architecture
summary: Organizations deploying agentic artificial intelligence must determine more than whether a model is trustworthy; they must establish what to validate, control, and observe for a use case to deliver its intended outcome while meeting applicable obligations. This paper proposes AI-GRACE (Agentic Intelligence-Governance, Risk, Assurance, Controls, and Evidence) as a use-case operationalization framework connecting organizational governance with technical implementation. The proposal draws on professional observations and a purposive synthesis of standards and literature, using design science to frame the method contribution and situational method engineering to guide contextual tailoring and reuse. The framework establishes objectives and obligations and then assesses risks in seven proposed domains, including mission and value realization. It derives requirements for assurance before deployment, runtime controls, and evidence, which guide capability qualification, gap assessment, and a logical architecture. An Agent Operating Envelope specifies permitted actions and escalation conditions, while Risk-Aligned Independence Levels (RAIL) summarize the authorized independence. A fictional retail banking application illustrates the method. The contribution is a traceable basis for deciding what an organization must implement, what it already supports, and what remains unresolved. Empirical evaluation must establish whether it improves deployment decisions, efficiency, and reuse.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes AI-GRACE, a use-case operationalization framework that connects organizational governance with technical implementation for deploying agentic AI, using design science and situational method engineering to specify assurance, controls, and evidence per use case.
AI.motivation: Organizations deploying agentic AI must determine not only whether a model is trustworthy but also what to validate, control, and observe for a use case to achieve its intended outcome while meeting applicable obligations.
AI.method: AI-GRACE is developed through professional observations and a purposive synthesis of standards and literature, framed by design science for the method contribution and situational method engineering for contextual tailoring and reuse. It establishes objectives and obligations, assesses risks across seven domains (including mission and value realization), derives requirements for pre-deployment assurance, runtime controls, and evidence, and guides capability qualification, gap assessment, and a logical architecture. An Agent Operating Envelope specifies permitted actions and escalation conditions, and Risk-Aligned Independence Levels (RAIL) summarize authorized independence.
AI.result: A fictional retail banking application illustrates the method, demonstrating AI-GRACE as a traceable basis for deciding what an organization must implement, what it already supports, and what remains unresolved.
AI.conclusion: AI-GRACE provides a traceable, use-case-level basis for operationalizing agentic AI governance. Empirical evaluation is still required to establish whether it improves deployment decisions, efficiency, and reuse.

title: Towards Effective Visual-Inertial SLAM with Passive-Only Sensors for Low-Cost Autonomous Underwater Vehicles
summary: Improvements to Visual-Inertial Simultaneous Localization and Mapping (VI-SLAM) for low-cost autonomous underwater vehicles (AUVs) are critical for transitioning advanced marine robotics from specialized labs to broader research and hobbyist applications. While high-end AUVs typically rely on expensive sensor suites - such as Doppler Velocity Logs (DVLs) and Ultra-Short Baseline (USBL) systems - this work demonstrates that robust, high-quality navigation is achievable using a sub-$10, 000(USD) platform equipped only with inexpensive consumer-grade sensors. By leveraging a similarly priced, open-source AUV, we evaluate the performance of stereo cameras, Micro-electromechanical System (MEMS)-based IMUs, and depth sensors in a fully unconstrained 6-degree-of-freedom (6-DOF) underwater environment. We analyze the efficacy of off-the-shelf SLAM packages and propose optimizations for sensor fusion to mitigate the visual and physical challenges of untethered underwater operation. Our results prove that a usable SLAM solution can be accessible to the masses, providing a benchmark for expectations in demanding, real-time maritime missions without the financial barrier of industrial-grade hardware.

AI.tldr: This work shows that robust 6-DOF VI-SLAM is achievable on a sub-$10,000 open-source AUV using only consumer-grade stereo cameras, MEMS IMUs, and depth sensors, with proposed sensor-fusion optimizations that make SLAM accessible without industrial-grade hardware.
AI.motivation: High-end AUVs depend on expensive sensor suites (DVLs, USBL), which restricts advanced marine robotics to specialized labs and prevents broader research and hobbyist adoption. Affordable, high-quality navigation is needed to democratize underwater SLAM.
AI.method: Using a similarly priced open-source AUV, the authors evaluate stereo cameras, MEMS-based IMUs, and depth sensors in a fully unconstrained 6-DOF underwater environment. They assess off-the-shelf SLAM packages and propose optimizations for sensor fusion to address the visual and physical challenges of untethered operation.
AI.result: A usable SLAM solution is demonstrated on a sub-$10,000 platform, proving that robust navigation can be achieved with inexpensive consumer-grade sensors and providing a benchmark for expectations in demanding, real-time maritime missions.
AI.conclusion: Robust, high-quality VI-SLAM is attainable without the financial barrier of industrial-grade hardware, making it accessible to the masses for low-cost AUV applications.

title: Information-Gain Rewards over Diversity-Pruned Tests: GT-Anchored Verifier Co-Training for Reliable Code Generation
summary: Self-play methods that co-train a single language model as both coder and test author promise to move code-generation RL beyond fixed test suites, but they suffer from two coupled pathologies: permissiveness collapse, where pass-rate rewards are maximised by trivial, non-discriminative tests, and concentration bias, where i.i.d. sampled tests cluster on modal inputs and inflate estimator variance. We introduce CoVer (Co-trained Coder and Verifier), a single-policy GRPO framework that addresses both failure modes. First, an information-gain (IG) reward scores each self-generated test by the mutual information between its pass/fail vector and a graded, ground-truth-anchored correctness signal y [0, 1] m, gated by the sign of their covariance so that only positively discriminative tests receive reward. Second, a three-stage diversity-aware selection step prunes a candidate pool to a behaviourally non-redundant suite (invalidity, input-string, execution-profile filtering), raising the effective sample size of the IG estimator at fixed execution budget. On five benchmarks (LiveBench, MBPP, LiveCodeBench, CodeContests, Code-Forces), CoVer raises one-shot pass@1 by +5.8 points at 7B and +7.1 points at 14B over the Qwen2.5-Instruct backbone, and achieves the highest macro-average among all compared methods at both scales. As a drop-in backbone inside the CodeT ranking pipeline, CoVer-7B adds +3.5 points, demonstrating the dual benefit of co-training for both generation and selection.

AI.tldr: CoVer is a single-policy GRPO framework that co-trains a language model as coder and test author, using an information-gain reward and diversity-aware test selection to overcome permissiveness collapse and concentration bias in self-play code-generation RL.
AI.motivation: Self-play methods co-training a single LM as coder and test author aim to move code-generation RL beyond fixed test suites, but suffer from two coupled pathologies: permissiveness collapse (pass-rate rewards maximised by trivial, non-discriminative tests) and concentration bias (i.i.d. sampled tests cluster on modal inputs, inflating estimator variance).
AI.method: CoVer uses an information-gain (IG) reward scoring each self-generated test by the mutual information between its pass/fail vector and a graded, ground-truth-anchored correctness signal y in [0,1]^m, gated by the sign of their covariance so only positively discriminative tests get reward. A three-stage diversity-aware selection step prunes a candidate pool to a behaviourally non-redundant suite via invalidity, input-string, and execution-profile filtering, raising the effective sample size of the IG estimator at fixed execution budget.
AI.result: On five benchmarks (LiveBench, MBPP, LiveCodeBench, CodeContests, CodeForces), CoVer raises one-shot pass@1 by +5.8 points at 7B and +7.1 points at 14B over the Qwen2.5-Instruct backbone, achieving the highest macro-average among all compared methods at both scales. As a drop-in backbone in the CodeT ranking pipeline, CoVer-7B adds +3.5 points.
AI.conclusion: CoVer demonstrates the dual benefit of co-training for both generation and selection, effectively addressing permissiveness collapse and concentration bias in self-play code-generation RL.

title: Catch Me If You Can: Real-Time Feedback Denoising for Responsive VLAs
comment: 10th Conference on Robot Learning (CoRL 2026), Austin TX, USA
summary: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have shown strong generalization in robotic manipulation by combining semantic knowledge from pretrained vision-language models with expressive action-generation policies. Diffusion-based action generators are particularly effective for modeling temporally coherent action chunks, but these chunks are typically executed open-loop after inference. This limits responsiveness when objects move, contacts change, or the scene evolves during execution. We propose VLA-Feedback, a two-timescale architecture that combines low-frequency diffusion planning with high-frequency visual feedback. Rather than fully denoising an action chunk before execution, VLA-Feedback retains its final denoising step as a lightweight feedback interface, allowing each action to be corrected using the latest observation before it is executed. This design preserves the expressiveness of the diffusion planner while enabling real-time action correction without rerunning the full vision-language diffusion model. VLA-Feedback matched GR00T on static LIBERO tasks while improving average success on dynamic simulation tasks from 27.5% to 85.0%. On real-robot tasks, it improved average success from 51% to 73%. Additional materials can be found on our project page: https://vla-feedback.github.io.

AI.tldr: VLA-Feedback is a two-timescale architecture combining low-frequency diffusion planning with high-frequency visual feedback by retaining the final denoising step as a lightweight feedback interface, enabling real-time action correction without rerunning the full model.
AI.motivation: Diffusion-based action generators in VLA models produce temporally coherent action chunks but execute them open-loop, limiting responsiveness when objects move, contacts change, or the scene evolves during execution.
AI.method: A two-timescale architecture that couples low-frequency diffusion planning with high-frequency visual feedback. Instead of fully denoising an action chunk before execution, it retains the final denoising step as a lightweight feedback interface, correcting each action with the latest observation before execution, preserving diffusion planner expressiveness while avoiding rerunning the full vision-language diffusion model.
AI.result: Matched GR00T on static LIBERO tasks; improved average success on dynamic simulation tasks from 27.5% to 85.0%; on real-robot tasks improved average success from 51% to 73%.
AI.conclusion: Retaining the final denoising step as a feedback interface enables real-time closed-loop action correction with minimal overhead, substantially improving robustness in dynamic and real-world manipulation settings.

title: Ability-Residual Decoupled Modeling for Affective Cognitive Diagnosis
summary: Cognitive diagnosis infers students' concept mastery from response logs. However, students' responses are not determined by mastery alone: non-cognitive factors such as emotion, engagement, and fatigue can also affect performance. Affective cognitive diagnosis therefore extends conventional cognitive diagnosis by incorporating affective states. Existing methods often assume that the cognitive diagnosis backbone has already explained ability, item, and concept effects, so the remaining errors can be attributed mainly to affect. We argue that this assumption can be insufficient in real educational data: item calibration bias, systematic concept bias, personalized student-concept deviations, and latent student-item matching can form stable cognitive residuals. Without an explicit modeling pathway, these residuals may leak into affective representations, producing affect contamination. To address this problem, we propose an ability-residual decoupled framework for affective cognitive diagnosis. The model first captures unmodeled cognitive residuals through student, item, concept, student-concept, and low-rank student-item components, and then uses an affective module to modulate guess/slip effects. A Q-matrix-constrained concept residual attention mechanism adaptively aggregates only item-relevant concept residuals. Experiments on ASSIST2017, ASSIST2012, ASSIST2009, and Junyi with six cognitive diagnosis backbones show response-prediction gains across the reported comparisons and generally improved affect alignment when affect labels are available. Ablation studies, leakage probes, principal component analysis visualization, long-tail analysis, and case studies further indicate that ability residuals absorb stable cognitive bias, reduce cognitive contamination in the affective branch, and enhance the robustness and predictive accuracy of cognitive diagnosis models.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes an ability-residual decoupled framework for affective cognitive diagnosis that explicitly models stable cognitive residuals (item calibration bias, concept bias, student-concept deviations, latent student-item matching) before an affective module modulates guess/slip effects, preventing affect contamination and improving response prediction and affect alignment.
AI.motivation: Cognitive diagnosis infers concept mastery from response logs, but responses also depend on non-cognitive factors like emotion, engagement, and fatigue, motivating affective cognitive diagnosis. Existing methods assume the cognitive backbone already explains ability, item, and concept effects, attributing remaining error mainly to affect. The authors argue this assumption fails in real educational data, where item calibration bias, systematic concept bias, personalized student-concept deviations, and latent student-item matching form stable cognitive residuals. Without explicit modeling, these residuals leak into affective representations, causing affect contamination.
AI.method: An ability-residual decoupled framework for affective cognitive diagnosis. The model captures unmodeled cognitive residuals via student, item, concept, student-concept, and low-rank student-item components, then uses an affective module to modulate guess/slip effects. A Q-matrix-constrained concept residual attention mechanism adaptively aggregates only item-relevant concept residuals.
AI.result: Experiments on ASSIST2017, ASSIST2012, ASSIST2009, and Junyi with six cognitive diagnosis backbones show response-prediction gains across reported comparisons and generally improved affect alignment when affect labels are available. Ablation studies, leakage probes, PCA visualization, long-tail analysis, and case studies further indicate that ability residuals absorb stable cognitive bias, reduce cognitive contamination in the affective branch, and enhance robustness and predictive accuracy.
AI.conclusion: Explicitly decoupling stable ability residuals from the affective branch mitigates affect contamination, yielding more robust and accurate cognitive diagnosis and better affect alignment across multiple datasets and backbones.

title: Adapting Rigid-Body Dynamics Derivatives for Constraint Embedding Closed-Chain Models
summary: This paper extends an existing algorithm for the first-order derivatives of rigid-body dynamics to the case of closed-chain kinematic systems modeled using constraint embed- ding. Many standard dynamics algorithms apply to both open- chain and constraint-embedded models, but existing efficient derivative methods assume joint velocity effects are locally config- uration invariant. We remove this assumption and derive adapted algorithms that extend dynamics derivatives to more general joint types, including those arising in constraint-embedded closed- chain models. Our results compare conventional pin-joint robot models with more complete actuation models that capture local closed chains. We show that the additional terms introduced by these generalizations have low computational impact when mod- eling actuation kinematics alone, but can incur higher cost when additional rigid bodies, such as motor rotors, are included in the actuation chain, or when considering non-local loops.
