Overall, these results enable more accurate dynamics computations for constraint-embedded actuation submechanisms to be adopted in model-predictive control and differentiable simulation.

AI.tldr: This paper generalizes an existing first-order derivative algorithm for rigid-body dynamics to closed-chain systems modeled via constraint embedding, removing the assumption that joint velocity effects are locally configuration-invariant.
AI.motivation: Standard efficient derivative methods for rigid-body dynamics assume joint velocity effects are locally configuration-invariant. This assumption fails for more general joint types, particularly those in constraint-embedded closed-chain models, limiting accurate dynamics computations for such systems.
AI.method: The authors extend an existing first-order derivative algorithm for rigid-body dynamics to closed-chain kinematic systems modeled using constraint embedding. They remove the locally configuration-invariant assumption and derive adapted algorithms that support general joint types, including those in constraint-embedded closed-chain models.
AI.result: The generalized algorithms were compared against conventional pin-joint robot models and more complete actuation models capturing local closed chains. The additional terms introduced by the generalization have low computational impact when modeling actuation kinematics alone, but incur higher cost when additional rigid bodies (e.g., motor rotors) are included in the actuation chain or when non-local loops are considered.
AI.conclusion: The results enable more accurate dynamics computations for constraint-embedded actuation submechanisms, suitable for adoption in model-predictive control and differentiable simulation.

title: A Fully Differentiable Neuro-Soft-Symbolic Framework for Perceptual Task Planning
summary: Perceptual planning tasks require two key capabilities: accurately perceiving uncertain scenes and planning valid action sequences following logical rules. Conventional methods convert perception into discrete symbolic facts and then plan, discarding perceptual uncertainty and severing task-level feedback to perception. We introduce a generic, fully differentiable neuro-soft-symbolic framework that connects visual perception and task planning within a single computational graph. The framework maintains a continuous soft symbolic state, lifts domain rules into a differentiable soft-$T_P$ transition operator, and optimizes action logits over a short planning horizon. Gradients from the planning objective can also update the perception parameters, allowing task-relevant perceptual representations to be refined during planning. On Blocksworld, our method solves 40/40 LatPlan-40 tasks and 596/600 PlanBench-600 tasks, compared with 33/40 for LatPlan and 587/600 for the reasoning-model baseline, while requiring substantially less computation and time. In the perceptual-uncertainty ablation, our method improves the success rate from 59\% with frozen perception to 83\%. We further conduct task-and-motion simulations on Blocksworld scenes, providing an execution-level validation of the compatibility between decoded task plans and downstream robotic motion execution.

AI.tldr: A fully differentiable neuro-symbolic framework unifies visual perception and task planning in one computational graph via continuous soft-symbolic states, enabling task-level gradients to refine perception and outperforming LatPlan and a reasoning-model baseline on Blocksworld tasks.
AI.motivation: Perceptual planning requires both accurate perception of uncertain scenes and valid action sequencing under logical rules. Conventional pipelines convert perception into discrete symbolic facts before planning, which discards perceptual uncertainty and severs task-level feedback from planning back to perception.
AI.method: The authors propose a generic, fully differentiable neuro-soft-symbolic framework linking visual perception and task planning in a single computational graph. It maintains a continuous soft-symbolic state, lifts domain rules into a differentiable soft-T_P transition operator, and optimizes action logits over a short planning horizon. Gradients from the planning objective also update perception parameters, refining task-relevant representations during planning.
AI.result: On Blocksworld, the method solves 40/40 LatPlan-40 tasks and 596/600 PlanBench-600 tasks, versus 33/40 for LatPlan and 587/600 for the reasoning-model baseline, with substantially less computation and time. In a perceptual-uncertainty ablation, success rate improves from 59% with frozen perception to 83%. Task-and-motion simulations on Blocksworld scenes validate compatibility between decoded task plans and downstream robotic motion execution.
AI.conclusion: The differentiable soft-symbolic formulation preserves perceptual uncertainty and enables end-to-end task feedback into perception, yielding higher planning success with lower compute and providing execution-level validation for downstream robotic motion.

title: MAPLE-RF: Efficient Probabilistic RF Source Localization in Partially Explored Environments
summary: Localizing a radio-frequency (RF) transmitter from received signals often requires a model of the environment to predict how obstacles block and reflect the signal. In many robotic applications, however, only a partial map is available, particularly when a robot localizes the source while exploring with simultaneous localization and mapping (SLAM). We study single-snapshot transmitter localization on such partially explored maps and compare two approaches that output a posterior over transmitter locations. The first extends a digital-twin method, which ray-traces every candidate location, to partial maps by treating unexplored space as free and training on mixed map coverage. The second, MAPLE-RF, encodes estimated path angles of arrival and signal-to-noise ratios as grid channels aligned with map knownness, occupancy, and line-of-sight visibility, and a U-Net scores all candidate positions in one pass without simulating propagation at inference. Ray-tracing simulations of indoor environments indicate that training on mixed map coverage is essential for both approaches. The digital-twin approach is more accurate on most single-snapshot metrics, while MAPLE-RF comes close at a query cost that does not depend on the propagation model and is more than two orders of magnitude below a fresh full-grid query with general-purpose ray tracing. Both outperform Gaussian and Gaussian-mixture baselines, and on exploration routes guided by its own estimates, fused MAPLE-RF posteriors place more probability near the source than the compared methods. Code and data will be released.

AI.tldr: The paper studies single-snapshot RF transmitter localization on partially explored maps (SLAM context), comparing an extended digital-twin ray-tracing approach against MAPLE-RF, a U-Net that fuses AoA/SNR grid channels with map knownness, occupancy, and LOS.
AI.motivation: Localizing an RF transmitter from received signals typically needs an environment model to predict obstacle blocking and reflection. In robotic applications, however, only a partial map is often available—especially when a robot localizes the source while exploring via SLAM—so existing full-map methods do not directly apply.
AI.method: Two approaches output a posterior over transmitter locations. (1) A digital-twin method that ray-traces every candidate location, extended to partial maps by treating unexplored space as free and training on mixed map coverage. (2) MAPLE-RF: encodes estimated path angles of arrival and signal-to-noise ratios as grid channels aligned with map knownness, occupancy, and line-of-sight visibility; a U-Net scores all candidate positions in one pass without simulating propagation at inference.
AI.result: Ray-tracing simulations of indoor environments show training on mixed map coverage is essential for both methods. The digital-twin approach is more accurate on most single-snapshot metrics, while MAPLE-RF comes close at a query cost independent of the propagation model and over two orders of magnitude below a fresh full-grid general-purpose ray-tracing query. Both outperform Gaussian and Gaussian-mixture baselines, and on exploration routes guided by its own estimates, fused MAPLE-RF posteriors place more probability near the source than compared methods.
AI.conclusion: Training on mixed map coverage is crucial for localization on partially explored maps. The digital-twin approach offers the highest single-snapshot accuracy, whereas MAPLE-RF provides a strong accuracy-efficiency trade-off and superior performance when its fused posteriors guide exploration. Code and data will be released.

title: CogGym: Towards Large-Scale Comparative Evaluation of Human and Machine Cognition
summary: Understanding and modeling human intelligence are parallel goals shared by artificial intelligence (AI) and cognitive science. As AI systems grow increasingly capable, in what ways do model responses resemble human responses, and where do they systematically diverge? The sheer breadth and diversity of the tasks humans can perform and think about pose a challenge for scalable and rigorous comparison between humans and models. We introduce CogGym, a scalable, unified framework grounded in cognitive science for systematically comparing model and human behavior on matched experimental trials. CogGym uses a semi-automated, human-in-the-loop pipeline to standardize diverse experimental paradigms into a task-agnostic Experiment Markup Language (EML), enabling reproducible and faithful comparison at scale. For initial release, we curate and standardize 258 cognitive experiments from 100 papers that focuses on human commonsense reasoning, and evaluate 50 large language models against human responses. We find a clear scaling trend where larger and more recent AI models better reproduce human judgments. Yet AI models' improvement on such common reasoning tasks is considerably slower than the gains observed on formal-reasoning benchmarks like math and coding, and model--human fit remains well below human splithalf reliability ($R^2 = 0.93$ on text, $0.95$ on image, and $0.92$ on video) with the best models achieving $R^2 = 0.59$ on text, $0.58$ on image, and $0.43$ on video experiments. We intend for CogGym to provide a living evaluation framework that continually incorporates new cognitive science experiments to characterize where model behavior resembles human behavior, where it systematically diverges, and how those patterns change as models and experiments evolve.

AI.tldr: CogGym is a scalable, cognitive-science-grounded framework that standardizes diverse experiments into a unified format to compare model and human behavior on matched trials, revealing that larger/newer models better mimic human judgment but still fall well short of human reliability.
AI.motivation: AI and cognitive science share the goal of understanding and modeling human intelligence, but comparing humans and models rigorously at scale is hard due to the breadth and diversity of tasks. There is a need for a unified, scalable, reproducible way to compare model and human behavior on matched experimental trials and to identify where they systematically diverge.
AI.method: CogGym uses a semi-automated, human-in-the-loop pipeline to standardize diverse experimental paradigms into a task-agnostic Experiment Markup Language (EML), enabling reproducible and faithful comparison at scale. The initial release curates and standardizes 258 cognitive experiments from 100 papers focused on human commonsense reasoning, then evaluates 50 large language models against human responses.
AI.result: A clear scaling trend emerges: larger and more recent models better reproduce human judgments. However, improvement on commonsense reasoning is much slower than on formal-reasoning benchmarks like math and coding. Model-human fit remains well below human split-half reliability (R² = 0.93 text, 0.95 image, 0.92 video), with best models only reaching R² = 0.59 (text), 0.58 (image), and 0.43 (video).
AI.conclusion: CogGym is intended as a living evaluation framework that continually incorporates new cognitive science experiments to characterize where model behavior resembles human behavior, where it systematically diverges, and how these patterns change as models and experiments evolve.

title: DEXTERA: From a Single Image to Deployable Dexterous Manipulation via Real-to-Sim-to-Real
summary: Collecting real-world robot data for dexterous manipulation is costly and time-consuming. While high-fidelity physics simulators enable scalable data synthesis and policy learning, constructing deployment-ready digital twins manually remains labor-intensive, and residual visual, geometric, and dynamics gaps hinder reliable sim-to-real transfer. We present DEXTERA, an automated real-to-sim-to-real framework that transforms a single RGB image into deployable policies for dexterous manipulation across four unified stages: (1) single-image scene factorization into a static Gaussian background and interactive rigid or articulated assets with VLM-inferred physical parameters; (2) metric scene global alignment, object canonicalization, and morphology-balanced robot calibration; (3) scalable simulator task primitive construction, VR teleoperation, and object-centric trajectory synthesis; and (4) a shared multimodal policy interface supporting both imitation learning and reinforcement learning. We evaluate DEXTERA across 13 task-embodiment pairs, 2 dexterous robot platforms, and 6 policy architectures. Experimental results demonstrate that DEXTERA achieves superior visual fidelity and 3D geometric reconstruction compared to generative baselines, while cross-domain trajectory replays validate strong physical interaction consistency. Furthermore, simulation-only trained policies enable viable zero-shot real-robot deployment, while simulation-real co-training substantially improves mean physical policy success from 29.2% to 61.9% across diverse policy architectures.

AI.tldr: DEXTERA is an automated real-to-sim-to-real framework that converts a single RGB image into deployable dexterous manipulation policies through four unified stages: single-image scene factorization, metric alignment and robot calibration, scalable simulator task construction, and a shared multimodal policy interface for IL and RL. It achieves high visual/geometric fidelity and enables zero-shot and co-trained real-robot deployment, raising mean success from 29.2% to 61.9%.
AI.motivation: Collecting real-world robot data for dexterous manipulation is costly and time-consuming. High-fidelity simulators enable scalable data synthesis, but manually constructing deployment-ready digital twins is labor-intensive, and residual visual, geometric, and dynamics gaps hinder reliable sim-to-real transfer.
AI.method: DEXTERA transforms a single RGB image into deployable dexterous manipulation policies across four stages: (1) single-image scene factorization into a static Gaussian background and interactive rigid/articulated assets with VLM-inferred physical parameters; (2) metric global alignment, object canonicalization, and morphology-balanced robot calibration; (3) scalable simulator task primitive construction, VR teleoperation, and object-centric trajectory synthesis; and (4) a shared multimodal policy interface supporting both imitation learning and reinforcement learning.
AI.result: Evaluated across 13 task-embodiment pairs, 2 dexterous robot platforms, and 6 policy architectures, DEXTERA attains superior visual fidelity and 3D geometric reconstruction versus generative baselines. Cross-domain trajectory replays confirm strong physical interaction consistency. Simulation-only trained policies enable viable zero-shot real-robot deployment, and simulation-real co-training improves mean physical policy success from 29.2% to 61.9%.
AI.conclusion: DEXTERA provides an automated, image-driven real-to-sim-to-real pipeline that yields high-fidelity digital twins and deployable dexterous manipulation policies, with co-training substantially improving real-robot success across diverse policy architectures.

title: PlaceReasoner-Beta: Reasoning-Driven Macro Placement and Benchmarking
summary: Automated macro placement remains a fundamental challenge in VLSI physical design. Despite decades of research, existing approaches predominantly optimize hand-crafted proxy objectives, such as estimated wirelength, and typically produce placements through one-shot numerical optimization, limiting their ability to incorporate visual layout context, codified design expertise, and downstream physical-design feedback in a unified loop. We present PlaceReasoner-Beta, a verifier-guided multi-agent framework that reformulates macro placement as a closed-loop reasoning problem rather than black-box optimization. A vision-language model (VLM) planner generates candidate placements from the floorplan image, macro specifications, and connectivity structure; a geometric verifier enforces physical legality and expert placement principles; a physical verifier refines candidates using early implementation feedback; and a post-route optimizer further improves promising layouts using final PPA. To enable reproducible evaluation, we introduce PlaceReasoner-Bench, a fully open end-to-end benchmark built from open RTL designs, EDA tools, and technology libraries. It comprises 8 designs at two aspect ratios, yielding 16 tasks with fixed floorplans and I/O assignments, so methods differ only in macro positions and orientations and are evaluated using routed PPA and DRC rather than pre-route proxies. Across the benchmark, PlaceReasoner-Beta achieves the best timing among DRC-clean methods on all square tasks, reducing post-route TNS by 61.2% at 1:1 and 53.0% at 2:1 relative to the classical baseline field. It also shortens routed wirelength on most designs despite never explicitly optimizing it, demonstrating that reasoning over spatial structure under physical-design feedback can improve end-to-end layout quality beyond proxy-objective optimization.

AI.tldr: PlaceReasoner-Beta reformulates macro placement as a closed-loop multi-agent reasoning problem using a VLM planner, geometric and physical verifiers, and a post-route optimizer, and introduces PlaceReasoner-Bench, a fully open routed-PPA-based benchmark. It achieves the best timing among DRC-clean methods on all square tasks, cutting post-route TNS by 61.2% (1:1) and 53.0% (2:1) versus the classical baseline.
AI.motivation: Automated macro placement remains a fundamental VLSI physical design challenge. Existing methods predominantly optimize hand-crafted proxy objectives (e.g., estimated wirelength) via one-shot numerical optimization, which prevents them from jointly incorporating visual layout context, codified design expertise, and downstream physical-design feedback in a unified loop. Additionally, evaluation based on pre-route proxies limits reproducibility and fidelity to true end-to-end quality.
AI.method: A verifier-guided multi-agent framework: (1) a vision-language model (VLM) planner generates candidate placements from the floorplan image, macro specifications, and connectivity structure; (2) a geometric verifier enforces physical legality and expert placement principles; (3) a physical verifier refines candidates using early implementation feedback; (4) a post-route optimizer further improves promising layouts using final PPA. The paper also introduces PlaceReasoner-Bench, an open end-to-end benchmark built from open RTL designs, EDA tools, and technology libraries.
AI.result: PlaceReasoner-Bench comprises 8 designs at two aspect ratios, yielding 16 tasks with fixed floorplans and I/O assignments, so methods differ only in macro positions and orientations and are evaluated using routed PPA and DRC rather than pre-route proxies. Across the benchmark, PlaceReasoner-Beta achieves the best timing among DRC-clean methods on all square tasks, reducing post-route TNS by 61.2% at 1:1 and 53.0% at 2:1 relative to the classical baseline field, and also shortens routed wirelength on most designs despite never explicitly optimizing it.
AI.conclusion: Reasoning over spatial structure under physical-design feedback can improve end-to-end layout quality beyond proxy-objective optimization.

title: Constraint-Unified MPC for Over-Actuated Surface Vehicles with Post-Detection Fault Reconfiguration
comment: 15 pages, 10 figures. Accepted for the International Symposium of Robotics Research (ISRR) 2026
summary: Choreographed aquatic performances require small autonomous surface vehicles to track precise paths under per-thruster force and rate limits, including after thruster failures. We report a deployed system in which trajectory tracking, thrust allocation, and the per-thruster force and rate limits are resolved in a single quadratic program over the per-thruster commands, with fault reconfiguration entering through one binary flag per thruster from an external detector. The system has driven a fleet in live performances on Lake Zürich and at the Time Space Existence 2025 exhibition in Venice. The field campaign measures 1.6 cm root mean square position error in a 10-minute hold and 4.3 cm over a 10 m square at 0.6 m/s. At 0.5 m/s, losing the front thruster increases the error to 11.6 cm, while losing the starboard-side thruster increases it to 11.5 cm. Losing two thrusters simultaneously leaves the craft tracking a 0.4 m/s square with a root mean square position error of 1.25 m. Compared to our own cascaded baseline, the unified formulation tracks the nominal square to the same few centimeters and holds station more tightly with roughly half the thruster force. The architectures separate after a thruster failure, where the unified controller stays within 24 cm of the reference path while the cascade leaves it.

AI.tldr: A unified quadratic-program controller jointly solves trajectory tracking, thrust allocation, and per-thruster force/rate limits, with a binary fault flag per thruster for reconfiguration, and is validated in live fleet performances on Lake Zürich and in Venice.
AI.motivation: Choreographed aquatic performances need small autonomous surface vehicles to follow precise paths while respecting per-thruster force and rate limits, and to remain functional after thruster failures. Existing cascaded architectures separate tracking, allocation, and limit handling, which degrades behavior under faults.
AI.method: A single quadratic program over per-thruster commands resolves trajectory tracking, thrust allocation, and per-thruster force and rate limits simultaneously. Fault reconfiguration is injected via one binary flag per thruster supplied by an external fault detector. The approach is compared against a cascaded baseline in a field campaign.
AI.result: Field results: 1.6 cm RMS position error in a 10-minute hold; 4.3 cm over a 10 m square at 0.6 m/s. At 0.5 m/s, front-thruster loss raises error to 11.6 cm and starboard-thruster loss to 11.5 cm. Simultaneous loss of two thrusters yields 1.25 m RMS error on a 0.4 m/s square. Versus the cascaded baseline, the unified formulation matches few-centimeter nominal tracking, holds station more tightly with roughly half the thruster force, and after a thruster failure stays within 24 cm of the reference path where the cascade departs from it.
AI.conclusion: Embedding tracking, allocation, and actuator limits in one QP with per-thruster fault flags yields accurate, force-efficient, fault-tolerant control, demonstrated in live performances and field trials; the unified and cascaded architectures diverge mainly after thruster failure.

title: Efficient Benchmarking in Production: A Study of an Evolving LLM Agent
comment: A study of efficient recurring evaluation of a production LLM agent based on real-world historical data
summary: Production LLM agents are evaluated repeatedly as they evolve, but full agent benchmarks are costly to rerun. We study efficient recurring evaluation for a production analytics agent serving tens of thousands of monthly active users and report first-hand deployment experience. Using 574 historical runs of the production benchmark, split chronologically into calibration and held-out periods, we compare random sampling, historical caching, fixed representative subsets, and IRT-based adaptive testing. The results show that multidimensional 2PL adaptive testing achieves the best overall score fidelity: executing 200 questions, 38.5% of a full run, yields 1.03 pp of MAE. We nevertheless deployed difficulty-stratified fixed subsets because of their operational simplicity, and show they transfer without recalibration to five other agent families and remain stable across calibration windows as short as one day. Drawing on this deployment experience, we report practical recommendations for recurring production-agent evaluation.

AI.tldr: The paper studies efficient recurring evaluation of a production analytics LLM agent using 574 historical benchmark runs, comparing sampling strategies and deploying difficulty-stratified fixed subsets for operational simplicity.
AI.motivation: Production LLM agents evolve continuously and are evaluated repeatedly, but rerunning full agent benchmarks is prohibitively costly. There is a need for efficient recurring evaluation methods validated in real deployment settings rather than only simulation.
AI.method: Using 574 historical runs of a production benchmark, split chronologically into calibration and held-out periods, the authors compare four evaluation strategies: random sampling, historical caching, fixed representative subsets, and IRT-based adaptive testing (multidimensional 2PL).
AI.result: Multidimensional 2PL adaptive testing achieves the best score fidelity, requiring only 200 questions (38.5% of a full run) to reach 1.03 pp MAE. Difficulty-stratified fixed subsets, chosen for deployment, transfer without recalibration to five other agent families and remain stable across calibration windows as short as one day.
AI.conclusion: Despite adaptive testing's superior fidelity, difficulty-stratified fixed subsets were deployed due to operational simplicity and demonstrated robust transferability and calibration stability. The authors distill practical recommendations for recurring production-agent evaluation.

title: PlantShade: Predicting Plant Shadows for Lighting-Aware Robotic Agricultural Operation
comment: This paper has been accepted by the 2026 IEEE/RSJ International Conference on Intelligent Robots and Systems (IROS 2026)
summary: Plant growth and agricultural production form the foundation of a country's sustainable development and directly impact human livelihoods. Recent advances in frontier artificial intelligence have enabled scientific agriculture with strong potential to improve crop productivity. In this paper, we identify the importance and inherent complexity of plant shade simulation, as shading is a critical factor influencing plant growth. To advance this field and promote broader societal benefits, we focus on two main contributions. First, we introduce a comprehensive plant growth and shade dataset covering four plant species, including soybean, tomato, sugarbeet, and strawberry. The dataset includes top-down viewpoints with a supplementary light along a circular trajectory, casting dynamic shadows across multiple growth stages and diverse observation complexities. Second, we propose generative shade simulation based on diffusion models, enabling realistic shade generation for unseen plants and supporting downstream robotic tasks such as perception, lighting control, and view planning. The model incorporates temporal conditioning to facilitate flexible shade simulation across different time stages. We conduct both quantitative and qualitative evaluations to assess model performance. This work provides a foundational study for plant-aware shade modeling and has meaningful implications for broader agricultural and robotic applications.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces a plant growth and shade dataset spanning four crop species and proposes a diffusion-based generative shade simulation model with temporal conditioning, supporting realistic shade generation for unseen plants and downstream agricultural robotic tasks.
AI.motivation: Plant growth and agricultural production underpin sustainable development and human livelihoods. While frontier AI has enabled scientific agriculture, plant shade simulation remains underexplored despite shading being a critical factor influencing plant growth. Advancing this field carries broad societal benefits.
AI.method: Two main contributions: (1) a comprehensive plant growth and shade dataset covering soybean, tomato, sugarbeet, and strawberry, captured from top-down viewpoints with a supplementary light moving along a circular trajectory to cast dynamic shadows across multiple growth stages and varying observation complexities; (2) a generative shade simulation approach based on diffusion models that incorporates temporal conditioning to enable flexible shade simulation across different time stages and generalization to unseen plants.
AI.result: Quantitative and qualitative evaluations assess model performance, demonstrating realistic shade generation for unseen plants and support for downstream robotic tasks including perception, lighting control, and view planning.
AI.conclusion: The work provides a foundational study for plant-aware shade modeling with meaningful implications for broader agricultural and robotic applications.

title: GameASG-Bench: Benchmarking Autonomous Software Generation for Game Development
summary: Autonomous software generation (ASG) aims to turn human requirements into executable applications, but delivering these applications does not necessarily establish that their interacting components satisfy the specified behavioral requirements. We introduce GameASG-Bench, a benchmark that makes behavioral testability part of the generation task for game development. Our design declares an evaluation interface specification before generation, fixing legal starting scenarios, player-level actions, stable snapshots, rejection behavior, and invariants while leaving private implementations open. Concretely, we include: (i) static L1 checks that assess source-level compliance; and (ii) browser-executed L2 checks that combine semantic observations with real input and runtime evidence. We implement this protocol as 47 browser-native game-generation tasks spanning 12 primary genres and both 2D and 3D interaction, each with executable checks and an independently verified reference implementation. Our experiments answer four key questions about end-to-end agent performance, tool access and nominal turn budget, reasoning effort, and harness choice. Across nine agent stacks, the highest observed mean L2 check pass rate is 93.2%, yet the highest observed strict task success rate, requiring all L1 and applicable L2 prerequisite and core requirement checks, is only 55.3% (26/47 tasks). For DeepSeek-V4-Flash, full tool access and larger nominal turn budgets yield more strict task successes, while the strict task success rate is not monotonic in reasoning effort. Both tested harnesses achieve 18 strict task successes, but only ten tasks succeed under both. These results expose task-level compliance gaps that high average check pass rates actually obscure.

AI.tldr: GameASG-Bench reframes autonomous software generation as a behaviorally testable task for game development. It fixes an evaluation interface specification before generation and grades agent outputs with static L1 source checks plus browser-executed L2 checks combining semantic observations with real input and runtime evidence, across 47 browser-native game tasks. Nine agent stacks reach up to 93.2% mean L2 check pass rate, yet strict task success tops out at 55.3% (26/47), revealing per-task compliance gaps hidden by average pass rates.
AI.motivation: Autonomous software generation (ASG) can turn requirements into executable applications, but executability does not entail that interacting components satisfy the specified behavioral requirements. Existing generation evaluations largely reward producing runnable artifacts rather than verifying behavioral compliance, so they can overstate agent capability. The paper argues behavioral testability should be part of the generation task itself, and builds a benchmark to measure it.
AI.method: The design declares an evaluation interface specification before generation: legal starting scenarios, player-level actions, stable snapshots, rejection behavior, and invariants are fixed while private implementations remain open. Two check layers are used: (i) static L1 checks assessing source-level compliance, and (ii) browser-executed L2 checks combining semantic observations with real input and runtime evidence. This protocol is instantiated as 47 browser-native game-generation tasks spanning 12 primary genres and both 2D and 3D interaction, each with executable checks and an independently verified reference implementation. Experiments assess four questions: end-to-end agent performance, tool access and nominal turn budget, reasoning effort, and harness choice.
AI.result: Across nine agent stacks, the highest observed mean L2 check pass rate is 93.2%, while the highest observed strict task success rate, requiring all L1 and applicable L2 prerequisite and core requirement checks, is only 55.3% (26/47 tasks). For DeepSeek-V4-Flash, full tool access and larger nominal turn budgets yield more strict task successes, whereas strict task success is not monotonic in reasoning effort. Both tested harnesses achieve 18 strict task successes, but only ten tasks succeed under both.
AI.conclusion: High average check pass rates obscure task-level compliance gaps: agents frequently satisfy many individual checks while failing the full prerequisite-and-core requirement set for a task. Behavioral testability must be built into generation benchmarks, and harness choice materially affects which tasks succeed, since agreement between harnesses is limited.

title: Design of Adaptive PID Controller Based On Asynchronous Advantage Actor Critic Learning Method for QuadCopter Control
summary: Quadcopters offer great utility in many applications, but their nonlinear nature and disturbance sensitivity present great control challenges. Basic PID controllers are generally not sophisticated enough to cope with these complexities. This paper suggests a control system that integrates the Asynchronous Advantage Actor-Critic (A3C) algorithm with a PID controller for quadcopter attitude and trajectory tracking. The A3C controller uses parallel agents to optimize PID parameters dynamically using a neural network. A system identification module for the complementary system makes predictions about system states for optimal control policy. The proposed framework was compared with a standard actor-critic (A2C) model. Simulation results verify that they both track accurately. However, the A3C-based controller converges much more for the loss function, as evidenced by reward figures and loss curves, demonstrating better parameter optimization. This shows that A3C-based approach results in improved performance for the control of quadcopter, effectively integrating reinforcement learning and traditional control to achieve higher adaptability.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes integrating the A3C reinforcement learning algorithm with a PID controller for quadcopter attitude and trajectory tracking, using parallel agents to dynamically optimize PID parameters and a system identification module for state prediction. Compared to an A2C model, the A3C-based controller achieves accurate tracking and significantly better convergence, demonstrating improved adaptability.
AI.motivation: Quadcopters are highly useful but their nonlinear dynamics and sensitivity to disturbances make control challenging. Basic PID controllers are not sophisticated enough to handle these complexities, motivating the need for a more adaptive control approach.
AI.method: The proposed control system integrates the Asynchronous Advantage Actor-Critic (A3C) algorithm with a PID controller. A3C uses parallel agents to dynamically optimize PID parameters via a neural network, while a system identification module predicts system states for optimal control policy.
AI.result: Simulation results show that both the proposed A3C-based framework and a standard A2C model track accurately. However, the A3C-based controller converges much more, as evidenced by reward figures and loss curves, indicating better parameter optimization.
AI.conclusion: The A3C-based approach improves quadcopter control performance by effectively integrating reinforcement learning with traditional control to achieve higher adaptability.

title: LEGIT: Credentialing Protocol for Trustworthy AI Agent Marketplaces
summary: Agentic marketplaces are emerging where AI agents with varying capabilities autonomously complete specialized tasks for buyers. A major challenge of such marketplaces is that buyers cannot easily determine which agent will perform best on their tasks. Reported benchmark scores may be difficult to verify or compare across tasks, software, and budgets. We introduce LEGIT, a credentialing protocol connecting certification, reputation, and proposed marketplace allocation. Certification binds measured quality and cost per solved task to an agent configuration, task domain, evaluation budget, and evidence through a signed record. Reputation links records of past task outcomes to the same identity, subject to the reliability of the reported feedback. Buyers and agents can verify credential records and inspect optional visual profiles. Evaluations reveal cost differences between agent configurations with similar observed task success, and show that comparisons depend on the evaluation budget. These results support binding performance measurements to the tested configuration and resource limits. A complementary analysis quantifies the deposits and fees required for reputation manipulation under a stated Sybil attack model.

AI.tldr: LEGIT is a credentialing protocol for agentic marketplaces that binds certified quality and cost to an agent configuration, task domain, and evaluation budget through signed records, links these to reputation, and informs marketplace allocation; evaluations show configuration-dependent cost differences and budget-dependent comparisons, plus deposit/fee requirements for reputation manipulation under a Sybil model.
AI.motivation: In emerging agentic marketplaces, autonomous AI agents of varying capabilities complete specialized tasks for buyers, but buyers cannot easily determine which agent will perform best on their tasks. Reported benchmark scores are hard to verify or compare across differing tasks, software, and budgets.
AI.method: LEGIT introduces a credentialing protocol connecting certification, reputation, and marketplace allocation. Certification binds measured quality and cost per solved task to an agent configuration, task domain, evaluation budget, and evidence via a signed record. Reputation links past task outcome records to the same identity, conditioned on reported feedback reliability. Buyers and agents verify credential records and may inspect optional visual profiles. A complementary analysis quantifies deposits and fees needed for reputation manipulation under a stated Sybil attack model.
AI.result: Evaluations reveal cost differences between agent configurations with similar observed task success, and show that comparisons depend on the evaluation budget. The Sybil-attack analysis quantifies the deposits and fees required for reputation manipulation.
AI.conclusion: The findings support binding performance measurements to the tested configuration and resource limits, establishing certification–reputation–allocation linkage as a credible basis for buyer decisions in agentic marketplaces.

title: Dynamic Modeling and LQR Control of a Single Coaxial Drone with 2DOF Thrust Vectoring Mechanism
summary: Coaxial rotor drones have generated considerable interest because of energy efficiency and small size, but they are afflicted with inherent underactuation for roll and pitch control, although systems like swashplates have circumvented this limitation at the cost of greater mechanical complexity. This work presents a novel coaxial drone supplemented by a two-degreesof-freedom pendulum mechanism for active thrust vectoring that offers a less mechanically complicated alternative. We develop a comprehensive Lagrangian dynamic model that does not ignore the inertial contributions of all the components, including body, servo arms, and motor assembly. A Linear Quadratic Regulator(LQR) is designed based on the linearized dynamics around the hover equilibrium. High-fidelity simulations taking actuator dynamics and sensor noise into account validate the proposed architecture. An Extended Kalman Filter (EKF) blends GPS, barometer, and IMU estimates with high accuracy for state estimation. The findings verify the potential and reliability of this approach for power-saving, rapid coaxial UAVs.

AI.tldr: A coaxial rotor drone with a 2-DOF pendulum thrust-vectoring mechanism is proposed as a mechanically simpler alternative to swashplates for overcoming roll/pitch underactuation; a full Lagrangian model, LQR control, and EKF-based state estimation are validated in simulation.
AI.motivation: Coaxial rotor drones are attractive for their energy efficiency and compact size, but they are inherently underactuated in roll and pitch. Swashplate-based solutions overcome this limitation only at the cost of significantly greater mechanical complexity. This work seeks a less mechanically complicated alternative for active thrust vectoring.
AI.method: The authors augment a coaxial drone with a two-degree-of-freedom pendulum mechanism for active thrust vectoring. They derive a comprehensive Lagrangian dynamic model that retains the inertial contributions of all components, including the body, servo arms, and motor assembly. A Linear Quadratic Regulator (LQR) is designed from the linearized dynamics about the hover equilibrium. High-fidelity simulations incorporate actuator dynamics and sensor noise, and an Extended Kalman Filter (EKF) fuses GPS, barometer, and IMU measurements for state estimation.
AI.result: High-fidelity simulations that account for actuator dynamics and sensor noise validate the proposed architecture. The EKF blends GPS, barometer, and IMU data with high accuracy for state estimation. The findings confirm the potential and reliability of the approach for power-saving, rapid coaxial UAVs.
AI.conclusion: The proposed pendulum-based thrust-vectoring coaxial drone offers a viable, mechanically simpler route to full roll/pitch actuation, and the validated modeling, LQR control, and EKF estimation demonstrate its promise for power-saving, high-speed coaxial UAV applications.

title: Offline Multimodal Large Language Models for Decision Support in Air Operations
summary: Air operations rely on complex rules, established procedures, and time-critical analysis under limited connectivity and strict security constraints. In such environments, analysts must combine written doctrine with images, often without access to external computing resources. This paper studies offline large language models as decision support tools, deployed in isolated and restricted environments to give analysts access to doctrinal knowledge that remains traceable to its original sources through natural language interaction. We describe a modular retrieval-augmented architecture suitable for operation without Internet connectivity, supporting both text and image input from technical manuals. As a first step toward evaluating this architecture, we report a pilot study with four image analysts of the Brazilian Air Force, combining (i) a doctrinal knowledge assessment based on their electronic-target identification doctrine, comparing human and proposed system performance on the same test, and (ii) a measurement of the cognitive workload involved in manually producing a reconnaissance target report (Relatório de Missão de Reconhecimento - REMIR) without AI assistance. The results show a demanding manual task, especially in terms of mental demand (6.0/7) and effort (5.0/7), while the proposed system matches the human score (8/10) and completes the assessment in 7.1 minutes (compared to a human average of 26.5 minutes), establishing a baseline for future AI-assisted evaluation. Finally, we describe a future evaluation protocol to systematically compare manual and AI-assisted workflows.

AI.tldr: This paper examines offline large language models as decision support for air operations analysts working in isolated, low-connectivity, secure environments. It proposes a modular retrieval-augmented architecture supporting text and image input from technical manuals without Internet access, and reports a pilot study with four Brazilian Air Force image analysts. The system matched human doctrinal assessment performance (8/10) while completing the task far faster (7.1 min vs. 26.5 min average), and manual reconnaissance reporting showed high cognitive workload (mental demand 6.0/7; effort 5.0/7), establishing a baseline and a future evaluation protocol.
AI.motivation: Air operations depend on complex rules, established procedures, and time-critical analysis under limited connectivity and strict security constraints. Analysts must combine written doctrine with images, often without external computing resources. This creates a need for offline, source-traceable decision support that gives analysts access to doctrinal knowledge through natural language interaction in isolated and restricted environments.
AI.method: The paper describes a modular retrieval-augmented architecture deployable without Internet connectivity, supporting both text and image input from technical manuals and providing traceability to original sources. As a first evaluation step, a pilot study was conducted with four image analysts of the Brazilian Air Force, combining (i) a doctrinal knowledge assessment based on electronic-target identification doctrine, comparing human and system performance on the same test, and (ii) measurement of the cognitive workload involved in manually producing a reconnaissance target report (Relatório de Missão de Reconhecimento - REMIR) without AI assistance.
AI.result: Manual production of the reconnaissance target report was a demanding task, particularly in mental demand (6.0/7) and effort (5.0/7). The proposed system matched the human doctrinal assessment score (8/10) and completed the assessment in 7.1 minutes, compared with a human average of 26.5 minutes.
AI.conclusion: The pilot study establishes a baseline for future AI-assisted evaluation and provides initial evidence that the offline retrieval-augmented system can match human doctrinal assessment accuracy while substantially reducing task time. The authors further describe a future evaluation protocol to systematically compare manual and AI-assisted workflows.

title: Dynamics-Induced Commitment in Learning-Based Robotic Penalty Kicks
summary: Learning in robotic games is constrained not only by strategic information but also by what the body can still execute. We study this coupling in a hierarchical humanoid-quadruped penalty system in which game-level self-play policies command fixed soccer whole-body controllers (S-WBCs). The humanoid shooting skill is initialized from self-collected motion-capture data, whereas the quadruped saving skill is learned by reinforcement learning. We introduce dynamics-induced commitment mapping (DIC-Map), a body-grounded analysis that estimates continuation capability, identifies the first persistent loss of a terminal alternative, and tests whether the remaining interaction admits a reduced zero-sum game. For symmetric terminal alternatives, the reduced game yields a closed-form bound on optimal strategy concentration determined by the responder's value of deferring. We further show that, when the responder acts through an estimator, equal response values eliminate the direct terminal-allocation gradient and leave an estimator-mediated first-order learning channel. Experiments locate commitment about 0.29 s before contact, and changing only ball speed shifts deferral coverage. Across four responder policies, replacing the estimator raises save rate from 0.240 to 0.472, whereas a comparable gain in read accuracy obtained by waiting raises it only to 0.246. Posterior analysis is used for the equilibrium comparison because the available coverage terms are observational proxies. Project website: https://chris-ruizegeng.github.io/penaltykick/

AI.tldr: This paper studies how bodily execution constraints couple with strategic decision-making in a hierarchical humanoid-quadruped penalty system, introducing DIC-Map to analyze continuation capability, commitment timing, and reduced-game structure.
AI.motivation: Robotic game learning is limited not only by strategic information but also by what the body can still execute, and this body-strategy coupling is underexplored.
AI.method: A hierarchical humanoid-quadruped penalty system where game-level self-play policies command fixed soccer whole-body controllers (S-WBCs); the humanoid shooting skill is initialized from self-collected motion-capture data and the quadruped saving skill is learned by reinforcement learning. Dynamics-induced commitment mapping (DIC-Map) estimates continuation capability, identifies the first persistent loss of a terminal alternative, and tests whether the remaining interaction admits a reduced zero-sum game; for symmetric terminal alternatives the reduced game yields a closed-form bound on optimal strategy concentration; an estimator-mediated first-order learning channel is analyzed for the responder acting through an estimator.
AI.result: Commitment is located about 0.29 s before contact; changing only ball speed shifts deferral coverage. Across four responder policies, replacing the estimator raises save rate from 0.240 to 0.472, whereas a comparable gain in read accuracy obtained by waiting raises it only to 0.246. Posterior analysis is used for equilibrium comparison because coverage terms are observational proxies.
AI.conclusion: Body-grounded commitment analysis reveals when terminal alternatives are irreversibly lost and how estimator identity, rather than read accuracy alone, dominates the responder's achievable save rate in this coupled robot game.

title: DENSE: Distilling Agent Trajectories into Evidence-Grounded Shortcut Trees for Self-Refinement
summary: Online agent deployments produce abundant execution traces, while task-specific verification and expert annotation are costly to scale. We study how to distill these traces into reusable feedback without post-hoc outcome labels, drawing on their evidence of local progress, recovery, and unfinished requirements. We introduce DENSE (Distilling Evidence from Nested Subtask Executions), which organizes this evidence into evidence-grounded nested shortcut trees. DENSE compresses redundant attempts, reconciles issues across levels using recovery evidence, and summarizes completed branches while expanding unresolved ones, linking reusable progress to remaining obligations. We introduce REFIT, a source-paired protocol comparing feedback from shared initial trajectories under post-hoc outcome blindness, with environments and model contexts reset for fresh attempts at the same tasks. On Terminal-Bench 2.1, DENSE achieves the highest strict pass rate among tested non-privileged feedback methods across four recipient models. Relative to initial executions, strict pass rate improves by 7.12-15.64 pp, with 19.0-43.6% fewer observed recipient tokens in reruns. GPT-5.5 ablations support combining nested subtask analysis with shortcut construction and issue reconciliation. These findings point toward agent self-refinement through evidence-grounded trajectory reuse with less reliance on external supervision.

AI.tldr: DENSE distills unlabeled agent execution traces into evidence-grounded nested shortcut trees for reusable feedback, validated by REFIT on Terminal-Bench 2.1.
AI.motivation: Online agent deployments generate abundant execution traces that encode local progress, recovery, and unfinished requirements, but scaling task-specific verification and expert annotation is costly. The paper seeks to convert these traces into reusable feedback without relying on post-hoc outcome labels.
AI.method: The authors propose DENSE (Distilling Evidence from Nested Subtask Executions), which organizes trace evidence into nested shortcut trees. It compresses redundant attempts, reconciles issues across levels via recovery evidence, and summarizes completed branches while expanding unresolved ones, linking reusable progress to remaining obligations. They also introduce REFIT, a source-paired protocol comparing feedback on shared initial trajectories under post-hoc outcome blindness, resetting environments and model contexts for fresh attempts.
AI.result: On Terminal-Bench 2.1, DENSE attains the highest strict pass rate among tested non-privileged feedback methods across four recipient models. Strict pass rate improves by 7.12-15.64 pp relative to initial executions, with 19.0-43.6% fewer observed recipient tokens in reruns. GPT-5.5 ablations support combining nested subtask analysis with shortcut construction and issue reconciliation.
AI.conclusion: The findings suggest that agent self-refinement can be achieved through evidence-grounded trajectory reuse, reducing dependence on external supervision.

title: Learning Scene-Aware Humanoid Locomotion through 3D Clutter from Immersive Human Demonstrations
summary: While learning from human motions has enabled highly dynamic humanoid skills such as dancing and martial arts in obstacle-free space, traversal through densely cluttered environments remains underexplored. These spaces are three-dimensional and geometrically constrained, requiring scene-aware locomotion that tightly couples whole-body motion with scene geometry for obstacle avoidance. To address these challenges, we present Moving Through Clutter (MTC), a learning-from-demonstration framework for scene-aware humanoid locomotion. To bypass costly physical scene construction, MTC uses procedurally generated Virtual Reality environments for immersive data collection. To transform these human motions into training-ready humanoid motions, we propose a scene-aware motion retargeting algorithm that converts human demonstrations into humanoid trajectories while strictly enforcing robot-scene clearance to guarantee collision-free traversal. These reference trajectories are then used to train a scene-aware locomotion policy that deploys on a Unitree G1 humanoid. Evaluated on our proposed MTC-Challenge for multi-obstacle traversal, the policy demonstrates a 70.2% collision-free rate across diverse scenarios, successfully traversing complex environments through diverse whole-body skills, including crawling through low-clearance passages and squeezing through narrow gaps.

AI.tldr: MTC is a learning-from-demonstration framework that enables scene-aware humanoid locomotion through densely cluttered 3D environments, using VR data collection and a clearance-enforcing motion retargeting algorithm to train a collision-free policy on a Unitree G1.
AI.motivation: Existing humanoid learning from human motion achieves dynamic skills (dancing, martial arts) only in obstacle-free space; traversal through densely cluttered, geometrically constrained 3D environments remains underexplored and requires tight coupling of whole-body motion with scene geometry for obstacle avoidance.
AI.method: MTC collects immersive demonstrations via procedurally generated VR environments (avoiding costly physical scene construction), then applies a scene-aware motion retargeting algorithm that converts human demonstrations into humanoid trajectories while strictly enforcing robot-scene clearance to guarantee collision-free traversal. These reference trajectories train a scene-aware locomotion policy deployed on a Unitree G1 humanoid.
AI.result: Evaluated on the proposed MTC-Challenge for multi-obstacle traversal, the policy achieves a 70.2% collision-free rate across diverse scenarios, using whole-body skills such as crawling through low-clearance passages and squeezing through narrow gaps.
AI.conclusion: MTC shows that learning from demonstration with scene-aware retargeting can enable robust scene-aware humanoid locomotion in cluttered environments, with a diverse whole-body skill repertoire, though collision-free performance (70.2%) leaves room for improvement.

title: GVPO++: Group Variance Policy Optimization for LLM Post-Training and On-Policy Distillation
comment: Extended version of the NeurIPS 2025 paper "GVPO: Group Variance Policy Optimization for Large Language Model Post-Training"
summary:
Post-training plays a pivotal role in enhancing the reasoning capabilities and task-specific expertise of large language models (LLMs). Despite recent advances in post-training methods, such as Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO), their practical deployment remains impeded by training instability arising from the reliance on importance sampling.
  We introduce Group Variance Policy Optimization (GVPO), a novel post-training method that integrates the analytical solution of KL-constrained reward maximization into its gradient weighting scheme. This formulation provides an intuitive interpretation: GVPO's gradient corresponds to the mean squared error between the central distance of implicit rewards and that of actual rewards. GVPO offers two key advantages: (1) it guarantees a unique optimal solution, exactly to the KL-constrained reward maximization objective, and (2) it enables flexible sampling distributions without requiring importance sampling.
  Beyond general post-training, we show that GVPO naturally extends to on-policy distillation (OPD). Furthermore, GVPO enables the optimization of a broad family of extended OPD objectives, providing a principled foundation for diverse objective design. By unifying theoretical guarantees with practical adaptability, GVPO establishes a new paradigm for reliable and versatile LLM post-training and on-policy distillation.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes Group Variance Policy Optimization (GVPO), a post-training method for LLMs that embeds the analytical solution of KL-constrained reward maximization into its gradient weighting, eliminating the need for importance sampling and guaranteeing a unique optimum.
AI.motivation: Existing post-training methods such as Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) suffer from training instability caused by their reliance on importance sampling, which impedes practical deployment despite their effectiveness in improving LLM reasoning and task-specific expertise.
AI.method: GVPO integrates the analytical solution of KL-constrained reward maximization into its gradient weighting scheme. This yields a gradient equal to the mean squared error between the central distance of implicit rewards and that of actual rewards. GVPO further extends to on-policy distillation (OPD) and supports a broad family of extended OPD objectives.
AI.result: GVPO guarantees a unique optimal solution exactly matching the KL-constrained reward maximization objective, and permits flexible sampling distributions without requiring importance sampling. It also naturally extends to OPD and enables optimization of diverse extended OPD objectives.
AI.conclusion: By unifying theoretical guarantees with practical adaptability, GVPO establishes a new paradigm for reliable and versatile LLM post-training and on-policy distillation.

title: Demonstration Synthesis from a Single Scan via Gaussian Splatting for Visuomotor Policy Learning
summary: Training a visuomotor policy calls for abundant demonstrations that closely match the target environment, yet collecting them anew remains expensive. Existing demonstration synthesis methods reduce this cost but remain constrained by high manual effort, limited visual fidelity, or heavy reliance on physics simulators. This paper introduces GaussianFactory, a high-fidelity data engine that mass-produces demonstrations with a single video scan as its only human input and no physics engine in the generation loop. Specifically, GaussianFactory reconstructs the scene as an editable 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) replica and samples from the object-combination tasks the scene affords. For each task, it plans grasps and trajectories purely kinematically on the geometric reconstruction, rendering photorealistic demonstrations that visually match the target environment. Physical dynamics enter the pipeline only where contact force interactions dictate the outcome---during grasp formation, via a learned contact model pretrained once on an interaction dataset. To evaluate the downstream utility of the synthesized demonstrations, we implement an end-to-end scan-to-deployment workflow in two setups: a simulated scene that stands in for the real world to enable reproducibility, and a real-world workspace with a physical UR10e robot. In each setup, a standard diffusion policy trained solely on the synthesized demonstrations achieves 95.1% and 84.2% success rates, respectively.

AI.tldr: GaussianFactory is a high-fidelity data engine that mass-produces visuomotor policy demonstrations from a single video scan, using an editable 3D Gaussian Splatting replica with no physics engine in the generation loop. Policies trained only on synthesized demonstrations reach 95.1% (sim) and 84.2% (real UR10e) success rates.
AI.motivation: Training visuomotor policies requires abundant demonstrations matching the target environment, but collecting them is expensive. Existing demonstration synthesis methods still suffer from high manual effort, limited visual fidelity, or heavy dependence on physics simulators.
AI.method: GaussianFactory takes a single video scan as its only human input and no physics engine in the generation loop. It reconstructs the scene as an editable 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) replica, samples object-combination tasks the scene affords, and for each task plans grasps and trajectories purely kinematically on the geometric reconstruction. Physical dynamics are introduced only where contact force interactions determine the outcome—during grasp formation—via a learned contact model pretrained once on an interaction dataset.
AI.result: A standard diffusion policy trained solely on synthesized demonstrations achieves 95.1% success in a simulated scene and 84.2% in a real-world workspace with a physical UR10e robot, evaluated through an end-to-end scan-to-deployment workflow in both setups.
AI.conclusion: GaussianFactory enables low-effort, high-fidelity, simulator-free mass production of demonstrations that transfer effectively to real-robot visuomotor policy deployment.

title: Risk-Aware Occupancy for Safety-Oriented End-to-End Autonomous Driving
comment: The first version of this research was completed in early 2025
summary: Sparse representation formulates the environment perception for the end-to-end driving system as a set of discrete elements like objects and lane lines. This formulation meets safety risks in crowded, occluded scenes dealing with unstructured obstacles, uncertain regions, and intricate interactions. In this paper, we propose a dense representation, risk-aware occupancy, to characterize planning-relevant risks in an explicit and uniform manner. It jointly encodes global scene occupancy, map-derived traffic constraints, and future dynamic agent occupancy into a unified BEV map. The unified BEV map captures the risk evidence for trajectory planning in both spatial and temporal dimensions. We design an E2E network, ROIDrive, to realize risk-aware occupancy. It predicts risk-aware occupancy with an independent branch and injects it into planning queries for safety-oriented trajectory generation. In addition, to quantify the safety problem, we introduce RiskOcc4D-nuScenes built upon nuscenes and occ3d-nuscenes. Our risk-aware occupancy yields relative open-loop collision reductions of 52.9% under the UniAD metric and 35.0% under the ST-P3 metric on nuScenes.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes risk-aware occupancy, a dense BEV representation integrating global scene occupancy, traffic constraints, and future dynamic occupancy for safer end-to-end planning, realized via the ROIDrive network and validated on the new RiskOcc4D-nuScenes benchmark with large collision reductions.
AI.motivation: Sparse representation in end-to-end driving models planning as discrete elements (objects, lane lines) encounters safety risks in crowded and occluded scenes, especially with unstructured obstacles, uncertain regions, and intricate interactions.
AI.method: The authors introduce a dense representation termed risk-aware occupancy that jointly encodes global scene occupancy, map-derived traffic constraints, and future dynamic agent occupancy into a unified BEV map, capturing risk evidence across spatial and temporal dimensions. They design an E2E network, ROIDrive, which predicts risk-aware occupancy via an independent branch and injects it into planning queries for safety-oriented trajectory generation. They also build RiskOcc4D-nuScenes upon nuScenes and Occ3D-nuScenes to quantify the safety problem.
AI.result: Risk-aware occupancy achieves relative open-loop collision reductions of 52.9% under the UniAD metric and 35.0% under the ST-P3 metric on nuScenes.
AI.conclusion: The dense risk-aware occupancy representation, implemented through ROIDrive, explicitly and uniformly characterizes planning-relevant risks, substantially improving safety-oriented trajectory generation for end-to-end driving.

title: Noctif3R: Feed-Forward Monocular Real-Time SLAM for Photon-Limited Scenes on Embedded Hardware
summary: Robots carrying out tasks in dark environments need to localize from a single RGB camera, in light so low that the per-pixel signal approaches the sensor's own noise, on a power-constrained onboard computer, in real time. Each of these constraints has matured pipelines, but the intersection does not. Offline low-light reconstruction now recovers structure below -4 dB but is far too slow to run in real time, while the real-time monocular systems a robot can actually carry (DROID-SLAM, DPV-SLAM, etc.) degrade or fail when SNR gets low. We measured how they fail: across the nine lowest darkness levels of our scenes, DROID-SLAM returns a full-length trajectory carrying no information about the camera's motion on all nine, VGGT-SLAM and CUT3R on eight, pi^3 on seven, and DPV-SLAM on four. We present SYS, a monocular pipeline built on a low-light feed-forward pointmap front end with an explicit match gate, which returns three tracked trajectories and no uninformative ones, at the lowest error of any method where it tracks (24-47% of the no-information ceiling against 56-73% for the strongest baseline), and at the narrowest coverage. On a real robot video take in which 86.5% of delivered frames are entirely black, every configuration of ours stops after the lit beginning, while DROID-SLAM and DPV-SLAM each emit a pose for all 1178 frames. Our method contribution is an embedded execution path for the Jetson AGX Orin: running the map, keyframes and backend at 384 pixels with tracking at 256, together with two fixes to the per-frame pose solve, is a replicated Pareto improvement, 1.28x throughput at 0.964x error on one scene and 1.42x at 0.68x on a second, with 47% less peak GPU memory and 29% less energy per pose. We evaluate on a calibrated, bit-exact regenerable noise ladder, on relabelled real-world dark exposures, and on a new dark-room video ladder recorded from a Boston Dynamics Spot robot.

AI.tldr: SYS is a real-time monocular SLAM pipeline for robots operating in near-darkness, combining a low-light feed-forward pointmap front end with an explicit match gate and an embedded Jetson AGX Orin execution path, achieving tracked trajectories with lower error and better throughput, memory, and energy than real-time baselines.
AI.motivation: Robots in dark environments must localize in real time from a single RGB camera on a power-constrained onboard computer, where per-pixel signal approaches sensor noise. Existing pipelines address individual constraints (offline low-light reconstruction is accurate but slow; real-time monocular SLAM like DROID-SLAM, DPV-SLAM degrade or fail at low SNR), but their intersection is unaddressed, and prior systems fail silently by returning full-length trajectories with no motion information.
AI.method: SYS is a monocular pipeline built on a low-light feed-forward pointmap front end with an explicit match gate. An embedded execution path for the Jetson AGX Orin runs the map, keyframes, and backend at 384 pixels with tracking at 256 pixels, plus two fixes to the per-frame pose solve. Evaluation uses a calibrated, bit-exact regenerable noise ladder, relabelled real-world dark exposures, and a new dark-room video ladder recorded from a Boston Dynamics Spot robot.
AI.result: Baselines fail by emitting full-length but uninformative trajectories: across the nine lowest darkness levels, DROID-SLAM produces no motion information on all nine, VGGT-SLAM and CUT3R on eight, pi^3 on seven, and DPV-SLAM on four. SYS returns three tracked trajectories and no uninformative ones, at the lowest error where it tracks (24-47% of the no-information ceiling vs 56-73% for the strongest baseline) and the narrowest coverage. On a real robot video with 86.5% entirely black frames, every SYS configuration stops after the lit beginning, while DROID-SLAM and DPV-SLAM emit poses for all 1178 frames. The embedded path is a replicated Pareto improvement: 1.28x throughput at 0.964x error on one scene and 1.42x at 0.68x error on a second, with 47% less peak GPU memory and 29% less energy per pose.
AI.conclusion: SYS addresses the unaddressed intersection of real-time, onboard, single-camera low-light localization by gating out unreliable matches to avoid uninformative trajectories, and by delivering a Pareto-improving embedded implementation for the Jetson AGX Orin. It trades coverage for reliability—stopping rather than emitting information-free poses—and achieves lower tracking error, higher throughput, and reduced memory and energy relative to real-time baselines.

title: Driving on Registers, Reasoning on Risk: Risk-Aware Occupancy for Register-Based End-to-End Autonomous Driving
comment: This version of this research was completed in early 2026
summary: Multimodal trajectory prediction improves behavioral coverage in end-to-end autonomous driving, but existing methods remain limited by sparse scene representations. Incomplete evidence leads to low-quality candidate generation and unreliable ranking among geometrically similar trajectories. On a register-based baseline, bad and poor candidates constitute 19.74% of the candidate set, while the oracle-best candidate ranks only 33.9th on average. We propose RRDrive, which introduces risk-aware occupancy as a dense, temporally aligned, and trajectory-queryable representation. Its global structure guides high-quality multimodal generation, while candidate-conditioned risk queries support fine-grained selection. We further construct RiskOcc4D-NAVSIM with automatic risk annotations. RRDrive achieves a selected-trajectory PDMS of 0.951, representing a 1.5% relative improvement over the baseline (0.937), and improves the average candidate PDMS by 7.7%. In challenging scenes, it improves candidate PDMS by 30.2% and increases the Spearman correlation among good candidates by 0.41, from 0.26 to 0.67. To move beyond this oracle setting, we further develop an external RiskOcc predictor, a perception module that estimates risk-aware occupancy directly from sensor inputs. The competitive performance validates the representation's feasibility.

AI.tldr: RRDrive introduces risk-aware occupancy as a dense, temporally aligned, trajectory-queryable representation to improve multimodal trajectory prediction, achieving 0.951 PDMS on NAVSIM and boosting candidate quality and ranking, with an external RiskOcc predictor validating feasibility beyond the oracle setting.
AI.motivation: Existing multimodal trajectory prediction methods are limited by sparse scene representations, which lead to incomplete evidence, low-quality candidate generation, and unreliable ranking among geometrically similar trajectories. On a register-based baseline, bad and poor candidates comprise 19.74% of the candidate set, and the oracle-best candidate ranks only 33.9th on average.
AI.method: The authors propose RRDrive, which uses risk-aware occupancy as a dense, temporally aligned, and trajectory-queryable representation. Its global structure guides high-quality multimodal generation, while candidate-conditioned risk queries support fine-grained selection. They also construct RiskOcc4D-NAVSIM with automatic risk annotations, and develop an external RiskOcc predictor that estimates risk-aware occupancy directly from sensor inputs as a perception module.
AI.result: RRDrive achieves a selected-trajectory PDMS of 0.951, a 1.5% relative improvement over the baseline (0.937), and improves the average candidate PDMS by 7.7%. In challenging scenes, it improves candidate PDMS by 30.2% and raises the Spearman correlation among good candidates from 0.26 to 0.67 (a gain of 0.41). The external RiskOcc predictor shows competitive performance, validating the representation's feasibility.
AI.conclusion: Risk-aware occupancy serves as an effective dense representation for multimodal trajectory prediction, improving both candidate generation and selection. The competitive performance of the external RiskOcc predictor further validates the feasibility of the representation beyond the oracle setting.

title: MetaPusher: Meta Learning and Planning for Nonprehensile Manipulation of Unseen Objects with Rapid Online Adaption
summary: Manipulating previously unseen objects remains challenging, as their dynamics depend on latent physical properties, such as friction and mass distribution, that cannot be inferred from perception alone. Prior experience across objects can provide an initial estimate of unseen object dynamics, but this estimate remains uncertain and can degrade further during sim-to-real transfer. Adapting the dynamics through interaction can progressively refine the estimation, however, updating the model may invalidate the planned trajectory. Successful and efficient manipulation therefore requires both rapid dynamics adaptation and a planning strategy that can incorporate this evolution. In this work, we introduce MetaPusher, a meta-learning and adaptive planning framework for nonprehensile manipulation of unseen objects without prior object-specific interactions. A meta-learned dynamics model rapidly adapts from interactions during task execution, while an adaptive kinodynamic planner updates long-horizon plans by reusing and refining its existing search tree. This coupling enables manipulation and adaptation without a separate data collection phase. We evaluate MetaPusher on unseen objects in simulation and in sim-to-real scenarios, comparing against fine-tuning and active learning methods, MPPI-based control, and a reinforcement learning policy. It achieves lower prediction error and improves task success rate by up to 20%.

AI.tldr: MetaPusher is a meta-learning plus adaptive planning framework for nonprehensile manipulation of unseen objects, enabling rapid dynamics adaptation and online replanning without object-specific prior interactions.
AI.motivation: Manipulating unseen objects is hard because their dynamics depend on latent physical properties (e.g., friction, mass distribution) not inferable from perception alone. Prior cross-object experience yields only uncertain initial estimates that degrade under sim-to-real transfer, and interaction-based adaptation can invalidate planned trajectories, requiring both rapid adaptation and planning that accommodates model evolution.
AI.method: A meta-learned dynamics model that rapidly adapts from interactions during task execution, coupled with an adaptive kinodynamic planner that updates long-horizon plans by reusing and refining its existing search tree, enabling simultaneous manipulation and adaptation without a separate data collection phase.
AI.result: On unseen objects in simulation and sim-to-real scenarios, MetaPusher achieves lower prediction error and improves task success rate by up to 20% compared to fine-tuning, active learning, MPPI-based control, and a reinforcement learning policy.
AI.conclusion: Coupling rapid meta-learned dynamics adaptation with tree-reuse adaptive planning enables efficient nonprehensile manipulation of unseen objects without prior object-specific interactions.

title: LogicTrack: Auditing Reasoning Trajectories of Large Language Models with Formal Logic Solvers
summary: Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning has been shown to improve the performance of large language models (LLMs), yet existing optimization methods largely rely on outcome-based feedback, leaving the logical validity of intermediate reasoning steps largely unverified. To address the gap whereby LLMs arrive at correct final answers through logically flawed intermediate reasoning chains, we propose LogicTrack, a neuro-symbolic framework that audits reasoning trajectories by auto-formalizing each reasoning step into symbolic representations and verifying it with automated theorem provers. LogicTrack introduces Solver-Based Backtracking Reward (SBR), a step-wise scoring mechanism that quantifies logical soundness and guides backtracking tree search at inference time. We further extend LogicTrack to construct supervised fine-tuning (SFT) data with backtracking traces from its trajectories, enabling fine-tuned models to internalize step-wise auditing as an intrinsic capability. Extensive experiments across 8 reasoning benchmarks and 7 LLMs demonstrate that LogicTrack effectively improves both the verifiability of reasoning chains and final answer pass rate, thereby enhancing overall CoT quality and trustworthiness in high-stakes domains.

AI.tldr: LogicTrack is a neuro-symbolic framework that audits LLM chain-of-thought by auto-formalizing each step and verifying it with automated theorem provers, using a Solver-Based Backtracking Reward to guide inference-time tree search and to build SFT data that internalizes step-wise auditing.
AI.motivation: Existing CoT optimization methods rely largely on outcome-based feedback, leaving the logical validity of intermediate reasoning steps unverified, so LLMs can reach correct final answers through logically flawed intermediate chains. This gap is especially problematic in high-stakes domains where trustworthy reasoning is required.
AI.method: A neuro-symbolic framework that audits reasoning trajectories by auto-formalizing each reasoning step into symbolic representations and verifying them with automated theorem provers. Its Solver-Based Backtracking Reward (SBR) provides step-wise scoring of logical soundness and guides backtracking tree search at inference time. The framework is further extended to construct supervised fine-tuning data with backtracking traces, letting fine-tuned models internalize step-wise auditing.
