AI.result: Across 8 reasoning benchmarks and 7 LLMs, LogicTrack improves both the verifiability of reasoning chains and the final answer pass rate.
AI.conclusion: LogicTrack enhances overall CoT quality and trustworthiness in high-stakes domains by combining symbolic verification, solver-based step-wise rewards, and fine-tuning on backtracking traces.

title: SAGE: Safety-Aligned Gradient Enforcement for Human--Robot Collaboration
summary: Multi-party human-robot collaboration poses a dual challenge: robot decisions should remain interpretable and auditable, while executed actions must satisfy safety constraints during physical interaction. Combining explainable decision-tree policies with control-barrier-function (CBF) filtering provides a promising architecture but creates two learning mismatches in multi-agent reinforcement learning. Safety projection changes the action applied to the environment, while the coupled proposal graph can misalign independently optimized actor updates with a team-level update. We present safety-aligned gradient enforcement (SAGE) to address both mismatches. Its shield-annealed internalization layer (SAIL) uses a differentiable finite-penalty proposal map while retaining the exact CBF quadratic program for execution, preserving constraint-normal sensitivity to internalize repeatedly active safety constraints. Team-averaged Lyapunov policy optimization (TALO) constructs a team-aware update reference and applies a Lyapunov half-space correction to regulate independent actor updates. Physical experiments with two humanoid robots and a human partner demonstrate deployment feasibility. Across nine simulation scenarios, SAGE achieves a 71.0% success rate with 0.5 collision steps per thousand environment steps. Ablations show that direct CBF filtering reduces collision frequency by 98.5% but decreases success from 67.3% to 59.3%. SAIL reduces proposal violation by 48.8% and proposal-execution correction by 85.2%, while TALO reduces the update-consistency gap by 50.8%.

AI.tldr: SAGE is a MARL framework that resolves two learning mismatches arising from combining explainable decision-tree policies with CBF safety filtering in multi-party human-robot collaboration, using a shield-annealed internalization layer (SAIL) and team-averaged Lyapunov policy optimization (TALO).
AI.motivation: Multi-party human-robot collaboration demands robot decisions that are both interpretable/auditable and safety-constrained during physical interaction. Explainable decision-tree policies combined with CBF filtering offer a promising architecture, but this combination introduces two learning mismatches in multi-agent reinforcement learning: (1) safety projection alters the action actually applied to the environment, and (2) the coupled proposal graph misaligns independently optimized actor updates with a team-level update.
AI.method: SAGE addresses both mismatches. Its shield-annealed internalization layer (SAIL) employs a differentiable finite-penalty proposal map while retaining the exact CBF quadratic program for execution, preserving constraint-normal sensitivity so that repeatedly active safety constraints are internalized. Team-averaged Lyapunov policy optimization (TALO) builds a team-aware update reference and applies a Lyapunov half-space correction to regulate independent actor updates.
AI.result: Physical experiments with two humanoid robots and a human partner demonstrate deployment feasibility. Across nine simulation scenarios, SAGE reaches a 71.0% success rate with 0.5 collision steps per thousand environment steps. Ablations show direct CBF filtering cuts collision frequency by 98.5% but lowers success from 67.3% to 59.3%. SAIL reduces proposal violation by 48.8% and proposal-execution correction by 85.2%, while TALO reduces the update-consistency gap by 50.8%.
AI.conclusion: SAGE effectively resolves the action-projection and team-update mismatches of coupling explainable decision-tree policies with CBF filtering, improving both safety and task success in multi-party human-robot collaboration, and is validated in real physical deployment.

title: PolyBridgeBench: Benchmarking Multimodal LLMs for Physics-Grounded Bridge Design
summary: Multimodal large language models, or MLLMs, perform well at visual understanding and structured generation, yet these capabilities do not establish whether an engineering design will work when executed. Existing benchmarks assess spatial reasoning, structural validity, or physics-grounded construction, but they do not determine whether MLLMs can synthesize complete load-bearing structures and repair them after simulator execution exposes a failure. We introduce PolyBridgeBench, an executable benchmark for multimodal bridge design. A model receives a visual scene and structured engineering constraints and generates a complete node--member--material topology. Deterministic legality checks gate execution in a native dynamic physics simulation. Following an execution failure, the benchmark returns temporal visual evidence from the failed rollout and evaluates repair under a fixed interaction budget. Separate measurements of deterministic validity, dynamic functional success, and post-failure recovery identify the stage at which design fails. Experiments with six representative MLLMs across 189 levels expose a substantial gap between deterministic validity and dynamic success, pronounced sensitivity to material budgets, and limited post-failure recovery under the primary strict-budget setting.

AI.tldr: PolyBridgeBench is an executable benchmark that tests whether MLLMs can synthesize and repair complete load-bearing bridge designs under dynamic physics simulation, revealing a large gap between deterministic validity and actual dynamic success.
AI.motivation: MLLMs excel at visual understanding and structured generation, but these abilities do not guarantee that an engineering design will function upon execution. Existing benchmarks cover spatial reasoning, structural validity, or physics-grounded construction, yet none determine whether MLLMs can synthesize complete load-bearing structures and repair them after a simulator exposes a failure.
AI.method: PolyBridgeBench provides a visual scene and structured engineering constraints; a model must generate a complete node-member-material topology. Deterministic legality checks gate entry into a native dynamic physics simulation. Upon execution failure, the benchmark supplies temporal visual evidence from the failed rollout and evaluates repair within a fixed interaction budget. It separately measures deterministic validity, dynamic functional success, and post-failure recovery.
AI.result: Testing six representative MLLMs across 189 levels reveals a substantial gap between deterministic validity and dynamic success, pronounced sensitivity to material budgets, and limited post-failure recovery under the primary strict-budget setting.
AI.conclusion: The three-stage measurement isolates where design fails and shows that current MLLMs, despite strong visual and structured generation, struggle to produce dynamically functional load-bearing structures or to repair them after simulated failure.

title: Diverse and Adaptable Arm Coordination for Octopus-Crawling via Diffusion-Based Uncertainty-Aware Optimization
summary: Octopus crawling motivates soft robots that exploit redundancy, yet discovering and organizing diverse coordination modes for adaptation remains challenging. To address this, we introduce a Diffusion-based Uncertainty-aware Optimization (DUO) algorithm that learns demonstration-free crawling controllers for a simulated, muscle-actuated CyberOctopus. This work represents the first application of diffusion-based control to soft multi-arm robots in contact-rich simulations. By embedding a variety of locomotion behaviors within a shared control distribution, this approach enables the simulated octopus to navigate dynamic physical constraints, demonstrating that learned coordination diversity inherently facilitates robust adaptation. The main contributions include: (i) a symmetry-structured policy representation that folds radially equivalent controllers into a canonical directional sector, (ii) an online black-box optimization strategy, the DUO algorithm, that discovers and retains diverse coordination modes, and (iii) a control editing technique that adapts existing controllers to novel actuator constraints without retraining. These results show how learned coordination diversity makes motor abundance a practical resource for adaptation in soft multi-arm robots.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces DUO, a diffusion-based, uncertainty-aware optimization algorithm that learns demonstration-free crawling controllers for a simulated muscle-actuated CyberOctopus, using coordination diversity to enable robust adaptation.
AI.motivation: Octopus crawling demonstrates how motor abundance (redundancy) supports diverse coordination modes, motivating soft multi-arm robots. However, discovering and organizing such diverse coordination modes for adaptation remains challenging, and prior diffusion-based control has not been applied to soft multi-arm robots in contact-rich simulations.
AI.method: DUO is a Diffusion-based Uncertainty-aware Optimization algorithm that learns demonstration-free crawling controllers for a simulated, muscle-actuated CyberOctopus. It embeds varied locomotion behaviors in a shared control distribution. Key components: (i) a symmetry-structured policy representation folding radially equivalent controllers into a canonical directional sector, (ii) an online black-box optimization strategy that discovers and retains diverse coordination modes, and (iii) a control editing technique adapting existing controllers to novel actuator constraints without retraining.
AI.result: The simulated octopus navigates dynamic physical constraints, showing that learned coordination diversity inherently facilitates robust adaptation; control editing adapts controllers to new actuator constraints without retraining.
AI.conclusion: Learned coordination diversity makes motor abundance a practical resource for adaptation in soft multi-arm robots, with DUO being the first diffusion-based control applied to soft multi-arm robots in contact-rich simulation.

title: The Communication Bottleneck: A Round-Trip Study of Tree-Structured Expression Serialization in Language Models
summary: When language models reason in chain-of-thought or exchange free-text intermediates, they serialize structured information into natural language. How much tree-structured compositional content survives this bottleneck? We propose a round-trip protocol that answers this question empirically for tree-structured expressions. A generator converts a procedurally generated arithmetic expression into a word problem, a separate extractor recovers the expression from the word problem alone, and symbolic equivalence provides an exact oracle. Evaluating all pairwise combinations of sixteen models yields a communication matrix whose marginals separate generation quality from extraction quality. Three main findings emerge. First, the channel is lossy and asymmetric: swapping which model generates and which extracts shifts accuracy by up to 60.4 points, and the best pair reaches 92.9% by combining different models on each end rather than the same model on both. Second, at least 73.6% of round-trip failures originate at generation, and difficulty is driven by tree structure (operator count, depth, right-branching) rather than model family. Third, the channel is trainable: ~3600 fine-tuning examples that share the evaluation's operators and tree shapes lift every open-weight model above untrained Gemini-3.1-Pro, an upper bound under matched semantics. A disjoint-domain regime with new operators and vocabulary also raises every open-weight model, confirming the gain is not an artifact of matched semantics, though a gap to the frontier remains. Together these results identify tree-structured expression serialization as a primary limiting factor when models communicate hierarchical structure through natural language.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a round-trip protocol (generator → word problem → extractor, with symbolic-equivalence oracle) to measure how much tree-structured compositional information survives serialization into natural language. Testing 16 models shows the channel is lossy and asymmetric, failures are mostly generation-side and driven by tree structure, and the channel is trainable via ~3600 fine-tuning examples.
AI.motivation: Language models serialize structured information into natural language during chain-of-thought reasoning and free-text exchange, but it is unclear how much tree-structured compositional content survives this natural-language bottleneck. The paper aims to empirically quantify this information loss for tree-structured arithmetic expressions.
AI.method: A round-trip protocol for tree-structured expressions: a generator converts a procedurally generated arithmetic expression into a word problem, a separate extractor recovers the expression from the word problem alone, and symbolic equivalence serves as an exact oracle. All pairwise combinations of sixteen models are evaluated, producing a communication matrix whose marginals separate generation quality from extraction quality. Additional fine-tuning experiments (~3600 examples with matched operators and tree shapes) and a disjoint-domain regime with new operators and vocabulary are conducted.
AI.result: (1) The channel is lossy and asymmetric: swapping generator/extractor roles shifts accuracy by up to 60.4 points, and the best pair reaches 92.9% using different models on each end rather than the same model on both. (2) At least 73.6% of round-trip failures originate at generation, with difficulty driven by tree structure (operator count, depth, right-branching) rather than model family. (3) The channel is trainable: ~3600 fine-tuning examples lift every open-weight model above untrained Gemini-3.1-Pro, and a disjoint-domain regime with new operators and vocabulary also raises every open-weight model, confirming the gain is not an artifact of matched semantics, though a gap to the frontier remains.
AI.conclusion: Tree-structured expression serialization is a primary limiting factor when models communicate hierarchical structure through natural language. The findings highlight the lossy, asymmetric, structure-driven, and trainable nature of this natural-language channel.

title: Same World, Different Knowledge: When Isolated Audits Misjudge World-Model Repairs
summary:
A repair favored under an isolated input fault can be inferior when deployed modules share the faulty information. We introduce an information-interface
  audit for world models, distinguishing fidelity gaps, where exact inputs become estimates, from availability gaps, where inputs are missing. Fixed-weight
  interventions measure prediction error, input dependence, and paired closed-loop benefit, including dependencies introduced by reconstruction. In
  simulated quadrotor model predictive control, coupled, opposite-sign 10% mass/thrust calibration errors reduce a physics-anchored model's success from 69%
  to 8%; uncertainty training restores 65%. Wind reconstruction recovers control benefit but inherits calibration dependence. For a positive calibration
  offset, reconstruction-only corruption favors uncertainty-trained reconstruction, whereas shared corruption favors the baseline. Acceleration diagnostics
  reveal compensation between reconstruction bias and nominal-model error, also observed with a disturbance observer. Repair selection therefore depends on
  the information paths used in deployment.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces an information-interface audit for world models that distinguishes fidelity gaps (inputs become estimates) from availability gaps (inputs are missing), and shows via fixed-weight interventions that repair selection must account for the information paths used in deployment.
AI.motivation: A repair that appears beneficial under an isolated input fault can become inferior when deployed modules share the faulty information, so repairs cannot be evaluated in isolation without considering how faulty information propagates through the deployment interface.
AI.method: The authors propose an information-interface audit that separates fidelity gaps from availability gaps. They apply fixed-weight interventions to measure prediction error, input dependence, and paired closed-loop benefit, including dependencies introduced by reconstruction. The audit is evaluated in simulated quadrotor model predictive control with coupled, opposite-sign 10% mass/thrust calibration errors, and cross-checked with acceleration diagnostics and a disturbance observer.
AI.result: Coupled, opposite-sign 10% mass/thrust calibration errors reduce a physics-anchored model's success from 69% to 8%, while uncertainty training restores it to 65%. Wind reconstruction recovers control benefit but inherits calibration dependence. For a positive calibration offset, reconstruction-only corruption favors uncertainty-trained reconstruction, whereas shared corruption favors the baseline. Acceleration diagnostics reveal compensation between reconstruction bias and nominal-model error, also observed with a disturbance observer.
AI.conclusion: Repair selection depends on the information paths used in deployment: the same repair can be favorable or unfavorable depending on whether corruption is isolated or shared, so audits must assess fidelity and availability gaps jointly with closed-loop consequences.

title: Learning-to-Optimize as the Missing Architectural Layer of AI-Native Networks
summary: Artificial Intelligence (AI) is becoming a fundamental design principle of future AI-native communication networks, enabling autonomous resource management, adaptive control, and zero-touch network operation. While current AI-native architectures increasingly embed intelligence across network functions, they provide little guidance on how optimisation knowledge should be systematically generated, transferred, and exploited by AI models. This paper argues that the Learning-to-Optimize (L2O) represents the missing architectural layer between optimisation and AI-native intelligence. Rather than viewing optimisation merely as an online decision engine, the proposed paradigm redefines optimisation algorithms as offline knowledge generators that produce high-quality supervisory information for neural surrogate models. The resulting models inherit optimisation expertise while enabling low-latency runtime inference suitable for dynamic network environments. A generic four-stage L2O workflow is introduced, comprising optimisation, knowledge generation, surrogate learning, and runtime inference. Unlike existing Learning-to-Optimize approaches, which primarily focus on algorithm acceleration, the proposed framework establishes L2O as an architectural abstraction applicable across heterogeneous communication and computing systems. The proposed paradigm is illustrated by an NR-V2X relay-selection problem, in which optimisation-generated solutions from a Mixed-Integer Linear Programming (MILP) solver are used to train a Graph Neural Network that can reproduce near-optimal decisions in real time. The presented perspective positions Learning-to-Optimize as a key architectural enabler for future AI-native networks.

AI.tldr: This paper positions Learning-to-Optimize (L2O) as the missing architectural layer between classical optimization and AI-native intelligence, redefining optimization algorithms as offline knowledge generators that produce supervisory data for neural surrogate models that then perform low-latency runtime inference in communication networks.
AI.motivation: AI is becoming a fundamental design principle of future AI-native communication networks, enabling autonomous resource management, adaptive control, and zero-touch operation. However, current AI-native architectures embed intelligence across network functions without providing guidance on how optimization knowledge should be systematically generated, transferred, and exploited by AI models. This gap motivates the need for a structured architectural abstraction linking optimization and AI-native intelligence.
AI.method: The paper proposes a paradigm that redefines optimization algorithms as offline knowledge generators rather than merely online decision engines, producing high-quality supervisory information for neural surrogate models that inherit optimization expertise while supporting low-latency runtime inference. A generic four-stage L2O workflow is introduced: optimization, knowledge generation, surrogate learning, and runtime inference. The framework is illustrated using an NR-V2X relay-selection problem, where solutions generated by a Mixed-Integer Linear Programming (MILP) solver are used to train a Graph Neural Network capable of reproducing near-optimal decisions in real time.
AI.result: The L2O paradigm is demonstrated on an NR-V2X relay-selection problem, where the Graph Neural Network trained on MILP-generated solutions reproduces near-optimal decisions in real time. Unlike existing L2O approaches focused primarily on algorithm acceleration, the proposed framework establishes L2O as an architectural abstraction applicable across heterogeneous communication and computing systems.
AI.conclusion: The paper concludes by positioning Learning-to-Optimize as a key architectural enabler for future AI-native networks, providing systematic guidance on how optimization knowledge can be generated, transferred, and exploited by AI models within an architectural abstraction spanning communication and computing systems.

title: MA-LIPP: Cooperative Multi-Agent Load-Aware Informative Path Planning for Heterogeneous Robot Teams
summary: Field robotics missions often require physical samples to be returned to laboratories for analysis, making path planning inherently load-aware and order-dependent as accumulated samples increase payload and traversal energy costs. In single-robot Load-Aware Informative Path Planning (LIPP), this rigidly couples sensing with hauling: a solitary robot must transport every collected sample, forcing frequent depot returns that severely restrict its spatial coverage. Heterogeneous multi-robot teams can overcome this bottleneck by dividing labor---enabling high-precision samplers to collect while high-capacity carriers handle transport. However, this introduces a complex coordination challenge regarding when, where, what, and to whom handoffs should occur on top of the LIPP problem. To address this tightly coupled problem, we introduce Multi-Agent LIPP (MA-LIPP), which enables teams to cooperate through asynchronous "dead drops," allowing one robot to deposit samples for another to retrieve later without requiring synchronous rendezvous. We formulate MA-LIPP as an exact Mixed-Integer Quadratic Program (MIQP) alongside a scalable Pairwise Large-Neighborhood Search (LNS) heuristic for complex real-world applications. The heuristic matches exact optima in $95.5\%$ of certified cases and reduces weighted posterior variance by $16.1$--$19.8\%$ relative to a sequential baseline on larger instances of up to 12 robots, providing a robust framework for cooperative physical-sampling missions.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Multi-Agent Load-Aware Informative Path Planning (MA-LIPP), which uses asynchronous "dead drops" to decouple sampling from hauling across heterogeneous robot teams, formulated as an MIQP with a scalable Pairwise LNS heuristic.
AI.motivation: Field robotics missions frequently require physical samples to be delivered to laboratories. This makes path planning load-aware and order-dependent: accumulated samples increase payload and traversal energy costs. In the single-robot LIPP setting, sensing and hauling are rigidly coupled—one robot must transport every sample, causing frequent depot returns that severely limit spatial coverage.
AI.method: The authors exploit heterogeneous multi-robot teams to divide labor, with high-precision samplers collecting and high-capacity carriers transporting. They introduce MA-LIPP, enabling cooperation via asynchronous "dead drops" where one robot deposits samples for later retrieval by another, avoiding synchronous rendezvous. The problem is formulated as an exact Mixed-Integer Quadratic Program (MIQP) plus a scalable Pairwise Large-Neighborhood Search (LNS) heuristic.
AI.result: The heuristic matches exact optima in 95.5% of certified cases and reduces weighted posterior variance by 16.1–19.8% relative to a sequential baseline on larger instances of up to 12 robots.
AI.conclusion: MA-LIPP provides a robust framework for cooperative physical-sampling missions, addressing the tightly coupled coordination of when, where, what, and to whom handoffs should occur on top of the LIPP problem.

title: Dual-Interest Sequential Product Recommendation With Multi-Granular SSM
summary: Sequential recommendation aims to predict the next item a user will interact with based on their historical behavior. Advances in Transformers have significantly improved sequential recommendation but are still limited by cost efficiency. Although State Space Models (SSMs) have recently enabled efficient long-range modeling, most existing methods encode each item with a single static contextual role, overlooking the phenomenon of item polysemy. In fact, the same item often plays different semantic roles depending on user context, and existing methods are limited in capturing dynamic behavior across different temporal granularities. In this work, we propose DSRec, a novel dual-interest cross-SSM model that explicitly disentangles item roles across long-term and short-term semantic context. Sequential items are encoded into long-term interest embeddings that capture stable preferences via historical aggregation, and a short-term interest branch that emphasizes local session intent modulated by inter-click time intervals. These interest embeddings are processed through distinct SSM encoders: a full-sequence Mamba for long-term modeling, and a time-modulated SSM that dynamically adjusts state evolution based on temporal gaps. To enable effective cross-granularity alignment, we adopt a residual cross-fusion mechanism that exchanges contextual information between the two branches while preserving semantic independence. Experiments on public benchmarks demonstrate that DSRec outperforms other state-of-the-art methods.

AI.tldr: DSRec, a dual-interest cross-SSM model, disentangles item roles into long-term and short-term interest branches, each processed by distinct SSM encoders and fused via residual cross-fusion, achieving SOTA sequential recommendation results.
AI.motivation: Transformer-based sequential recommendation is cost-inefficient, and existing SSM methods encode each item with a single static contextual role, ignoring item polysemy (the same item serving different semantic roles depending on user context) and failing to capture dynamic behavior across temporal granularities.
AI.method: DSRec encodes items into a long-term interest branch (historical aggregation for stable preferences, modeled by a full-sequence Mamba) and a short-term interest branch (local session intent modulated by inter-click time intervals, modeled by a time-modulated SSM whose state evolution adapts to temporal gaps). A residual cross-fusion mechanism exchanges contextual information between branches while preserving semantic independence for cross-granularity alignment.
AI.result: Experiments on public benchmarks demonstrate that DSRec outperforms other state-of-the-art methods.
AI.conclusion: Explicitly disentangling item roles across long- and short-term semantic contexts and aligning them via dual SSM encoders with residual cross-fusion yields superior sequential recommendation performance.

title: OpenRoIS: A Community-Driven Open-Source Middleware Implementing the Robotic Interaction Service (RoIS) Framework for Physical Robots and Virtual Agents
comment: Submitted for presentation at the 2027 IEEE/SICE International Symposium on System Integration (SII), Kobe, Japan
summary: Service applications for human-robot interaction are commonly written against the hardware-specific interfaces of one platform, so a change of hardware forces a rewrite of the application. The Robotic Interaction Service (RoIS) Framework 2.0, standardized by the Object Management Group (OMG), addresses this fragmentation by defining a platform-independent model in which Service Applications interact with Human-Robot Interaction (HRI) Engines through standardized interfaces and hardware-independent symbolic messages. A specification alone, however, does not provide the maintained implementation, Software Development Kits (SDKs), and adapters needed for practical adoption. This paper presents OpenRoIS, a community-driven open-source middleware providing a concrete implementation of the RoIS Framework 2.0. It takes the position that an openly developed, paradigm-neutral implementation is what carries the standard from specification to practice. OpenRoIS contributes a recursive engine architecture in which a single engine class realizes the main and sub HRI Engine roles, an internal five-method component contract distinct from the five external RoIS interfaces, a mapping of those interfaces onto JSON-RPC 2.0 over WebSocket, a single-source-of-truth type pipeline that generates three consistent language stacks, TypeScript and C# client SDKs that include web and Unity support, and a Python adapter SDK that includes ROS 2 support. Through the common RoIS interfaces, a Service Application can address physical robots and virtual agents over the internet. All source code, interface types, and documentation are released under the Apache-2.0 license and openly developed at https://openrois.org/.

AI.tldr: OpenRoIS is a community-driven open-source middleware that turns the OMG-standardized RoIS Framework 2.0 from a specification into practice, offering a recursive engine architecture, internal component contracts, JSON-RPC 2.0/WebSocket interface mapping, a single-source type pipeline generating three language stacks, and TypeScript/C#/Python SDKs.
AI.motivation: HRI service applications are typically written against one platform's hardware-specific interfaces, so changing hardware forces a rewrite. The OMG-standardized RoIS Framework 2.0 defines a platform-independent model with standardized interfaces and hardware-independent symbolic messages, but a specification alone lacks the maintained implementation, SDKs, and adapters required for practical adoption.
AI.method: OpenRoIS provides a concrete open-source implementation of RoIS Framework 2.0, taking the position that an openly developed, paradigm-neutral implementation is what carries the standard into practice. Contributions include: a recursive engine architecture where one engine class realizes both main and sub HRI Engine roles; an internal five-method component contract distinct from the five external RoIS interfaces; mapping of those interfaces onto JSON-RPC 2.0 over WebSocket; a single-source-of-truth type pipeline generating three consistent language stacks; TypeScript and C# client SDKs with web and Unity support; and a Python adapter SDK with ROS 2 support.
AI.result: Through the common RoIS interfaces, a Service Application can address both physical robots and virtual agents over the internet. All source code, interface types, and documentation are released under the Apache-2.0 license and openly developed at https://openrois.org/.
AI.conclusion: OpenRoIS demonstrates that an openly developed, paradigm-neutral implementation can operationalize the RoIS Framework 2.0 standard for HRI, enabling hardware-independent service applications that span physical robots and virtual agents.

title: Beyond Accuracy: Centroid-Guided Contrastive Loss for Structured Fraudulent Job Posting Detection
comment: 12 pages, 6 figures, 8 tables. Submitted to IEEE Open Journal of the Computer Society. Code: https://github.com/ali-ahmed925/CGCL_code
summary: Fraudulent job posting detection aims to identify job advertisements that are corrupted either through fake content, misleading information, or negative intent, disrupting the online eco-system of job-seekers and employers. Existing studies in this domain lack effective methods to simultaneously achieve high accuracy and meaningful structure of latent-space representations that capture subtleties among fake posts. To this end, we propose Centroid-Guided Contrastive Loss (CGCL), a loss function which unifies classification with densely formulated clustering to consistently reshape latent-space through a centroid-driven top-$k$ push-and-pull mechanism. The complementary nature of CGCL enables the model to enforce accurate decision boundaries and maintain high clustering compactness, effectively capturing both class separability and latent structure. Extensive experiments demonstrate the state-of-the-art (SOTA) performance of our method on EMSCAD, a public benchmark dataset. The code associated with this work is available at: https://github.com/ali-ahmed925/CGCL_code

AI.tldr: The paper proposes Centroid-Guided Contrastive Loss (CGCL), a loss function unifying classification with clustering via a centroid-driven top-k push-and-pull mechanism for fraudulent job posting detection, achieving SOTA on EMSCAD.
AI.motivation: Existing fraudulent job posting detection methods fail to simultaneously achieve high accuracy and meaningful latent-space representations that capture subtleties among fake posts.
AI.method: CGCL unifies classification with densely formulated clustering, consistently reshaping the latent space through a centroid-driven top-k push-and-pull mechanism.
AI.result: Extensive experiments show state-of-the-art (SOTA) performance on EMSCAD, a public benchmark dataset.
AI.conclusion: CGCL's complementary nature enables the model to enforce accurate decision boundaries while maintaining high clustering compactness, effectively capturing both class separability and latent structure.

title: When to Waddle: A Comparative Study of Bipedal Torso-Stabilization on Low-Friction Surfaces
summary: Low-friction surfaces challenge bipedal locomotion by limiting the contact forces available during stepping. Inspired by penguin waddling, we investigate how lateral torso motion and center of mass (COM) placement affect locomotion as surface friction changes. Using a five-actuator biped, we compare an upright-gait strategy with a penguin-inspired torso-over-stance-leg strategy across multiple COM placements in simulation and hardware. In the 3-D simulator MuJoCo, we sweep through sinusoidal leg and hip actuation parameters across four friction coefficients mu = 0.1, 0.3, 0.5, 0.7. In simulation, torso-over-stance-leg motion produces more successful controllers and higher forward speeds at low friction, with the highest speed occurring for the high-COM configuration. Hardware experiments show the same low-friction speed trend: at mu=0.12, torso-over-stance-leg motion increases forward speed and reduces cost of transport at both tested COM ratios, and the higher COM also improves both measures. The high-COM penguin configuration is the fastest and most energy efficient while maintaining low sideways foot motion. At mu=0.45, the COM trend reverses: the lower-COM configurations are faster and more energy efficient, while gait strategy has little effect on forward speed but still changes sideways foot motion. These results show that the effects of lateral torso motion and COM placement depend on the available friction, and that forward speed, energy use, and slip-related foot motion can be modulated with a penguin-inspired torso motion on hardware.

AI.tldr: Inspired by penguin waddling, this study tests how lateral torso motion and COM placement affect bipedal locomotion under varying friction, finding that a high-COM penguin-inspired gait is fastest and most efficient at low friction but the trend reverses at higher friction.
AI.motivation: Low-friction surfaces limit available contact forces during stepping, posing a challenge to bipedal locomotion. Penguins are hypothesized to exploit lateral torso motion and COM placement to cope with such conditions, motivating an investigation into whether these strategies improve locomotion as friction changes.
AI.method: Using a five-actuator biped, the authors compare an upright-gait strategy against a penguin-inspired torso-over-stance-leg strategy across multiple COM placements, both in simulation and hardware. In MuJoCo, they sweep sinusoidal leg and hip actuation parameters across four friction coefficients (mu = 0.1, 0.3, 0.5, 0.7). Hardware experiments validate the trends.
AI.result: In simulation, torso-over-stance-leg motion yields more successful controllers and higher forward speeds at low friction, peaking for the high-COM configuration. Hardware confirms this: at mu=0.12, torso-over-stance-leg motion raises forward speed and lowers cost of transport at both COM ratios, with higher COM further improving both. At mu=0.45, the COM trend reverses lower-COM configurations are faster and more efficient, gait strategy barely affects speed but still alters sideways foot motion.
AI.conclusion: The effects of lateral torso motion and COM placement on bipedal locomotion are friction-dependent. A penguin-inspired torso motion can modulate forward speed, energy use, and slip-related foot motion on hardware, with a high-COM configuration optimal at low friction and a lower-COM configuration optimal at higher friction.

title: Reducing Barriers to Academic Support: Evaluating a Course-Specific RAG System for Addressing Help-Seeking Disparities in Higher Education
summary: Access to academic support is a key determinant of student success, yet students experience it unequally: some readily seek help from lecturers or tutors, while others hesitate due to anxiety, fear of judgement, uncertainty about expectations, or low confidence in their understanding. This may be especially evident in computing education, where programming tasks are cumulative and cognitively demanding. Although students increasingly turn to general-purpose generative AI tools, these can produce responses that are inaccurate, insufficiently contextualised, or misaligned with module expectations. This study presents and evaluates Beacon, a course-specific Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) system providing private, immediate, module-aligned academic support. Grounding responses in approved teaching materials, Beacon was designed to lower barriers to help-seeking while encouraging independent learning. Using a design-based research approach, Beacon was developed iteratively and evaluated via mixed methods, combining questionnaires and semi-structured interviews with students and staff at a Higher Education institution. Students described Beacon's responses as closely aligned with module content and more trustworthy than unrestricted generative AI tools, valuing its use of pseudocode and scaffolded explanations over direct solutions. Although participants remained cautious about trusting AI-generated responses without verification, they viewed the system as a valuable first point of support before consulting lecturers or official resources. The findings suggest that carefully designed course-specific AI systems may reduce barriers to academic support by occupying an intermediary space between independent study and formal support. Rather than replacing educators, educational AI may be most valuable when it broadens access to guidance while preserving the pedagogical role of lecturers.

AI.tldr: Beacon, a course-specific RAG system grounded in approved teaching materials, was developed via design-based research and evaluated with mixed methods. Students found it module-aligned and more trustworthy than general generative AI, valuing pseudocode and scaffolded explanations, and treated it as a first point of support before formal help.
AI.motivation: Access to academic support is unequal: some students readily seek help, while others hesitate due to anxiety, fear of judgement, uncertain expectations, or low confidence—especially in computing education, where programming tasks are cumulative and cognitively demanding. General-purpose generative AI tools are increasingly used but can be inaccurate, insufficiently contextualised, or misaligned with module expectations.
AI.method: Design-based research: Beacon, a course-specific Retrieval-Augmented Generation system, was developed iteratively to provide private, immediate, module-aligned academic support by grounding responses in approved teaching materials. It was evaluated through mixed methods combining questionnaires and semi-structured interviews with students and staff at a Higher Education institution.
AI.result: Students described Beacon's responses as closely aligned with module content and more trustworthy than unrestricted generative AI tools, valuing pseudocode and scaffolded explanations over direct solutions. Participants remained cautious about trusting AI responses without verification but saw the system as a valuable first point of support before consulting lecturers or official resources.
AI.conclusion: Carefully designed course-specific AI systems may reduce barriers to academic support by occupying an intermediary space between independent study and formal support. Rather than replacing educators, educational AI may be most valuable when it broadens access to guidance while preserving the pedagogical role of lecturers.

title: Robust Structureless Monocular Visual Inertial Initialization Exploiting Line Features and Vanishing Points
summary: Accurate initialization is essential for reliable visual-inertial odometry (VIO), but it is often ill-conditioned under degenerate motions. Existing methods typically require restrictive excitation motions to ensure sufficient observability or rely on computationally expensive 3D structure reconstruction, limiting efficient and practical deployment. To address these limitations, we propose SLIM-init, a structureless monocular VIO initializer that directly exploits geometric constraints from tracked 2D line features without explicit 3D landmark reconstruction. Specifically, SLIM-init leverages line-derived vanishing points (VPs) as translation-invariant orientation cues to provide robust rotation-only constraints under degenerate scenarios such as low-parallax or translation-dominant motions. It further incorporates a line epipolar residual to constrain translation and a line-normal projection residual to improve the conditioning of linear alignment, enhancing the accuracy and robustness of initial state estimation. Extensive experiments on a public benchmark and challenging custom degenerate-motion sequences demonstrate improved accuracy and robustness over state-of-the-art initialization methods. The source code is available at: https://github.com/cjunwan/SLIM-init.

AI.tldr: SLIM-init is a structureless monocular VIO initializer that uses tracked 2D line features—via vanishing points, line epipolar residuals, and line-normal projection residuals—to achieve accurate, efficient initialization even under degenerate motions, without 3D landmark reconstruction.
AI.motivation: Accurate initialization is crucial for reliable VIO, yet it is often ill-conditioned under degenerate motions. Existing approaches either demand restrictive excitation motions for observability or rely on computationally expensive 3D structure reconstruction, hindering practical deployment.
AI.method: SLIM-init is structureless and monocular, exploiting geometric constraints from tracked 2D line features without explicit 3D landmark reconstruction. It uses line-derived vanishing points as translation-invariant orientation cues for robust rotation-only constraints under degenerate scenarios (low parallax, translation-dominant motion), plus a line epipolar residual to constrain translation and a line-normal projection residual to improve conditioning of linear alignment.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on a public benchmark and challenging custom degenerate-motion sequences show improved accuracy and robustness over state-of-the-art initialization methods.
AI.conclusion: SLIM-init enhances the accuracy and robustness of initial state estimation for monocular VIO under degenerate motions while avoiding expensive structure reconstruction. Source code: https://github.com/cjunwan/SLIM-init.

title: Calibrating Teacher--Student Discrepancy for On-Policy Distillation
summary: On-policy distillation (OPD) improves reasoning models by learning the token-level discrepancy between a stronger teacher and an on-policy student. However, this discrepancy does not purely reflect the capability gap between the teacher and the student: it also contains deviations arising from the teacher itself, which are consequently mixed into the observed teacher--student discrepancy and indiscriminately learned by standard OPD during training. This issue is further exacerbated by privileged OPD, where privileged information induces larger teacher-side likelihood shifts, thereby encouraging the student to learn more of the teacher's own deviation. We introduce \textbf{Calibrated On-Policy Distillation (Cal-OPD)}, which estimates the teacher's self-deviation region through positive and negative privileged interventions and calibrates the original teacher--student discrepancy by retaining only the component that lies beyond this region. Experiments on mathematical reasoning benchmarks show that, while retaining only about 52--65\% of the original teacher--student discrepancy as the optimization signal, Cal-OPD consistently outperforms standard OPD and its variants across model scales.

AI.tldr: Cal-OPD calibrates on-policy distillation by estimating the teacher's self-deviation region via positive/negative privileged interventions and retaining only the teacher-student discrepancy beyond this region, outperforming standard OPD across model scales.
AI.motivation: In on-policy distillation, the observed teacher-student discrepancy conflates the genuine capability gap with deviations originating from the teacher itself. Standard OPD indiscriminately learns both, and privileged OPD exacerbates this by inducing larger teacher-side likelihood shifts, causing students to absorb the teacher's own deviations.
AI.method: Cal-OPD estimates the teacher's self-deviation region through positive and negative privileged interventions, then calibrates the original teacher-student discrepancy by retaining only the component lying beyond this region as the optimization signal.
AI.result: On mathematical reasoning benchmarks, Cal-OPD consistently outperforms standard OPD and its variants across model scales, while using only about 52-65% of the original teacher-student discrepancy as the optimization signal.
AI.conclusion: Filtering out teacher self-deviation from the distillation signal yields a cleaner, more effective optimization target, improving reasoning performance over standard and privileged OPD.

title: Stochastic Neural Signed Swept Volume for Real-time Chance-Constrained Trajectory Optimization
summary: Collision-free motion planning requires reliable collision models from sensed environments and validation of states along a continuous trajectory. To make this tractable, most planners check for collision at discrete states along continuous trajectories against a single determinized model of the environment, introducing a trade-off between safety and computational efficiency. While continuous collision checking approaches that approximate the swept volume of the robot exist, they are computationally expensive or overly conservative. Data-driven approaches can learn the swept volume; however, these neural models are susceptible to approximation errors and are therefore often limited to serving as coarse filters for downstream collision checkers. In this work, we propose to learn a signed distance function of the swept volume as a probabilistic field, enabling quantification of epistemic uncertainty, incorporation of perception noise, and eventual integration into a chance-constrained trajectory optimization framework. We demonstrate our approach on challenging high-dimensional manipulation problems with significant sensor noise, both in simulation and on real hardware.

AI.tldr: The paper learns a signed distance function (SDF) of the swept volume as a probabilistic field to enable uncertainty quantification, perception-noise incorporation, and chance-constrained trajectory optimization for collision-free motion planning.
AI.motivation: Most planners check collisions at discrete states against a single determinized environment model, creating a safety-efficiency trade-off. Continuous collision checking that approximates the swept volume is either computationally expensive or overly conservative. Existing data-driven swept-volume models suffer approximation errors and serve only as coarse filters.
AI.method: The authors propose learning a signed distance function of the swept volume represented as a probabilistic field, allowing quantification of epistemic uncertainty and incorporation of perception noise. This model is then integrated into a chance-constrained trajectory optimization framework.
AI.result: The approach is demonstrated on challenging high-dimensional manipulation problems with significant sensor noise, both in simulation and on real hardware.
AI.conclusion: Learning the swept-volume SDF as a probabilistic field yields a reliable collision model that supports uncertainty-aware, chance-constrained planning, overcoming limitations of determinized and conservative continuous collision checking.

title: One Prompt Does Not Fit All: Self-Meta-Evolve for Personalized Information Extraction
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed for enterprise information extraction (IE), where the same document must be reorganized differently for each user. Existing prompt optimization methods, however, rely on a single prompt optimized against a global objective, which is misaligned with the inherent user heterogeneity of real workplaces. We formulate enterprise IE as per-user prompt adaptation under interaction feedback and propose Self-Meta-Evolve, a hierarchical framework that maintains a dedicated prompt for each user and continuously refines it through a dual-loop process: an inner loop that edits structured prompts based on persona-conditioned feedback, and an outer loop that evolves the meta-prompt itself by distilling successful editing patterns. To enable scalable training and evaluation, we release a persona-driven IE benchmark of 292 simulated enterprise users, paired with a reproducible persona-generation pipeline grounded in O*NET occupational taxonomies. On this benchmark, Self-Meta-Evolve achieves a 74.58% success rate, outperforming the strongest prompt-optimization baseline by 13.56 absolute points, and reaches 52.54\% within only two iterations. A double-blind human study with twenty real professionals further confirms that prompts adapted by our framework win against static baselines in 71% of pairwise comparisons.

AI.tldr: The paper formulates enterprise information extraction as per-user prompt adaptation and proposes Self-Meta-Evolve, a hierarchical dual-loop framework that maintains and refines a dedicated prompt per user, achieving 74.58% success on a new persona-driven benchmark.
AI.motivation: LLMs are increasingly used for enterprise information extraction, where the same document must be reorganized differently per user. Existing prompt optimization methods optimize a single prompt against a global objective, which conflicts with real workplace user heterogeneity.
AI.method: Self-Meta-Evolve is a hierarchical framework maintaining a dedicated prompt per user, refined via a dual-loop process: an inner loop edits structured prompts based on persona-conditioned feedback, and an outer loop evolves the meta-prompt by distilling successful editing patterns. Evaluation uses a released persona-driven IE benchmark of 292 simulated enterprise users with a reproducible persona-generation pipeline grounded in O*NET occupational taxonomies.
AI.result: On the benchmark, Self-Meta-Evolve reaches 74.58% success rate, 13.56 absolute points above the strongest prompt-optimization baseline, and 52.54% within two iterations. A double-blind human study with twenty real professionals confirms adapted prompts win against static baselines in 71% of pairwise comparisons.
AI.conclusion: Per-user prompt adaptation via a dual-loop self-evolving framework substantially outperforms global single-prompt optimization, validated by both benchmark and human study results.

title: Visual Navigation Transformer with Pose Attention
summary: Learned navigation policies typically consume observations as a temporally ordered history, with positional encodings tying each observation to when it was seen, making it difficult to reuse experience from earlier traversals of an environment. Systems that do reuse such experience usually construct an explicit representation, such as a map or a topological graph, and plan on it. We propose VNT-PA (Visual Navigation Transformer with Pose Attention), a transformer planner whose context is a set of depth keyframes indexed by camera pose. With camera poses as positional encoding, attention depends on the pose differences between keyframes rather than on their temporal order. VNT-PA is trained to imitate a shortest-path planner operating on the ground-truth scene mesh, predicting actions by querying the spatial context with only its current pose and the goal position. On point-goal navigation in HM3D validation scenes, VNT-PA reaches 93.3% success and 90.4% success weighted by path length (SPL), outperforming baselines that encode the same context as a temporal sequence or treat pose as an input feature, in both navigation performance and training efficiency. Because the spatial context is a pose-indexed set, frames from different trajectories can be fused at test time. The planner also degrades more gracefully under localization noise than a conventional baseline which plans on explicit maps. These results show that pose-stamped experience can serve directly as the environment representation for a learned planner, and that making attention depend on pose differences, rather than on temporal order, speeds up training and improves long-horizon navigation.

AI.tldr: VNT-PA is a transformer navigation planner that uses camera poses as positional encodings over a set of depth keyframes, so attention depends on pose differences rather than temporal order, enabling experience reuse across trajectories and achieving 93.3% success / 90.4% SPL on HM3D point-goal navigation.
AI.motivation: Learned navigation policies consume observations as a temporally ordered history, tying each observation to when it was seen, which hinders reusing experience from earlier traversals of the same environment. Systems that reuse experience typically build explicit representations (maps or topological graphs) and plan on them, adding complexity and sensitivity to localization noise.
AI.method: VNT-PA (Visual Navigation Transformer with Pose Attention) is a transformer planner whose context is a set of depth keyframes indexed by camera pose. Camera poses serve as positional encodings, so attention depends on pose differences between keyframes rather than temporal order. It is trained to imitate a shortest-path planner operating on the ground-truth scene mesh, predicting actions by querying the spatial context using only its current pose and the goal position.
AI.result: On point-goal navigation in HM3D validation scenes, VNT-PA achieves 93.3% success and 90.4% SPL, outperforming baselines that encode the same context as a temporal sequence or treat pose as an input feature, in both navigation performance and training efficiency. Frames from different trajectories can be fused at test time, and the planner degrades more gracefully under localization noise than a conventional explicit-map baseline.
AI.conclusion: Pose-stamped experience can serve directly as the environment representation for a learned planner. Making attention depend on pose differences rather than temporal order speeds up training and improves long-horizon navigation.

title: Accelerating Dense LLMs via L0-regularized Mixture-of-Experts
summary: Large language models (LLMs) achieve strong performance but suffer from slow and costly inference. Existing acceleration methods often lead to noticeable performance degradation, while Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models require extensive computational resources. In this paper, we propose L0-MoE, a lightweight MoE approach using L0-regularization to accelerate dense LLMs nearly without performance loss. Our method introduces a cluster confusion matrix for domain-aware dataset curation and applies dynamic batching for efficient training. Experiments show that L0-MoE achieves up to 2.5x speedup over dense models while maintaining competitive performance, outperforming existing LLM acceleration baselines.

AI.tldr: L0-MoE is a lightweight Mixture-of-Experts approach that uses L0-regularization to accelerate dense LLMs with up to 2.5x speedup and nearly no performance loss.
AI.motivation: Dense LLMs achieve strong performance but suffer from slow and costly inference. Existing acceleration methods cause noticeable performance degradation, and standard MoE models demand extensive computational resources.
AI.method: The authors propose L0-MoE, a lightweight MoE approach employing L0-regularization to convert/accelerate dense LLMs. It introduces a cluster confusion matrix for domain-aware dataset curation and applies dynamic batching for efficient training.
AI.result: Experiments show L0-MoE achieves up to 2.5x speedup over dense models while maintaining competitive performance, outperforming existing LLM acceleration baselines.
AI.conclusion: L0-MoE offers an effective, lightweight acceleration strategy for dense LLMs, delivering substantial speedup with minimal performance loss and surpassing prior acceleration baselines.

title: Fewer Steps, Better Actions: Rethinking Flow-Matching Inference for VLA Policies
summary: Vision-language-action (VLA) policies based on flow matching generate action chunks through repeated evaluations of an action expert. Increasing the number of integration steps raises inference cost, but does not necessarily improve closed-loop success. We propose Coda, which reallocates part of this integration budget to a single learned endpoint correction. A frozen policy first completes a few-step noise-to-action trajectory; a lightweight Transformer then predicts a demonstration-supervised residual using the candidate action, source noise, and shared observation-prefix cache. Only the corrector is trained. On 50 RoboTwin Easy tasks, five-step Coda improves success from 71.64% to 74.68% over the matched five-step baseline, while reducing forward latency by 30.2% relative to the default ten-step policy. A two-step configuration achieves 71.88% success with a 2.12$\times$ speedup. An independent 13-task control shows a 5.69-percentage-point gain at nearly equal latency, supporting correction as an effective alternative to additional integration. The same design also improves frozen official SmolVLA, raising two-step success from 60.8% to 69.4%. These results show that endpoint correction improves the quality-latency trade-off of frozen flow-matching policies.

AI.tldr: Coda reallocates part of a flow-matching VLA policy's integration budget to a single learned endpoint correction: a frozen policy runs a few-step trajectory and a lightweight Transformer predicts a demonstration-supervised residual. It improves success (71.64%→74.68% at five steps) while cutting latency (30.2% vs ten-step), and generalizes to frozen SmolVLA.
AI.motivation: Flow-matching VLA policies generate action chunks via repeated action-expert evaluations. Adding integration steps raises inference cost without reliably improving closed-loop success, so there is a need for a better quality-latency trade-off than simply increasing integration steps.
AI.method: Coda keeps the policy frozen and lets it complete a few-step noise-to-action trajectory, then uses a lightweight Transformer corrector to predict a demonstration-supervised residual from the candidate action, source noise, and a shared observation-prefix cache. Only the corrector is trained.
AI.result: On 50 RoboTwin Easy tasks, five-step Coda raises success from 71.64% to 74.68% over the matched five-step baseline and reduces forward latency by 30.2% versus the default ten-step policy. A two-step configuration reaches 71.88% success with a 2.12× speedup. An independent 13-task control shows a 5.69-point gain at nearly equal latency. The design also lifts frozen official SmolVLA two-step success from 60.8% to 69.4%.
AI.conclusion: Endpoint correction is an effective alternative to additional integration steps for frozen flow-matching policies, improving both success and latency and transferring to frozen official SmolVLA.

title: GUARD: Natural Forgetting in Large Reasoning Models via Guided Answer-Reasoning Distillation
summary: Recent advances in large reasoning models (LRMs) have made machine unlearning more challenging, as protected facts or unsafe rationales may surface in intermediate chain-of-thought (CoT) traces before the final answer is produced. Existing unlearning objectives typically suppress the target content or redirect internal representations, but they never specify how the post-forgetting trajectory should continue, which can lead to hallucinated substitutes, malformed boundaries, or repetitive outputs. We argue that LRM unlearning should instead learn a natural forgetting trajectory: a coherent non-disclosing CoT followed by a stable refusal-style answer that replace the original disclosure. To this end, we propose Guided Answer-Reasoning Distillation (GUARD), which converts model-generated unsafe disclosures into safe-exit trajectories, aligns a frozen LRM via guidance tokens, and distills the guided behavior into model parameters.To address the lack of metrics for replacement quality beyond leakage, we further introduce Natural Forgetting Reasoning Score (NFRS), which captures structural stability, fluency, and unsupported substitutes in forgotten outputs. Extensive experiments on R-TOFU and a STAR-1-derived harmful-intent setting show that GUARD substantially reduces unsafe and privacy disclosures across two widely adopted distilled LRMs while preserving reasoning utility. Codes are available at https://github.com/zeyu-Yan/GUARD

AI.tldr: GUARD reframes LRM unlearning as learning a "natural forgetting trajectory" — a coherent non-disclosing chain-of-thought plus a stable refusal answer — via guided answer-reasoning distillation, and introduces the NFRS metric to evaluate replacement quality.
AI.motivation: In large reasoning models, protected facts or unsafe rationales can leak through intermediate chain-of-thought traces before the final answer. Existing unlearning objectives only suppress target content or redirect internal representations without specifying how the post-forgetting trajectory should proceed, causing hallucinated substitutes, malformed boundaries, or repetitive outputs.
AI.method: GUARD converts model-generated unsafe disclosures into safe-exit trajectories, aligns a frozen LRM using guidance tokens, and distills the guided behavior into model parameters. The Natural Forgetting Reasoning Score (NFRS) is proposed to measure structural stability, fluency, and unsupported substitutes in forgotten outputs.
AI.result: Experiments on R-TOFU and a STAR-1-derived harmful-intent setting show GUARD substantially reduces unsafe and privacy disclosures across two widely adopted distilled LRMs while preserving reasoning utility.
AI.conclusion: Guiding LRM unlearning toward a natural forgetting trajectory with a dedicated replacement-quality metric (NFRS) is an effective approach for reducing disclosure leakage while maintaining reasoning performance.

title: Safe Real-Time Policy Steering via Noise-Space Trajectory Optimization for One-Step Generative Policies
summary: Generative robot policies can represent diverse, multimodal behaviors, but adapting pretrained policies to deployment-time constraints such as collision avoidance and orientation maintenance remains challenging. Existing inference-time steering methods typically apply gradient guidance through iterative diffusion or flow processes, which can be computationally expensive for real-time control. We propose INSPO, which formulates inference-time steering of one-step generative policies as trajectory optimization in the policy's input noise space. By optimizing the input noise while evaluating constraints on the induced state trajectory, INSPO searches the policy-induced behavior space without directly modifying generated actions. The optimization includes a regularization term that encourages solutions to remain consistent with the policy's input distribution and is solved online using population-based particle optimization. We evaluate INSPO on state- and image-based task-specific policies and generalist vision-language-action policies across Push-T, Can pick-and-place, and LIBERO-Spatial. INSPO improves task success and constraint satisfaction over best-of-N sampling and action projection, while comparing favorably with gradient-guided generation at lower runtime.

AI.tldr: INSPO steers one-step generative robot policies at inference time by optimizing in the input noise space, treating constraint satisfaction as trajectory optimization solved online via population-based particle optimization with a regularization term, achieving better success and constraint satisfaction at lower runtime than baselines.
AI.motivation: Pretrained generative robot policies can produce diverse, multimodal behaviors, but adapting them to deployment-time constraints such as collision avoidance and orientation maintenance is difficult. Existing inference-time steering methods use gradient guidance through iterative diffusion or flow processes, which are computationally expensive for real-time control.
AI.method: INSPO formulates inference-time steering of one-step generative policies as trajectory optimization in the policy's input noise space. It optimizes the input noise while evaluating constraints on the induced state trajectory, thereby searching the policy-induced behavior space without directly modifying generated actions. A regularization term keeps solutions consistent with the policy's input distribution, and the optimization is solved online using population-based particle optimization.
AI.result: Evaluated on state- and image-based task-specific policies and generalist vision-language-action policies across Push-T, Can pick-and-place, and LIBERO-Spatial. INSPO improves task success and constraint satisfaction over best-of-N sampling and action projection, and compares favorably with gradient-guided generation at lower runtime.
AI.conclusion: Steering one-step generative policies by searching the input noise space is an effective and efficient alternative to iterative gradient-guided steering, yielding higher task success and better constraint satisfaction at reduced runtime.

title: Listen Before You Speak: Response Planning from Listener Facial Reactions for Conversational Speech Generation
comment: 15 pages, 2 figures, 2026 ECCV Workshop (11th ABAW) Best Student Paper Award
summary: Conversational speech depends on dialogue context and the listener's immediately preceding behavior. We propose ReACT-TTS, a two-stage framework that uses a one-second pre-response listener facial sequence to plan the next utterance's emotion and prosody before speech realization. On a strict dyadic MELD protocol, Temporal conditioning yields higher mean macro-F1 and VAD concordance than Text-only across ten seeds, while accuracy remains essentially unchanged. Ablations show that temporal modeling performs best among the visual variants and that an explicit early-to-late difference is unnecessary; correct listener reactions also outperform cyclic mismatches on average. In a contextual-appropriateness study with 20 speech researchers, 76% of judgments prefer Temporal, 9% Text-only, and 15% report no preference. We further connect the predicted response style to a Grad-TTS backbone for end-to-end speech realization. Overall, the results support pre-response listener dynamics as complementary cues for conversational response planning. The source code is available at https://github.com/CYJ1/ReACT-TTS_public.

AI.tldr: ReACT-TTS is a two-stage framework that leverages a one-second pre-response listener facial sequence to plan the emotion and prosody of the next utterance before speech realization, showing improved contextual appropriateness over text-only conditioning.
AI.motivation: Conversational speech depends not only on dialogue context but also on the listener's immediately preceding behavior, yet conventional TTS systems typically ignore such listener-side temporal cues when planning a response.
AI.method: The authors propose ReACT-TTS, a two-stage pipeline: (1) a response-planning stage that uses a one-second pre-response listener facial sequence to predict the next utterance's emotion and prosody, and (2) a speech realization stage connecting the predicted response style to a Grad-TTS backbone. Evaluation is conducted on a strict dyadic MELD protocol, comparing Temporal (visual temporal) conditioning against Text-only conditioning across ten seeds, supplemented by ablations over visual variants (including an explicit early-to-late difference) and cyclic mismatch controls, plus a contextual-appropriateness study with 20 speech researchers.
AI.result: Temporal conditioning achieves higher mean macro-F1 and VAD concordance than Text-only across ten seeds, while accuracy remains essentially unchanged. Ablations indicate that temporal modeling is the best-performing visual variant and that an explicit early-to-late difference is unnecessary; correct listener reactions also outperform cyclic mismatches on average. In the perceptual study, 76% of judgments prefer Temporal, 9% prefer Text-only, and 15% report no preference.
AI.conclusion: Pre-response listener dynamics serve as complementary cues for conversational response planning, supporting their integration into two-stage TTS pipelines for more contextually appropriate speech synthesis. Source code is publicly available.

title: SafeStage: Evaluating Safety Before, During, and After Vision-Language-Conditioned Robot Manipulation
summary: Vision-language-conditioned robot policies integrate perception, language understanding, and control for general-purpose manipulation. However, existing evaluations often focus on task success, isolated physical constraints, semantic refusal, or realized physical damage, providing limited insight into where safety fails during closed-loop manipulation. We introduce SafeStage, a lifecycle-structured benchmark for evaluating manipulation safety before, during, and after task execution. SafeStage contains 97 purpose-built risk scenarios organized into three stages. Initial-State Hazards captures safety-relevant relations that must be resolved before manipulating the target. Execution-Time Safety evaluates unsafe contacts, trajectories, region entries, and object interactions during execution. Final-State Hazards capture unstable or otherwise unsafe conditions remaining after nominal task completion. The benchmark evaluates realized interactions using event-based and state-based checks and reports native task success independently from stage-specific safety outcomes. We evaluate representative direct-action Vision-Language-Action (VLA) policies and policies with world-model-based policies under a common closed-loop protocol. Our results demonstrate that nominal task completion frequently coexists with safety violations and that different policies exhibit distinct failure profiles across the three stages. By separating task success from safety and localizing when violations occur, SafeStage provides a unified diagnostic testbed for evaluating and improving vision-language-conditioned robot manipulation policies.

AI.tldr: SafeStage is a lifecycle-structured benchmark with 97 risk scenarios that evaluates robot manipulation safety before, during, and after task execution, separating task success from stage-specific safety outcomes and revealing that nominal completion often coexists with safety violations.
AI.motivation: Existing evaluations of vision-language-conditioned robot policies focus on task success, isolated physical constraints, semantic refusal, or realized physical damage, offering limited insight into where safety fails during closed-loop manipulation.
AI.method: SafeStage organizes 97 purpose-built risk scenarios into three stages: Initial-State Hazards (relations to resolve before manipulation), Execution-Time Safety (unsafe contacts, trajectories, region entries, object interactions), and Final-State Hazards (unsafe conditions remaining after nominal completion). It uses event-based and state-based checks and reports native task success independently from stage-specific safety outcomes, evaluating direct-action VLA policies and world-model-based policies under a common closed-loop protocol.
AI.result: Nominal task completion frequently coexists with safety violations, and different policies exhibit distinct failure profiles across the three stages.
AI.conclusion: By separating task success from safety and localizing when violations occur, SafeStage provides a unified diagnostic testbed for evaluating and improving vision-language-conditioned robot manipulation policies.

title: World Modeling in Transformers
summary: Behavioral failures can make a transformer appear to lack a world model even when it has learned faithful representations of its environment. We demonstrate this in TaxiGPT, a transformer trained on random walks through Manhattan whose failures have been interpreted as evidence of an incoherent internal map. Through mechanistic analysis and causal interventions, we show that the model represents intersections and streets, tracks its position, and uses a goal compass to navigate. We trace its failures to interference between superposed intersection features, which disrupts localization within the internal map. Affordance packing, which groups representations of intersections with the same legal moves, helps limit the consequences of these errors. Finally, we propose mechanistic indicators that we use to compare models and show that world-modeling capacities emerge at different stages of training. Our findings motivate a shift from asking whether a model has a world model to mechanistically studying its world modeling: the interacting capacities through which it represents its environment and uses those representations to guide behavior.

AI.tldr: Transformers can possess faithful internal world models yet still fail behaviorally; the paper traces TaxiGPT's failures to feature interference rather than an incoherent map, reframing world-model evaluation mechanistically.
AI.motivation: Prior work interprets a transformer's behavioral failures (e.g., TaxiGPT navigating Manhattan) as evidence that it lacks a coherent internal world model. The authors argue this inference is flawed: behavioral failure does not imply absent or unfaithful representations, so evaluation should probe internal mechanisms instead of relying on behavior alone.
AI.method: Mechanistic analysis and causal interventions on TaxiGPT, a transformer trained on random walks through Manhattan. The authors dissect how the model encodes intersections and streets, tracks its position, and employs a goal compass for navigation, and they test interventions such as affordance packing, which groups representations of intersections sharing the same legal moves.
AI.result: The model does represent intersections and streets, track position, and use a goal compass. Its failures stem from interference between superposed intersection features that disrupts localization within the internal map. Affordance packing limits the downstream consequences of these errors, and proposed mechanistic indicators reveal that world-modeling capacities emerge at different stages of training.
AI.conclusion: Behavioral failures should not be read as evidence of a missing world model. The authors advocate shifting from the binary question of whether a model has a world model to mechanistically studying its world modeling—the interacting capacities by which it represents its environment and uses those representations to guide behavior.

title: AirSplan: Risk-Aware Motion Planning for Quadrotors in Cluttered 3D Gaussian Splats
comment: To appear in the proceedings of IROS 2026
summary: Quadrotors are increasingly deployed in applications such as agriculture, infrastructure inspection, and maintenance. In each of these applications, the robot must navigate complex scene geometry while remaining strictly collision-free. Unlike in ground domains, even minor collisions for aerial vehicles can result in the loss of the robot. This safety requirement induces a pair of technical challenges. First, the environment must be represented with sufficient fidelity to encode complex structure, even when no ground-truth obstacle data is available. Second, a motion planner must leverage this representation to determine a collision-free path to the goal. This paper proposes a system that addresses these complementary challenges. The proposed method, AirSplan, adopts a normalized variant of 3D Gaussian Splatting that encodes high-fidelity scene geometry. It then applies a novel reachability-based motion planner that leverages the differential flatness of quadrotors to compute continuous-time collision constraints that tightly overapproximate the robot's occupancy. Experiments demonstrate that AirSplan successfully finds a path in 81.2% of challenging test cases, a significant improvement over the nearest baseline method's 51.2%.

AI.tldr: AirSplan combines normalized 3D Gaussian Splatting scene representation with a reachability-based motion planner using quadrotor differential flatness to generate continuous-time collision constraints, achieving 81.2% success on challenging test cases versus 51.2% for the nearest baseline.
AI.motivation: Quadrotors are increasingly used in agriculture, infrastructure inspection, and maintenance, where they must navigate complex scene geometry while remaining strictly collision-free. Unlike ground robots, even minor aerial collisions can cause loss of the robot. This safety requirement creates two challenges: representing the environment with enough fidelity to encode complex structure even without ground-truth obstacle data, and leveraging that representation in a motion planner to find a collision-free path to the goal.
AI.method: AirSplan adopts a normalized variant of 3D Gaussian Splatting to encode high-fidelity scene geometry, and applies a novel reachability-based motion planner that exploits the differential flatness of quadrotors to compute continuous-time collision constraints tightly overapproximating the robot's occupancy.
AI.result: AirSplan finds a path in 81.2% of challenging test cases, a significant improvement over the nearest baseline's 51.2%.
