AI.conclusion: AirSplan addresses the complementary challenges of high-fidelity scene representation and collision-free planning for quadrotors, demonstrating substantially higher success rates than the nearest baseline on challenging test cases.

title: ECG Mirage: Revealing and Mitigating the Underutilisation of ECGs in Vision-Language Models for Clinical Prediction
summary: Emergency department (ED) decision-making relies on heterogeneous clinical information, including patient history, vital signs, laboratory results, and electrocardiograms (ECGs). Vision--language models (VLMs) can jointly process these modalities, but strong predictive performance does not necessarily imply meaningful use of the correct patient's ECG. We term this failure mode ECG Mirage: apparent multimodal capability without useful dependence on patient-specific ECG information. We distinguish two forms: ECG neglect, where ECGs provide little predictive benefit, and ECG confusion, where matched ECGs outperform no-image inputs but not mismatched ECGs. To evaluate these behaviours, we compare predictions obtained with matched ECGs, outcome-discordant mismatched ECGs, and no-image inputs while holding the clinical text and prediction targets fixed. Across four VLMs on MDS-ED, matched ECGs provide no consistent advantage for either ICU admission or clinical deterioration prediction. We then train four restricted visual prompts using supervised learning followed by conditional direct preference optimisation, while keeping the VLM backbone frozen. The resulting models achieve balanced accuracies of 70.6% for ICU admission and 67.5% for deterioration and increase the matched-versus-mismatched performance gap to approximately 16.5 and 5.5 percentage points, respectively. Overall, our study identifies ECG Mirage in multimodal clinical prediction and introduces visual prompt tuning as an efficient mitigation strategy.

AI.tldr: This study identifies "ECG Mirage," a failure mode where vision-language models (VLMs) appear to leverage ECG data in emergency department prediction but actually do not depend on patient-specific ECG information; it distinguishes ECG neglect from ECG confusion, demonstrates the problem across four VLMs on the MDS-ED dataset, and mitigates it via restricted visual prompt tuning (supervised learning plus conditional DPO) with a frozen backbone.
AI.motivation: ED decision-making integrates heterogeneous clinical data (history, vital signs, labs, ECGs), and VLMs can process these modalities jointly. However, strong predictive performance does not guarantee that a model meaningfully uses the correct patient's ECG, so the authors aim to formalize and detect this misleading behavior—termed ECG Mirage—and to provide an efficient mitigation strategy.
AI.method: The authors define ECG Mirage with two forms: ECG neglect (ECGs give little predictive benefit) and ECG confusion (matched ECGs beat no-image inputs but not mismatched ECGs). They compare predictions under three conditions—matched ECGs, outcome-discordant mismatched ECGs, and no-image inputs—while holding clinical text and prediction targets fixed. They evaluate four VLMs on the MDS-ED dataset for ICU admission and clinical deterioration prediction. To mitigate the issue, they train four restricted visual prompts using supervised learning followed by conditional direct preference optimisation, keeping the VLM backbone frozen.
AI.result: Across four VLMs on MDS-ED, matched ECGs provide no consistent advantage for either ICU admission or clinical deterioration prediction. The trained visual-prompt models achieve balanced accuracies of 70.6% for ICU admission and 67.5% for deterioration, and increase the matched-versus-mismatched performance gap to approximately 16.5 and 5.5 percentage points, respectively.
AI.conclusion: The study identifies ECG Mirage in multimodal clinical prediction and introduces visual prompt tuning as an efficient mitigation strategy, showing that restricted visual prompts can induce genuine, patient-specific ECG dependence without fine-tuning the VLM backbone.

title: FOCAL-VLA: Subtask-Guided Geometry Distillation and Implicit World Modeling for Vision-Language-Action Models
summary: Vision-language-action (VLA) models built on pretrained vision-language models have demonstrated strong performance across diverse robotic manipulation tasks. However, VLA models that directly map current 2D observations to actions often lack sufficient spatial and temporal understanding, limiting their performance in precise and long-horizon manipulation. Recent methods enhance VLA models through geometric supervision and future-state prediction across the entire scene. However, these methods can suffer from redundant scene information, distracting the model from learning the geometry and dynamics relevant to the current interaction. To address this issue, we propose FOCAL-VLA, a framework that combines subtask-guided geometry distillation with implicit world modeling to learn representations of current spatial structure and future interaction dynamics. To focus geometric learning on the current subtask, we transfer geometric knowledge from VGGT to the VLA model by aligning geometry latents with features from subtask-relevant image regions. To capture the future 3D evolution of the current interaction, we incorporate implicit world modeling using Track4World features from current and future demonstration frames. The two complementary representations jointly guide action generation without running VGGT or Track4World at inference time. Experiments show that FOCAL-VLA outperforms baselines on both simulation benchmarks and real-world manipulation tasks. Project website: https://zhiyuan-gao.github.io/FOCAL-VLA/.

AI.tldr: FOCAL-VLA is a vision-language-action framework that combines subtask-guided geometry distillation with implicit world modeling to improve precise and long-horizon robotic manipulation, achieving gains on simulation benchmarks and real-world tasks.
AI.motivation: VLA models mapping current 2D observations directly to actions lack spatial and temporal understanding. Existing enhancement methods using geometric supervision and future-state prediction suffer from redundant scene information, which distracts the model from learning geometry and dynamics relevant to the current interaction.
AI.method: FOCAL-VLA combines subtask-guided geometry distillation with implicit world modeling. It transfers geometric knowledge from VGGT to the VLA model by aligning geometry latents with features from subtask-relevant image regions, and incorporates implicit world modeling using Track4World features from current and future demonstration frames. These complementary representations jointly guide action generation without running VGGT or Track4World at inference.
AI.result: FOCAL-VLA outperforms baselines on both simulation benchmarks and real-world manipulation tasks.
AI.conclusion: Focusing geometric and dynamic learning on the current subtask and interaction yields more effective VLA representations, improving precise and long-horizon manipulation while avoiding inference-time overhead from auxiliary models.

title: LLM-Generated Feature Pools for Time Series Anomaly Detection
summary: We study how far a simple statistical pipeline can go on univariate time series anomaly detection under a strict selection protocol. The method extracts a small pool of statistics over sliding windows, scores each window with a transductive robust (MAD) model, and selects a feature subset per domain on a held-out tuning split. On TSB-AD-U it reaches $0.529$ per-series VUS-PR, above the best neural ($0.45$) and statistical ($0.44$) entries on the public leaderboard and within $0.06$ of the strongest pretrained foundation model, several of which use more supervision than ours. Ablations locate the cause: across three selection strategies and a hindsight oracle the score moves by $0.031$, and across the aggregation grid by $0.096$, while changing the candidate pool moves it by $0.226$. The candidate pool sets the ceiling; the search over it is second-order. We therefore generate a pool per domain by prompting a multimodal LLM with in-context example windows from that domain. The generated pools match the hand-crafted one under matched selection, and the two cover different domains: selecting over their union improves on the generated pool in all twelve generator-seed pairs and lifts the pipeline to $0.588$, matching the performance of the best entry on the leaderboard.

AI.tldr: A simple statistical pipeline with MAD scoring and per-domain feature selection achieves 0.529 VUS-PR on TSB-AD-U, and generating the candidate feature pool via a multimodal LLM plus union selection lifts it to 0.588, matching the best leaderboard entry.
AI.motivation: The paper asks how far a simple statistical pipeline can go on univariate time series anomaly detection under a strict selection protocol, and investigates which design choice limits performance.
AI.method: Extract a small pool of statistics over sliding windows, score each window with a transductive robust (MAD) model, and select a feature subset per domain on a held-out tuning split. Ablations compare three selection strategies, a hindsight oracle, and an aggregation grid vs. the candidate pool. A pool is also generated per domain by prompting a multimodal LLM with in-context example windows from that domain.
AI.result: TSB-AD-U: 0.529 per-series VUS-PR, above best neural (0.45) and statistical (0.44) entries, within 0.06 of the strongest pretrained foundation model. Ablations: selection strategy varies score by 0.031, aggregation grid by 0.096, candidate pool by 0.226. Generated pools match hand-crafted under matched selection and cover different domains; selecting over their union improves on the generated pool in all twelve generator-seed pairs and lifts the pipeline to 0.588, matching the best leaderboard entry.
AI.conclusion: The candidate pool sets the ceiling while the search over it is second-order. LLM-generated pools are complementary to hand-crafted ones, and selecting over their union delivers leaderboard-best performance.

title: KnowDemo: Knowledge-Guided Robot Demonstration Generation from Human Videos
summary: Learning robot manipulation policies typically requires substantial demonstration data, which are costly to collect on real robots. Recent methods generate robot demonstrations from human videos by adapting recovered motion and validating the resulting trajectories in simulation. However, methods centered on motion-reference adaptation can limit behavioral diversity by retaining the demonstrated contact strategies and subtask orders, while insufficient understanding of task requirements and scene relations can reduce demonstration generation efficiency by generating invalid candidates. To address these limitations, we propose KnowDemo, a framework that uses structured manipulation knowledge from human videos to generate diverse robot demonstrations for a target workspace. To distinguish task requirements from demonstration-specific choices, we develop a knowledge extraction and reasoning module based on a vision-language model (VLM) that associates object and action descriptions with inferred task conditions, demonstration references, and permissible execution variations. To translate this knowledge into executable demonstrations, we resolve the descriptions against target-scene entities and geometry to guide candidate generation and screening before motion planning and simulation. The resulting demonstrations exhibit multimodal behavior through alternative contact strategies and valid subtask orders, with structured execution labels. Experiments demonstrate additional verified execution modes beyond a reference-only configuration and improved candidate planning success through task-guided grasp sampling. To validate the generated data for policy learning, we fine-tune the pretrained $π_{0.5}$ model on simulation data, achieving sim-to-real transfer across three tasks. Project page: https://zhiyuan-gao.github.io/knowdemo/

AI.tldr: KnowDemo uses structured manipulation knowledge extracted from human videos via a VLM to generate diverse, valid robot demonstrations for a target workspace, improving execution-mode coverage and planning success, and enabling sim-to-real policy transfer on three tasks.
AI.motivation: Collecting robot demonstration data on real hardware is costly. Existing human-video-to-robot demonstration methods rely on motion-reference adaptation, which limits behavioral diversity by preserving demonstrated contact strategies and subtask orders, and suffers from low generation efficiency due to insufficient understanding of task requirements and scene relations, producing invalid candidates.
AI.method: KnowDemo extracts structured manipulation knowledge from human videos using a VLM-based extraction and reasoning module that links object and action descriptions to inferred task conditions, demonstration references, and permissible execution variations, separating task requirements from demonstration-specific choices. This knowledge is then grounded against target-scene entities and geometry to guide candidate generation and screening prior to motion planning and simulation, yielding demonstrations with structured execution labels covering alternative contact strategies and valid subtask orders.
AI.result: Experiments show additional verified execution modes beyond a reference-only configuration and improved candidate planning success via task-guided grasp sampling. Fine-tuning the pretrained π0.5 model on the generated simulation data achieves sim-to-real transfer across three tasks.
AI.conclusion: Structured, task-level manipulation knowledge from human videos can drive diverse and valid robot demonstration generation and produce data effective for policy learning and sim-to-real transfer.

title: MIST: Multimodal Survival Prediction with Genomic-Guided Histology Attention
comment: Accepted at the COMPAYL 2026 Workshop on Computational Pathology and Multimodal Data at MICCAI 2026. 11 pages, 2 figures, 4 tables
summary: Multimodal survival models can combine complementary prognostic information from whole-slide images and genomic profiles, but effective fusion remains challenging amid external cohort shift and computational complexity. To address these challenges, we propose MIST, multimodal survival prediction with genomic-guided histology attention. MIST represents genomic features as tokens and allows them to query compact foundation-model-derived histology context tokens before survival prediction. This design enriches molecular information with histology context rather than merging separately encoded modalities only at the final stage. Training combines discrete-time survival prediction with genomic feature masking, WSI dropout, and paired WSI-genomics contrastive alignment. Across four external evaluations in colon, renal, lung, and glioblastoma cohorts, MIST improves external C-index over standard fusion baselines in the primary comparisons. These results support genomic-guided histology attention as a compact and effective strategy for multimodal oncology outcome prediction. Our code is available at https://github.com/samiyavuuz/MIST .

AI.tldr: MIST is a multimodal survival prediction model that uses genomic features as query tokens to attend over compact histology context tokens derived from foundation models, improving external generalization over standard late-fusion baselines across four cancer cohorts.
AI.motivation: Multimodal survival models can combine complementary prognostic information from whole-slide images (WSIs) and genomic profiles, but effective fusion is difficult due to external cohort shift (poor generalization) and computational complexity. Existing approaches typically merge separately encoded modalities only at the final stage.
AI.method: MIST represents genomic features as tokens and lets them query compact foundation-model-derived histology context tokens before survival prediction, enriching molecular information with histology context early rather than late merging. Training combines discrete-time survival prediction with genomic feature masking, WSI dropout, and paired WSI-genomics contrastive alignment.
AI.result: Across four external evaluations in colon, renal, lung, and glioblastoma cohorts, MIST improves external C-index over standard fusion baselines in the primary comparisons.
AI.conclusion: Genomic-guided histology attention is a compact and effective strategy for multimodal oncology outcome prediction. Code is available at https://github.com/samiyavuuz/MIST.

title: VLA-Scope: Shift-Aware Failure Prediction for Vision-Language-Action Models
summary: Vision-language-action (VLA) models map visual observations and natural-language instructions to robotic actions, but distribution shifts can compromise their reliability. Because these models may still succeed under out-of-distribution (OOD) conditions, detecting OOD inputs alone is insufficient to predict execution failure. In this paper, we introduce VLA-Scope, a two-stage framework that combines input-shift characterization with execution history to predict failure during OOD rollouts. The first stage uses pooled image and language representations to detect OOD inputs and classify their shift categories. For inputs flagged as OOD, the second stage combines the predicted category, action-prefix features, and execution progress features. A logistic regression model shared across shift categories updates failure risk as execution proceeds. We evaluate the framework with OpenVLA on ten LIBERO-Spatial tasks using leave-one-group-out cross-validation. OOD detection achieves a ROC-AUC of 0.9454, and shift classification achieves 91% accuracy. Evaluated independently of the OOD gate on all 1,400 OOD rollouts, the failure predictor achieves a ROC-AUC of 0.8497 after 60 executed actions, compared with 0.7906 without execution progress features. It also achieves a higher ROC-AUC than the evaluated ActProbe and SAFE-MLP baselines. These results suggest that combining action features with temporally aggregated execution step representations improves failure prediction under input shifts.

AI.tldr: VLA-Scope is a two-stage framework that detects out-of-distribution inputs and predicts execution failure during OOD rollouts by combining shift category, action-prefix, and execution-progress features, achieving high OOD detection and competitive failure prediction on OpenVLA/LIBERO-Spatial.
AI.motivation: VLA models can fail under distribution shifts, yet they may also still succeed under OOD conditions, so detecting OOD inputs alone cannot reliably predict execution failure. A method is needed that predicts failure during OOD rollouts rather than only flagging shifted inputs.
AI.method: A two-stage framework: Stage 1 detects OOD inputs and classifies their shift categories using pooled image and language representations. Stage 2, applied to flagged OOD inputs, combines the predicted shift category, action-prefix features, and execution-progress features, using a logistic regression model shared across shift categories that updates failure risk as execution proceeds.
AI.result: Evaluated with OpenVLA on ten LIBERO-Spatial tasks using leave-one-group-out cross-validation. OOD detection reaches ROC-AUC 0.9454; shift classification reaches 91% accuracy. Evaluated independently of the OOD gate on all 1,400 OOD rollouts, the failure predictor reaches ROC-AUC 0.8497 after 60 executed actions (vs. 0.7906 without execution-progress features) and outperforms ActProbe and SAFE-MLP baselines.
AI.conclusion: Combining action features with temporally aggregated execution-step representations improves failure prediction under input shifts, showing that input-shift characterization plus execution history is effective for predicting VLA execution failure during OOD rollouts.

title: EnterpriseVal: Quantifying the Efficacy, Reliability and Value of Generative AI in the Enterprise
summary: Frontier language models now produce professional deliverables that expert graders judge to match human work on a substantial share of economically valuable tasks, yet most enterprise GenAI initiatives fail to show a measurable business effect and a large fraction of agentic projects are expected to be cancelled. We argue that this is substantially a measurement problem: public benchmarks answer "what can the model do?", whereas a deployment decision requires "is this workflow fit, reliable, safe and worth scaling - here, on our data, under our controls?". We present EnterpriseVal, a use-case-level evaluation system that closes this gap. It comprises (i) a formal specification of the use case and of the frozen socio-technical configuration under test, model, prompts, retrieval, tools, guardrails and human oversight, with an autonomy level and consequence tier that jointly set the required evaluation intensity; (ii) a metric catalogue spanning fidelity, utility, efficiency, reliability, assurance and oversight; (iii) a grading protocol that scales blinded expert judgement with calibrated LLM-as-judge scoring through prediction-powered inference; (iv) a two-tier threshold gate, stated as an executable algorithm, that maps metric vectors with confidence bounds to REJECT/CONDITIONAL/SCALE decisions; and (v) a value-and-risk model in which the reviewer catch rate is a measured parameter. We report a pilot across three workflows in a global bank. In credit-memo drafting, human-graded citation precision reached 88% and hallucination rate 1.6% for the best model against gates of 70% and 5%; in procedure transformation, analyst refinement effort fell from an estimated 27.4 to 2.9 hours per document. We separate established results, documented pilot evidence, the proposed system and open hypotheses, and specify the experiments required for full validation

AI.tldr: EnterpriseVal is a use-case-level evaluation system that reframes enterprise GenAI deployment as a measurement problem, combining a formal specification of the frozen socio-technical configuration, a six-dimension metric catalogue, calibrated expert/LLM-as-judge grading via prediction-powered inference, an executable two-tier threshold gate mapping metric vectors to REJECT/CONDITIONAL/SCALE decisions, and a value-and-risk model, piloted across three banking workflows.
AI.motivation: Frontier models now match human work on many economically valuable tasks, yet most enterprise GenAI initiatives show no measurable business effect and many agentic projects face cancellation. The authors attribute this to a measurement gap: public benchmarks answer what a model can do, whereas deployment decisions require knowing whether a specific workflow is fit, reliable, safe, and worth scaling on the organization's own data and controls.
AI.method: The proposed system has five components: (i) formal specification of the use case and the frozen socio-technical configuration under test (model, prompts, retrieval, tools, guardrails, human oversight), with an autonomy level and consequence tier setting required evaluation intensity; (ii) a metric catalogue covering fidelity, utility, efficiency, reliability, assurance, and oversight; (iii) a grading protocol scaling blinded expert judgement with calibrated LLM-as-judge scoring through prediction-powered inference; (iv) a two-tier threshold gate stated as an executable algorithm mapping metric vectors with confidence bounds to REJECT/CONDITIONAL/SCALE decisions; (v) a value-and-risk model treating reviewer catch rate as a measured parameter.
AI.result: A pilot across three workflows at a global bank is reported. In credit-memo drafting, the best model reached human-graded citation precision of 88% and a 1.6% hallucination rate, against gates of 70% and 5%. In procedure transformation, analyst refinement effort dropped from an estimated 27.4 to 2.9 hours per document.
AI.conclusion: The work separates established results, documented pilot evidence, the proposed system, and open hypotheses, and specifies the experiments required for full validation of the evaluation framework. Interpretation should be constrained accordingly, since only the pilot evidence is empirically documented.

title: LOInK: Learned Optimal Inverse Kinematics via Structured Neural Surrogate Models
summary: We introduce Learned Optimal Inverse Kinematics (LOInK), a method to generate approximately optimal solutions to an inverse kinematics problem. When trained on data consisting of sampled configurations and associated task variables and a given cost function, LOInK learns a bi-Lipschitz invertible mapping from configuration space to a decoupled task/latent space, and moreover, the latent space is structured so as to place cost-minimizing solutions at the origin. This enables efficient sampling of cost-minimizing solutions via a network-inversion algorithm based on operator splitting. We demonstrate the proposed approach on three problems: an illustrative three degree-of-freedom manipulator problem; a quadrupedal climbing robot for which LOInK can generate near-optimal solutions on average 31 times faster and up to 100 times faster than a constrained optimization approach; and a simulated soft actuator as a purely data-driven example, in which LOInK can explicitly generate high-quality solutions, unlike existing generative approaches that require diverse sampling and evaluation of candidate solutions.

AI.tldr: LOInK learns a bi-Lipschitz invertible mapping from configuration space to a decoupled task/latent space, placing cost-minimizing solutions at the origin, enabling efficient near-optimal inverse kinematics sampling via an operator-splitting network-inversion algorithm.
AI.motivation: Optimal inverse kinematics requires solving constrained optimization, which is computationally expensive. The paper seeks a fast, data-driven approach that yields approximately optimal solutions without costly online optimization or sampling-and-evaluation of candidates.
AI.method: Train on sampled configurations, associated task variables, and a given cost function to learn a bi-Lipschitz invertible mapping from configuration space to a decoupled task/latent space. Structure the latent space so cost-minimizing solutions lie at the origin, then sample cost-minimizing solutions via a network-inversion algorithm based on operator splitting.
AI.result: Evaluated on three problems: an illustrative 3-DoF manipulator; a quadrupedal climbing robot, where LOInK generates near-optimal solutions on average 31x faster and up to 100x faster than constrained optimization; and a simulated soft actuator, a purely data-driven case where LOInK explicitly generates high-quality solutions, unlike generative approaches requiring diverse sampling and candidate evaluation.
AI.conclusion: LOInK provides an efficient, data-driven method for generating approximately optimal inverse kinematics solutions, outperforming constrained optimization in speed and explicitly producing high-quality solutions where sampling-based generative methods cannot.

title: AutoRecLab: Describe the Experiment, Get the Code!
comment: Accepted at the 20th ACM Conference on Recommender Systems (RecSys '26), Demo Track. 4 pages, 2 figures
summary: Empirical evaluation is central to recommender-systems (RecSys) research, but turning experimental designs into executable code remains a manual and error-prone task. We present AutoRecLab, a Python-based autonomous RecSys lab that automates RecSys experiments from natural-language prompts. Given a research idea, AutoRecLab derives explicit experiment requirements, builds and validates a prototype, and iteratively expands it into the requested full experiment. The workflow combines retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) for documentation lookup, static type verification, and execution-steered tree search. In our demonstration, AutoRecLab autonomously implements an explicit-to-implicit feedback conversion study. In a baseline comparison across six algorithms and three datasets, 8 of 9 runs succeed at an average cost of approx- imately $1 per run with GPT-5.4-mini.

AI.tldr: AutoRecLab is a Python-based autonomous RecSys lab that turns natural-language research ideas into executable recommender-systems experiments via RAG, static type verification, and execution-steered tree search, achieving 8/9 successful baseline runs at ~$1 each with GPT-5.4-mini.
AI.motivation: Empirical evaluation is central to RecSys research, yet converting experimental designs into executable code remains manual and error-prone, motivating an autonomous system to automate this process.
AI.method: Given a natural-language prompt, AutoRecLab derives explicit experiment requirements, builds and validates a prototype, then iteratively expands it into the full experiment. The workflow integrates retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) for documentation lookup, static type verification, and execution-steered tree search.
AI.result: In a demonstration, AutoRecLab autonomously implemented an explicit-to-implicit feedback conversion study. In a baseline comparison across six algorithms and three datasets, 8 of 9 runs succeeded at an average cost of approximately $1 per run with GPT-5.4-mini.
AI.conclusion: AutoRecLab demonstrates that autonomous, cost-effective automation of RecSys experiments from natural-language prompts is feasible, reducing manual and error-prone implementation effort.

title: Stability-aware Residual Reinforcement Learning Framework for Robotic Manipulator Disturbance Compensation
summary: Although conventional controllers and disturbance observers (DOBs) are the standard for precision tracking in manipulators, they suffer from parameter uncertainty, nonlinear friction, and compound disturbances. This study proposes a residual reinforcement learning DOB framework that pairs an analytical observer with an RL policy. The deterministic baseline operates within a reliable region, whereas the RL policy explicitly targets the residuals that the model cannot capture. To make this compensation disturbance-aware, an estimator network aligns the observation history with a privileged disturbance context, organizing the latent space by disturbance regime and enabling rapid adaptation across disturbance transitions. To guarantee stability, we derived and enforced a state-dependent action bound on the RL policy from an input-to-state stability (ISS) analysis such that the closed loop provably confines the tracking error to a certified envelope for arbitrary policy outputs. Experiments on a 6-DOF manipulator demonstrated consistent improvements in disturbance estimation and tracking, including a 27.8% tracking-error reduction on real hardware under zero-shot sim-to-real transfer and a 38.0% reduction under a base-vibration disturbance that was not observed during training.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a residual RL disturbance-observer framework: an analytical DOB handles the reliable baseline while an RL policy compensates unmodeled residuals, guided by a disturbance-aware estimator network and constrained by an ISS-derived state-dependent action bound that certifies a bounded tracking error.
AI.motivation: Conventional controllers and disturbance observers, though standard for precision tracking in manipulators, degrade under parameter uncertainty, nonlinear friction, and compound disturbances. Purely model-based observers cannot capture residual dynamics, motivating a hybrid approach that augments the analytical observer with learned compensation.
AI.method: The framework pairs a deterministic analytical observer (operating in a reliable region) with an RL policy that explicitly targets residuals the model cannot capture. A disturbance-aware estimator network aligns observation history with a privileged disturbance context, organizing the latent space by disturbance regime to enable fast adaptation across disturbance transitions. Stability is guaranteed by deriving a state-dependent action bound on the RL policy from an input-to-state stability (ISS) analysis, provably confining tracking error to a certified envelope for arbitrary policy outputs.
AI.result: Experiments on a 6-DOF manipulator showed consistent improvements in disturbance estimation and tracking, including a 27.8% tracking-error reduction on real hardware under zero-shot sim-to-real transfer and a 38.0% reduction under a base-vibration disturbance unseen during training.
AI.conclusion: Residual RL compensation layered on an analytical DOB, combined with disturbance-aware latent organization and ISS-based action bounding, delivers certified stability and robust precision tracking under unmodeled and unseen disturbances, with effective zero-shot sim-to-real transfer.

title: What Should We Ask Next? Retrieval-Aware Question Learning under Partial Evidence
summary: Interactive retrieval under partial evidence is a sequential information-acquisition problem: an agent must decide which question will create the most useful evidence for the next retrieval update. Existing systems train this decision by imitating an offline ordering of candidate QA pairs, although question value is determined by the response it elicits and its downstream effect on retrieval. We establish that candidate discriminativeness and perceived usefulness provide weak supervision for this objective, then introduce RAVEL, a retrieval-aware online reinforcement learning framework for interactive person re-identification. RAVEL initializes from supervised question generation, observes the current Top-4 candidates directly, and optimizes the question policy with rank feedback from the full question-answer-retrieval loop. Experiments on Interactive-PEDES show that RAVEL delivers progressively stronger retrieval performance across five interaction rounds. Further analysis shows that RAVEL reallocates the questioning budget toward localized open-ended attributes, which provide more useful retrieval evidence and yield the largest gains on initially difficult queries.

AI.tldr: RAVEL frames interactive retrieval under partial evidence as sequential information acquisition and trains the question policy with online reinforcement learning using rank feedback from the full question-answer-retrieval loop.
AI.motivation: Existing systems train the question-selection decision by imitating an offline ordering of candidate QA pairs. However, question value is actually determined by the response it elicits and its downstream effect on retrieval, making candidate discriminativeness and perceived usefulness only weak supervision for this objective.
AI.method: RAVEL is a retrieval-aware online reinforcement learning framework for interactive person re-identification. It initializes from supervised question generation, directly observes the current Top-4 candidates, and optimizes the question policy using rank feedback from the full question-answer-retrieval loop.
AI.result: On Interactive-PEDES, RAVEL delivers progressively stronger retrieval performance across five interaction rounds. Analysis shows it reallocates the questioning budget toward localized open-ended attributes, which provide more useful retrieval evidence and yield the largest gains on initially difficult queries.
AI.conclusion: Modeling question value through online reinforcement learning on downstream retrieval rank feedback, rather than offline QA-pair imitation, improves interactive retrieval, especially for difficult queries.

title: NaViRrator: Robot Navigation from Human-Readable Maps through a Learned Visual Route
summary: Human-readable maps provide an intuitive interface for specifying robot destinations, but connecting their schematic geometry to egocentric observations remains challenging. We present NaViRRator, a framework that translates user-specified start and goal locations on such maps into navigation instructions for a pretrained vision-and-language navigation (VLN) policy. Its core method, RouteScribe, separates route inference from verbalization by first generating an explicit route scaffold in map-image coordinates, which a pretrained vision-language model (VLM) converts into a navigation instruction. We construct the scaffold with start--goal line conditional flow matching (SGL-CFM), which deforms a straight start--goal waypoint sequence into a map-conditioned route. During execution, the VLN policy receives only the instruction and egocentric observations, while the map and scaffold remain upstream, allowing executor replacement without retraining the map-to-language modules. Real-world experiments show higher success rates and success weighted by path length (SPL) than direct map-to-instruction generation, A*-based scaffolding, and Gaussian-source conditional flow matching. Qualitative results further show clearer salient turns and better preservation of the intended maneuver sequence, supporting route-grounded language as a modular interface between human-readable maps and pretrained navigation policies.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces NaViRRator, a framework that converts user-specified start/goal points on human-readable maps into navigation instructions for a pretrained VLN policy, using RouteScribe to separate route inference (via SGL-CFM) from verbalization (via a VLM).
AI.motivation: Human-readable maps offer an intuitive way to specify robot destinations, but linking their schematic geometry to egocentric observations is difficult. Bridging this gap would let users leverage such maps with pretrained navigation policies.
AI.method: NaViRRator's core is RouteScribe, which decouples route inference from verbalization. It first generates an explicit route scaffold in map-image coordinates using start-goal line conditional flow matching (SGL-CFM), deforming a straight start-goal waypoint sequence into a map-conditioned route. A pretrained VLM then converts this scaffold into a navigation instruction. At execution, the VLN policy receives only the instruction and egocentric observations, keeping map and scaffold upstream and enabling executor replacement without retraining the map-to-language modules.
AI.result: Real-world experiments show higher success rates and SPL than direct map-to-instruction generation, A*-based scaffolding, and Gaussian-source conditional flow matching. Qualitative results show clearer salient turns and better preservation of the intended maneuver sequence.
AI.conclusion: Route-grounded language serves as a modular interface between human-readable maps and pretrained navigation policies, improving navigation performance and instruction quality.

title: AutoViewMem: Self-Configuring Orthogonal Views for Conversational Long-Term Memory
summary: Long-term memory is essential for large language model (LLM) agents to maintain consistency and personalization over extended interactions. Existing memory systems typically rely on fixed granularities or static schemas, but these designs struggle when heterogeneous information, such as preferences, events, constraints, and temporal updates, is embedded in a single mixed representation. The resulting semantic interference makes top-K retrieval sensitive to noise and often leaves relevant evidence poorly ranked. We present AutoViewMem, a data-driven framework that organizes long-term conversational memory into self-configuring, low-overlap semantic views before indexing. AutoViewMem discovers candidate views from interaction traces, selects a compact complementary view set, and uses these views to guide write-time structured extraction of provenance-grounded memories. This representation-first design moves semantic disentanglement from retrieval time to write time, allowing standard top-K similarity search to retrieve focused evidence without explicit routing or iterative retrieval. We further apply offline consolidation to improve memory compactness and consistency. Experiments on the LoCoMo and PersonaMem benchmarks, under both Qwen3-8B and Qwen3-14B backbones, show that AutoViewMem improves long-horizon question answering and personalization over strong memory baselines while preserving a simple inference pipeline.

AI.tldr: AutoViewMem is a data-driven memory framework that organizes long-term conversational memory into self-configuring, low-overlap semantic views at write time, enabling standard top-K retrieval to surface focused evidence without routing or iterative retrieval.
AI.motivation: LLM agents need long-term memory for consistency and personalization, but existing systems use fixed granularities or static schemas. When heterogeneous information (preferences, events, constraints, temporal updates) is mixed into one representation, semantic interference makes top-K retrieval noise-sensitive and misranks relevant evidence.
AI.method: AutoViewMem discovers candidate views from interaction traces, selects a compact complementary view set, and uses these views to guide write-time structured extraction of provenance-grounded memories. This representation-first design shifts semantic disentanglement from retrieval time to write time. Offline consolidation is additionally applied to improve memory compactness and consistency.
AI.result: On LoCoMo and PersonaMem benchmarks with Qwen3-8B and Qwen3-14B backbones, AutoViewMem improves long-horizon question answering and personalization over strong memory baselines while keeping a simple inference pipeline.
AI.conclusion: Organizing memory into self-configuring, low-overlap semantic views at write time is an effective, data-driven alternative to fixed-granularity or static-schema memory, delivering better long-horizon QA and personalization without added inference complexity.

title: LEMCA: LLM-Guided Synthesis of Efficient Mode-Switching Control Architectures
summary: Physical control tasks in the natural world, such as driving or object manipulation, frequently exhibit dramatic variations in sensory and compute complexity over time. Correspondingly, a natural resource-efficient choice for robot control is to dynamically switch between control modes with varying resource allocations. However, such "mode-switching controllers" (MSCs) have historically required laborious, expert-driven design and synthesis for each new task. Driven by these design difficulties, modern robotic control architectures often fall back to a wasteful "monolithic" one-size-fits-all structure, where resource allocation is permanently anchored to the hardest, most resource-intensive task phases. To facilitate the design of performant yet efficient MSCs, we propose LLM-Guided synthesis of Efficient Mode-Switching Control Architectures (LEMCA). LEMCA represents MSC designs as interpretable programs to be iteratively refined in an evolutionary loop. To evaluate design fitness, we propose MSC-compatible extensions of automated controller synthesis approaches, such as reinforcement learning in simulation. LEMCA then leverages the semantic priors, reasoning, and coding capabilities of Large Language Models (LLMs) to iteratively edit controller modes, their corresponding sensory-compute resource allocations, and mode transitions. Our experiments across diverse control benchmarks show that LEMCA consistently discovers strategies that surpass the Pareto frontier of monolithic designs by reclaiming wasted resources during "easy" task phases. LEMCA thus presents an automated, low-effort path to synthesize resource-efficient MSC designs.

AI.tldr: LEMCA uses LLMs to automatically synthesize mode-switching robot control architectures that dynamically reallocate sensory and compute resources, outperforming monolithic controllers on the Pareto frontier.
AI.motivation: Physical control tasks vary greatly in sensory and compute complexity over time, so switching between control modes with different resource allocations is naturally efficient. However, designing such mode-switching controllers (MSCs) has required laborious expert effort per task, leading modern architectures to adopt wasteful monolithic designs permanently sized for the hardest phases.
AI.method: LEMCA represents MSC designs as interpretable programs refined in an evolutionary loop. Fitness is evaluated via MSC-compatible extensions of automated controller synthesis (e.g., reinforcement learning in simulation). LLMs then iteratively edit controller modes, their sensory-compute resource allocations, and mode transitions using semantic priors, reasoning, and coding abilities.
AI.result: Across diverse control benchmarks, LEMCA consistently discovered strategies surpassing the Pareto frontier of monolithic designs by reclaiming resources wasted during easy task phases.
AI.conclusion: LEMCA offers an automated, low-effort path to synthesize resource-efficient mode-switching control designs.

title: Learning Cardiac Features: ECG Biometrics Across Time and~Exercise
summary: Electrocardiograms (ECGs) carry subject-specific patterns enabling reliable individual discrimination, forming the basis of ECG biometrics. Beyond authentication, this paradigm holds significant potential to secure sensitive cardiac data and to serve as a pretext task in self-supervised learning. Yet, most studies remain confined to singlesession, resting data, leaving robustness to temporal and physiological variations largely untested. We address this gap by evaluating ECG biometrics under realistic conditions involving exercise-induced stress and cross-session variability. A Siamese ResNet with late multi-lead fusion strategy is trained on a large ECG dataset extracted from cardiopulmonary exercise tests and evaluated with a exercise-and time-aware protocol, as well as on public benchmarks. This first extensive assessment of ECG biometrics under combined physiological and temporal variability achieves an intra-session rest-to-peak EER of 1.7% and stateof-the-art 3.9% on the CYBHi dataset. Findings support the presence of an intrinsic cardiac signature resilient to physiological and temporal drift.

AI.tldr: This work benchmarks ECG biometrics under realistic exercise-induced stress and cross-session variability using a Siamese ResNet with late multi-lead fusion, achieving 1.7% intra-session rest-to-peak EER and 3.9% on CYBHi, supporting an intrinsic cardiac signature robust to physiological and temporal drift.
AI.motivation: Most ECG biometrics studies are limited to single-session, resting data, so robustness to temporal and physiological variations remains largely untested. This limits the reliability of ECG-based authentication and its use in securing sensitive cardiac data and as a self-supervised pretext task.
AI.method: A Siamese ResNet with a late multi-lead fusion strategy is trained on a large ECG dataset extracted from cardiopulmonary exercise tests. It is evaluated using an exercise- and time-aware protocol as well as on public benchmarks (including CYBHi).
AI.result: The proposed approach achieves an intra-session rest-to-peak EER of 1.7% and a state-of-the-art 3.9% on the CYBHi dataset. This constitutes the first extensive assessment of ECG biometrics under combined physiological and temporal variability.
AI.conclusion: The findings support the existence of an intrinsic cardiac signature that is resilient to physiological and temporal drift, indicating that ECG biometrics can remain reliable under realistic, non-resting, cross-session conditions.

title: The EventCV Library for Event-Based Robotic Vision
summary: Event cameras detect per-pixel brightness changes asynchronously on microsecond timescales, with high dynamic range and low power draw. These are desirable properties for robots that move fast or work in difficult lighting conditions. However, integrating an event camera into a real-world robotic pipeline still requires substantial effort: plug-and-play drivers do not exist, event streams are recorded in a variety of incompatible file formats, and most projects rely on custom research-grade code. Here, we present EventCV, an open-source and extensible Rust library with OpenCV-style Python bindings that lowers the entry barrier to working with event cameras. EventCV provides a wide range of features: denoising filters and geometric transforms, augmentations, corner detection and unsupervised feature learning, contrast-maximization motion estimation, a video-to-events simulator, and Open Neural Network Exchange (ONNX) inference for deployment in robotic stacks. EventCV integrates the Neuromorphic Drivers package, allowing an event camera stream to be processed directly in real time. No existing toolkit covers this range of operations in one package, and EventCV builds representations and decodes files 1.1x to 3.7x faster than the currently available libraries. We deploy EventCV on a Jetson Orin AGX and present three robotics case studies spanning object detection, on-device model inference, and localization. Project webpage: https://eventcv.net.

AI.tldr: EventCV is an open-source Rust library with OpenCV-style Python bindings that provides an end-to-end toolkit for event-camera processing and robotics deployment.
AI.motivation: Event cameras offer microsecond temporal resolution, high dynamic range, and low power, ideal for fast-moving or poorly lit robots, but integration into real robotic pipelines is hard: no plug-and-play drivers, incompatible file formats, and reliance on custom research-grade code.
AI.method: EventCV is implemented in Rust with OpenCV-style Python bindings and unifies denoising filters, geometric transforms, augmentations, corner detection and unsupervised feature learning, contrast-maximization motion estimation, a video-to-events simulator, and ONNX inference. It integrates the Neuromorphic Drivers package for real-time streaming.
AI.result: EventCV covers a broader operation range than existing toolkits in a single package, builds representations and decodes files 1.1x-3.7x faster than available libraries, and was deployed on a Jetson Orin AGX across three robotics case studies: object detection, on-device model inference, and localization.
AI.conclusion: EventCV lowers the entry barrier to event-camera robotics by consolidating drivers, processing, learning, and deployment in one open-source, extensible library.

title: A Lie Detector Test for Language Models: Reading Knowledge a Model Won't Reveal
summary: Large language models can hold knowledge they do not report. A model may sandbag on a capability evaluation, or answer against what it internally knows, and its outputs alone cannot tell whether it is hiding an answer or simply does not have one. We borrow the Concealed Information Test, a forensic method that identifies guilty knowledge by presenting a suspect with the true detail among plausible decoys and measuring a stronger response to the item they recognize. Our method, Probe of Internal Recognition (PIR), does the same inside a model. It presents a question with its candidate answers and reads, from the model's internal states, which candidate the model recognizes as correct. PIR is reference-free, needing no honest reference model and no labeled truth corpus. Across eight models from five families (Gemma, Qwen, Llama, Mistral, and Phi), PIR recovers the recognized answer at 0.70 to 0.87 balanced accuracy, well above the 0.28 to 0.40 unknown-item baseline and the 0.25 chance rate. It stays readable across every form of concealment we test, from prompted deception and trained sandbagging to external password-locked and circuit-broken checkpoints, with recognition between 0.85 and 0.93. When the model hides a known answer, recognition stays high. When unlearning removes the knowledge, recognition drops to the level of a question the model never knew. PIR therefore separates a model that will not answer from one that cannot, which supports sandbagging audits and unlearning verification. The signal is causal, adds information beyond black-box behavioral cues, and extends from multiple-choice questions to free-form generation.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Probe of Internal Recognition (PIR), a reference-free method that detects knowledge a model holds but does not report, by reading which candidate answer the model's internal states recognize. PIR distinguishes concealment from genuine ignorance and supports sandbagging audits and unlearning verification.
AI.motivation: Large language models can conceal knowledge they possess: they may sandbag on capability evaluations or answer against their internal beliefs. Outputs alone cannot distinguish whether a model is hiding an answer or genuinely lacks it, creating a gap for auditing deception and verifying unlearning.
AI.method: PIR borrows the Concealed Information Test from forensics: it presents a question with candidate answers and reads from the model's internal states which candidate it recognizes as correct. It is reference-free, requiring no honest reference model and no labeled truth corpus.
AI.result: Across eight models from five families (Gemma, Qwen, Llama, Mistral, Phi), PIR recovers the recognized answer at 0.70–0.87 balanced accuracy vs. 0.28–0.40 unknown-item baseline and 0.25 chance. It remains readable under prompted deception, trained sandbagging, and external password-locked and circuit-broken checkpoints (0.85–0.93). Recognition stays high when hiding a known answer but drops to ignorance level when unlearning removes knowledge.
AI.conclusion: PIR separates a model that will not answer from one that cannot. The signal is causal, adds information beyond black-box behavioral cues, and extends from multiple-choice questions to free-form generation, supporting sandbagging audits and unlearning verification.

title: FAN: Foresight Action Normalization for Continual Adaptation of Vision-Language-Action Models
summary: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models pre-trained on large-scale, closed datasets have demonstrated remarkable success across diverse robotic manipulation tasks. However, their long-term real-world deployment necessitates continuously acquiring new skills while retaining previously learned capabilities. While pioneering works have explored continual VLA adaptation using techniques such as experience replay and reinforcement fine-tuning, they overlook a foundational mechanism: action normalization, which determines the underlying coordinate system in which policies perceive and execute physical actions. To bridge this gap, we systematically evaluate five normalization strategies across four real-world task streams covering single-arm and bimanual manipulation. Our analysis reveals that existing protocols induce severe failure modes due to inter-task coordinate drift, limited motion coverage, or train-test coordinate mismatches. Motivated by these insights, we formulate three core design principles: consistency, coverage, and causality (3C), and introduce foresight action normalization (FAN). FAN estimates normalization statistics once from a small, task-independent calibration set prior to continual learning and freezes them throughout adaptation. Across all evaluated streams, FAN achieves the highest performance and demonstrates consistent robustness, providing insightful guidance for building stable action representations in achieving effective lifelong VLA adaptation.

AI.tldr: This paper identifies action normalization as an overlooked yet foundational mechanism in continual Vision-Language-Action (VLA) adaptation, systematically studies it, and proposes Foresight Action Normalization (FAN) guided by three design principles.
AI.motivation: Pre-trained VLA models succeed broadly but require continual skill acquisition while retaining prior capabilities for long-term deployment. Prior continual VLA work relies on experience replay and reinforcement fine-tuning, yet ignores action normalization—the coordinate system in which policies perceive and execute physical actions—leaving a critical gap.
AI.method: The authors systematically evaluate five normalization strategies across four real-world task streams spanning single-arm and bimanual manipulation. From observed failure modes they derive three design principles—consistency, coverage, and causality (3C)—and introduce Foresight Action Normalization (FAN), which estimates normalization statistics once from a small, task-independent calibration set before continual learning and freezes them throughout adaptation.
AI.result: Existing normalization protocols induce severe failure modes stemming from inter-task coordinate drift, limited motion coverage, or train-test coordinate mismatches. FAN achieves the highest performance across all evaluated streams and demonstrates consistent robustness.
AI.conclusion: Action normalization is a foundational mechanism for stable action representations in lifelong VLA adaptation; freezing calibration-derived statistics (FAN) provides actionable guidance for effective continual VLA learning.

title: CodeMidas: Scaling Agentic Coding RL Environments from Code Itself
summary: Training capable coding agents via reinforcement learning (RL) requires diverse tasks with reliable verifiers. Open-source codebases offer a rich source of such tasks, while existing methods typically rely on development artifacts such as issues and commits, limiting the range of tasks that can be extracted. To better scale RL environments, we present CodeMidas, an agentic pipeline that turns implemented functionality in existing codebases into executable RL environments using source code as its only task-specific input. CodeMidas allocates agentic compute to every stage of environment construction: agents explore implemented functionality to formulate behavioral specifications, construct tests grounded in execution of the original code, and validate and filter candidate tasks through execution checks and repeated solution rollouts. The resulting dataset has 5,545 training tasks from 3,185 open-source codebases spanning 23 programming languages and 15 technical domains. Training MiMo-V2.5 on these tasks with GRPO improves performance on all five diverse benchmarks, covering issue repair (DeepSWE + 11.7%), whole-program construction (ProgramBench +17%), and terminal work (Terminal-Bench v2.1 +8.5%). Ablations show that increasing the number of high-quality training tasks improves performance. Trajectory analysis shows the RL-trained agent demonstrates better behaviors like increasing codebase exploration and more diverse self-verification. These results establish source code as a scalable foundation for constructing RL environments that improve coding agents across diverse software tasks.

AI.tldr: CodeMidas is an agentic pipeline that converts implemented functionality in existing codebases—using source code alone—into 5,545 executable RL training tasks across 3,185 repos, 23 languages, and 15 domains; RL training with GRPO on these tasks improves coding agents across five benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Training capable coding agents via RL requires diverse tasks with reliable verifiers. Open-source codebases are a rich task source, but existing extraction methods depend on development artifacts like issues and commits, restricting the range of extractable tasks. The goal is to scale RL environments beyond these artifact-dependent approaches.
AI.method: CodeMidas is an agentic pipeline that uses source code as the only task-specific input. It allocates agentic compute to every construction stage: agents explore implemented functionality to formulate behavioral specifications, build tests grounded in execution of the original code, and validate/filter candidate tasks via execution checks and repeated solution rollouts.
AI.result: The dataset contains 5,545 training tasks from 3,185 open-source codebases spanning 23 programming languages and 15 technical domains. Training MiMo-V2.5 with GRPO improves all five benchmarks: DeepSWE (issue repair) +11.7%, ProgramBench (whole-program construction) +17%, Terminal-Bench v2.1 +8.5%. Ablations show more high-quality tasks yield better performance; trajectory analysis shows the RL-trained agent explores codebases more and performs more diverse self-verification.
AI.conclusion: Source code alone can serve as a scalable foundation for constructing RL environments, enabling coding-agent improvement across diverse software tasks without relying on issues or commits.

title: MicroHookACT: Monocular Microscopic Vision Guided Visuomotor Policy for Flexible Microelectrode Hooking
summary: Automated needle-loop hooking is a critical step in flexible microelectrode (FME) implantation. This paper presents MicroHookACT, an imitation learning-based visuomotor policy for automated 3D hooking under monocular microscopic vision. First, a unidirectional hooking strategy exploits defocus cues and optical-axis guidance to enable palpation-free precise alignment and contact-rich threading. Second, an action-supervised object attention module built on a frozen ViT backbone learns to focus on the micro-needle tip and micro-loop directly from human demonstrations, without requiring manual visual annotations for training. Third, attention-centered global coarse and local fine features are dynamically weighted according to predicted action progress, enabling a single ACT policy to adapt to changing defocus blur and visual requirements throughout the operation. In the experiments, visuomotor policies were trained on 60 human demonstrations and evaluated under five setups with varying difficulties. Our MicroHookACT framework achieved the highest overall success rate of 96.7\% with an average execution time of 11.5 s. These results demonstrate the potential of visuomotor policy learning for micron-level control under varying operating conditions.

AI.tldr: MicroHookACT is an imitation learning-based visuomotor policy for automated 3D needle-loop hooking under monocular microscopic vision, achieving 96.7% success rate and 11.5 s average execution time.
AI.motivation: Automated needle-loop hooking is a critical yet challenging step in flexible microelectrode (FME) implantation, requiring micron-level precision and handling of defocus blur under monocular microscopic vision.
AI.method: The framework combines: (1) a unidirectional hooking strategy using defocus cues and optical-axis guidance for palpation-free alignment and contact-rich threading; (2) an action-supervised object attention module on a frozen ViT backbone that learns to focus on the micro-needle tip and micro-loop from demonstrations without manual visual annotations; and (3) attention-centered global coarse and local fine features dynamically weighted by predicted action progress, enabling a single ACT policy to adapt to changing defocus blur and visual requirements.
AI.result: Trained on 60 human demonstrations and evaluated across five setups of varying difficulty, MicroHookACT achieved the highest overall success rate of 96.7% with an average execution time of 11.5 s.
AI.conclusion: The results demonstrate the potential of visuomotor policy learning for micron-level control under varying operating conditions.

title: Designer-RSI: Evolving Procedural Memory from User Traffic for Agentic Graphic Design
summary: Professional graphic design is a long-horizon agentic task in which structured, editable artifacts emerge from many interdependent actions, yet outcomes admit no reliable programmatic oracle. We introduce a continual adaptation framework in which a frozen frontier model operates professional design software through more than 230 tools, while an external procedural memory of natural-language skills accumulates and refines reusable design procedures from experience. The memory widens by acquiring procedures for recurring uncovered subtasks and deepens by revising existing procedures against their own successful and failed executions, while a matched replay gate admits only changes that repair failures without regressing observed successes. Five rounds over 1,406 real user briefs and 1,869 automatically graded trajectories, with no weight updates and no human labels, grow the bank from 76 documentation-derived skills to 139 and raise GenEval2 execution success on Claude-Sonnet-4 from 72.7% to 99.3% (+11.99 points in generation quality), with 61.8% and 67.6% win rates against the no-skill agent across four specialized design benchmarks on Claude-Sonnet-4 and Claude-Opus-4.6. We further show the two mechanisms are effective in combination: on 200 held-out briefs from user-traffic benchmark, widening or deepening alone reaches a 49.4% / 48.6% win rate over the no-skill agent, while their combination reaches 58.5% (p = 0.025). Procedural memory offers a practical route to continual adaptation of agents under noisy, unverifiable feedback.

AI.tldr: A frozen frontier model driving professional design software via 230+ tools is continually adapted through an external natural-language procedural memory that widens (adds new skills) and deepens (refines existing ones) under a matched replay gate, raising GenEval2 success from 72.7% to 99.3% without weight updates or human labels.
AI.motivation: Professional graphic design is a long-horizon agentic task where editable artifacts arise from many interdependent actions, yet no reliable programmatic oracle exists to verify outcomes. This makes standard reward-based or label-based adaptation impractical, motivating a memory-based mechanism that can learn from noisy, unverifiable feedback.
AI.method: A continual adaptation framework keeps the frontier model frozen and operates professional design software through more than 230 tools. An external procedural memory of natural-language skills accumulates reusable design procedures: it widens by acquiring procedures for recurring uncovered subtasks and deepens by revising existing procedures based on their own successful and failed executions. A matched replay gate admits only updates that repair failures without regressing observed successes. Adaptation proceeds over five rounds on 1,406 real user briefs and 1,869 automatically graded trajectories, with no weight updates and no human labels.
AI.result: The skill bank grows from 76 documentation-derived skills to 139. GenEval2 execution success on Claude-Sonnet-4 rises from 72.7% to 99.3% (+11.99 points in generation quality). Win rates against the no-skill agent are 61.8% and 67.6% across four specialized design benchmarks on Claude-Sonnet-4 and Claude-Opus-4.6. On 200 held-out briefs from a user-traffic benchmark, widening or deepening alone yields 49.4% / 48.6% win rates, while their combination reaches 58.5% (p = 0.025), showing the two mechanisms are effective in combination.
AI.conclusion: Procedural memory provides a practical route to continual adaptation of agents under noisy, unverifiable feedback, allowing a frozen frontier model to substantially improve on long-horizon professional design tasks without weight updates or human labels.

title: ProTracer: Proprioception-Guided Failure Diagnosis in Robot Manipulation
summary: This paper presents a comprehensive framework for robot manipulation failure analysis that includes binary failure detection, failure categorization, explanation generation, and the additional capability of failure onset localization, which aims to identify the earliest moment at which a robot execution deviates from a valid task-completion trajectory and is ultimately followed by task failure. To address these tasks, we propose ProTracer, a training-free framework that leverages existing Vision-Language Models (VLMs) together with proprioceptive signals for failure analysis. Our method uses proprioceptive dynamics to identify temporally informative action boundaries and converts richer robot-state signals into structured natural-language descriptions that can be jointly analyzed together with visual observations by the VLM. This design combines the temporal precision of proprioceptive signals with the multimodal reasoning capabilities of modern VLMs without requiring additional model training. We further introduce FailTime, a benchmark with synchronized visual and proprioceptive observations for evaluating conventional failure diagnosis tasks as well as failure onset localization. Experiments demonstrate that ProTracer achieves strong performance across both conventional failure diagnosis tasks and the newly introduced failure onset localization task, highlighting the importance of proprioceptive reasoning for fine-grained temporal failure analysis.

AI.tldr: ProTracer is a training-free VLM-based framework that fuses proprioceptive signals with visual observations to perform robot manipulation failure detection, categorization, explanation, and failure onset localization, supported by the new FailTime benchmark.
AI.motivation: Robot manipulation failure analysis is typically limited to coarse diagnosis (detection, categorization, explanation) and lacks fine-grained temporal reasoning, particularly identifying the earliest moment an execution deviates from a valid task-completion trajectory. Existing approaches also often require task-specific training and underutilize the rich temporal information in robot proprioceptive signals.
AI.method: The authors propose ProTracer, a training-free framework that leverages existing Vision-Language Models jointly with proprioceptive signals. Proprioceptive dynamics are used to detect temporally informative action boundaries, and robot-state signals are converted into structured natural-language descriptions that the VLM analyzes together with visual observations. This combines proprioceptive temporal precision with VLM multimodal reasoning without additional model training. They also introduce FailTime, a benchmark with synchronized visual and proprioceptive observations.
AI.result: Experiments show that ProTracer achieves strong performance on conventional failure diagnosis tasks (binary detection, categorization, explanation) as well as the newly introduced failure onset localization task, demonstrating the value of proprioceptive reasoning for fine-grained temporal failure analysis.
AI.conclusion: The work establishes failure onset localization as a valuable task for robot manipulation and shows that a training-free, proprioception-augmented VLM framework, together with the FailTime benchmark, can effectively support both conventional and temporally fine-grained failure analysis.

title: AVT-Fabric: Active Visuo-Tactile Perception via Adaptive Evidence Selection for Efficient Robotic Fabric Comparison
summary: Robotic fabric comparison needs to actively combine visual appearance and tactile cues. Here, we present AVT-Fabric, an RGB-first framework that allocates tactile evidence according to the difficulty of each comparison. A dual-scale gate evaluates answer-token confidence and raw logit separation to determine whether another force-tagged GelSight observation is needed. Compact textual memory preserves the executed history, and majority voting consolidates the selected predictions. On 400 held-out comparisons, AVT-Fabric achieves 98.0% accuracy with a compact 7B Multimodal Large Language Model (MLLM), surpassing the 94.0% reported by the 90B MLLM-Fabric baseline by 4.0 percentage points while processing only 1.60 of five available stages on average. It improves on matched passive inference by 9.25 percentage points and reduces model-side latency by 61.8%, while also improving on RGB-only accuracy. Four additional MLLM backbones support the generalizability, accuracy, and efficiency of the framework. This framework is also deployed on a real robotic system, achieving 78.1% pairwise ranking accuracy and correct fabric selection in seven of eight application scenarios. AVT-Fabric demonstrates that adaptive evidence selection can improve both the accuracy and efficiency of robotic visuo-tactile reasoning.

AI.tldr: AVT-Fabric is an RGB-first framework that selectively acquires tactile evidence based on comparison difficulty, achieving 98.0% accuracy on fabric comparison with a 7B MLLM while using only 1.60 of five stages on average.
AI.motivation: Robotic fabric comparison requires actively combining visual appearance with tactile cues, yet existing approaches either rely on passive inference or exhaustively query tactile observations, incurring unnecessary cost. A large multimodal baseline (90B MLLM-Fabric) reaches only 94.0%, motivating a more efficient, adaptive evidence-selection strategy.
AI.method: The framework uses a dual-scale gate that evaluates answer-token confidence and raw logit separation to decide whether an additional force-tagged GelSight tactile observation is needed. A compact textual memory preserves the executed history, and majority voting consolidates selected predictions.
AI.result: On 400 held-out comparisons, AVT-Fabric reaches 98.0% accuracy with a 7B MLLM, exceeding the 90B MLLM-Fabric baseline (94.0%) by 4.0 percentage points while using only 1.60 of five stages on average. It improves over matched passive inference by 9.25 percentage points, cuts model-side latency by 61.8%, and beats RGB-only accuracy. Four additional MLLM backbones confirm generalizability, and a real robotic deployment achieves 78.1% pairwise ranking accuracy with correct selection in seven of eight scenarios.
AI.conclusion: Adaptive evidence selection improves both accuracy and efficiency of robotic visuo-tactile reasoning, allowing a compact 7B model to outperform a much larger 90B baseline.

title: MarineCraft: Enabling Rapid Prototyping of Underwater Robots via Modular Construction
summary: Underwater robot development is often hindered by the complexities of waterproofing and wiring, which significantly delay the rapid prototyping process. This paper presents MarineCraft, a modular toolkit designed to accelerate the development cycle through structural reconfiguration. The system features self-contained, waterproof propulsion modules that integrate power, wireless communication, and actuation. By eliminating centralized wiring and the need for repeated sealing, MarineCraft allows diverse robot geometries to be assembled and tested in minutes rather than days. Experimental results demonstrate that this reconfigurable architecture enables fast, iterative design cycles while maintaining reliable operation and leak-free performance at depths of up to 2.5 meters. Our toolkit effectively lowers the barrier to underwater robotics by transforming modularity into a vehicle for rapid physical prototyping.

AI.tldr: MarineCraft is a modular toolkit of self-contained, waterproof propulsion modules that eliminates wiring and repeated sealing, enabling underwater robots to be assembled and tested in minutes and operating reliably to 2.5 m depth.
AI.motivation: Underwater robot development is slowed by waterproofing complexity and wiring, which delay rapid prototyping.
AI.method: A modular toolkit with self-contained waterproof propulsion modules integrating power, wireless communication, and actuation, supporting structural reconfiguration into diverse geometries without centralized wiring.
AI.result: Fast, iterative design cycles with reliable, leak-free operation at depths up to 2.5 meters.
AI.conclusion: MarineCraft lowers the barrier to underwater robotics by turning modularity into a vehicle for rapid physical prototyping.

title: Stabilizing Trajectory Outputs in End-to-End Autonomous Driving via SC-IMM Based Teacher Signals
summary: End-to-End autonomous driving models commonly predict future waypoints from sensor inputs and convert them into vehicle control commands through a downstream controller. However, conventional waypoint-based imitation learning mainly minimizes coordinate-level errors, making it difficult to capture scene-dependent path-speed changes and temporal instability across waypoint outputs. In this paper, we propose an offline teacher-signal generation and learning method for trajectory-output stabilization based on a Scene-Conditioned Interacting Multiple Model (SC-IMM) to mitigate this issue. The proposed method converts expert trajectories into path-speed states and performs IMM updates conditioned on scene cues to generate path-speed teacher labels and mode posterior probabilities. The generated signals are added to the original trajectory loss as auxiliary supervision during training, while the inference structure and waypoint controller remain unchanged. In closed-loop evaluation on 100 short routes in CARLA Town12, the proposed method improved the driving score by 28.0% and reduced Collision/km by 62.3% compared with the baseline, while also improving jerk and trajectory-variation metrics. These results demonstrate that offline teacher signals embedding scene-conditioned motion-model cues can guide trajectory-output driving models toward more stable closed-loop behavior.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes an offline teacher-signal generation and learning method based on a Scene-Conditioned Interacting Multiple Model (SC-IMM) to stabilize waypoint outputs in end-to-end autonomous driving, improving closed-loop performance without changing inference structure.
AI.motivation: Conventional waypoint-based imitation learning mainly minimizes coordinate-level errors, making it difficult to capture scene-dependent path-speed changes and temporal instability across waypoint outputs. This limits closed-loop driving stability.
AI.method: The method converts expert trajectories into path-speed states and performs IMM updates conditioned on scene cues to generate path-speed teacher labels and mode posterior probabilities. These generated signals are added to the original trajectory loss as auxiliary supervision during training, while the inference structure and waypoint controller remain unchanged.
AI.result: In closed-loop evaluation on 100 short routes in CARLA Town12, the proposed method improved the driving score by 28.0% and reduced Collision/km by 62.3% compared with the baseline, while also improving jerk and trajectory-variation metrics.
AI.conclusion: Offline teacher signals embedding scene-conditioned motion-model cues can guide trajectory-output driving models toward more stable closed-loop behavior.

title: A Unified Dynamic Force Guidance Framework for Performance-Optimized Kinesthetic Teaching
summary: Collaborative robots are increasingly deployed in industrial scenarios characterized by frequent product changeovers. As an intuitive programming method, kinesthetic teaching facilitates rapid robot deployment. However, users may overlook the configuration of the robot during kinesthetic teaching, leading to degradation in operational performance. Operational performance refers to the capability of the robot to generate motion and can be quantified by the Minimum Singular Value of the Jacobian matrix. To address this issue, this paper proposes an online dynamic force guidance method that integrates performance constraint and optimization mechanisms. Specifically, variable admittance control maintains the operational performance of the robot above a predefined threshold, while a virtual force actively guides the user to drag the robot towards configurations with improved performance. Experiments are conducted on a 6-DOF collaborative robot, comparing three typical paths in the task space. To evaluate the quality of the taught trajectories, trajectory playback experiments are conducted to analyze the relationship between the operational performance of the robot and the work efficiency. The results demonstrate that the proposed method effectively enhances the operational performance of the robot and consequently improves the work efficiency, holding significant value for reducing production takt time in industrial deployment.
