AI.tldr: This paper proposes an online dynamic force guidance method combining variable admittance control with virtual force to keep a collaborative robot's operational performance above a threshold during kinesthetic teaching, improving work efficiency.
AI.motivation: Collaborative robots are increasingly used in industrial scenarios with frequent product changeovers, and kinesthetic teaching enables rapid deployment. However, users may overlook robot configuration during teaching, degrading operational performance (quantified by the Minimum Singular Value of the Jacobian matrix).
AI.method: An online dynamic force guidance method integrating performance constraint and optimization mechanisms: variable admittance control maintains operational performance above a predefined threshold, while a virtual force actively guides the user to drag the robot toward configurations with improved performance.
AI.result: Experiments on a 6-DOF collaborative robot comparing three typical task-space paths, with trajectory playback experiments analyzing the relationship between operational performance and work efficiency, show the method effectively enhances operational performance and improves work efficiency.
AI.conclusion: The proposed method holds significant value for reducing production takt time in industrial deployment.

title: FootQuery: Future-Touchdown-Guided Retrieval from Depth History for Perceptive Humanoid Locomotion
summary: Humanoid locomotion over complex terrain requires anticipating footholds that may no longer be visible at touchdown. Limited camera coverage and self-occlusion make it necessary to retrieve relevant terrain information from earlier observations. We present FootQuery, a perceptive locomotion framework that queries depth history using each foot's predicted next touchdown. The policy predicts touchdown locations and uncertainty from proprioception and uses these distributions, together with per-foot features, to query sparsely sampled historical depth frames. During training, realized contacts are projected into historical images to supervise retrieval at the regions where those contacts were visible. The retrieved per-foot features are fused with global visual memory to generate control actions. A progressive force-assistance curriculum supports early exploration, while event-consistent tread-midline shaping encourages coordinated stair contacts. Deployment requires only proprioception and onboard depth images. In simulation, the complete framework outperforms its component ablations on the most challenging tested stairs, gaps, and platforms. Real-world experiments on a Unitree G1 demonstrate continuous traversal with a single policy across outdoor stairs and indoor routes combining stair ascent and descent, platforms, and gaps. These results support organizing visual history around anticipated contacts for perceptive humanoid locomotion.

AI.tldr: FootQuery queries historical depth frames using each foot's predicted next touchdown, fusing retrieved per-foot features with global visual memory for perceptive humanoid locomotion over complex terrain.
AI.motivation: Humanoid locomotion over complex terrain requires anticipating footholds that may be invisible at touchdown due to limited camera coverage and self-occlusion, making it necessary to retrieve relevant terrain information from earlier observations.
AI.method: The policy predicts touchdown locations and uncertainty from proprioception and uses these distributions, together with per-foot features, to query sparsely sampled historical depth frames. During training, realized contacts are projected into historical images to supervise retrieval at regions where contacts were visible. Retrieved per-foot features are fused with global visual memory to generate control actions. A progressive force-assistance curriculum supports early exploration, and event-consistent tread-midline shaping encourages coordinated stair contacts. Deployment requires only proprioception and onboard depth images.
AI.result: In simulation, the full framework outperforms its component ablations on the most challenging stairs, gaps, and platforms. Real-world experiments on a Unitree G1 demonstrate continuous traversal with a single policy across outdoor stairs and indoor routes combining stair ascent/descent, platforms, and gaps.
AI.conclusion: Organizing visual history around anticipated contacts is effective for perceptive humanoid locomotion.

title: Robotic Multiphase Interaction: Manipulating Coupled Liquid and Solid Dynamics with a World Model
summary: This work presents \textit{Robotic Multiphase Interaction (RMI)}, a setting in which liquid enters a porous material and interacts mechanically with its deforming solid skeleton. Manipulation can therefore change pore volume, expel or redistribute retained liquid, and alter grasp stability at the same time. Spilled liquid can also create safety risks in domestic and manufacturing settings. This differs from most manipulation of solid objects and from tasks that involve both liquid and solid while keeping the phases spatially separate. We study a sponge filled with water as the first RMI example. We use implicit incompressible porous flow with smoothed particle hydrodynamics as the dynamics engine and enable robotic manipulation by adding Coulomb contact memory, hybrid velocity and force regulation, and a stability gate for lifting. The resulting environment connects robot commands to changes in the coupled liquid and solid state. A world model conditioned on actions predicts how this state evolves under candidate commands, while a temporal UNet generates actions using either Diffusion Policy or rectified flow matching. Our world model reduces retained water prediction error by more than $60\%$ compared with the baseline. The best action sequence selected by the world model from policy proposals further reduces the predicted terminal water error by about half. These improvements show that modelling the coupled liquid and solid state helps the robot predict how its actions affect both the porous object and the liquid held inside.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Robotic Multiphase Interaction (RMI), where liquid inside a porous deformable solid is manipulated through the robot's actions, and demonstrates a world model plus generative policy that substantially reduces retained-water prediction error.
AI.motivation: Most robotic manipulation research focuses on solid objects, or on liquid and solid tasks where the two phases stay spatially separate. RMI is different because manipulating the porous object changes pore volume, expels or redistributes the retained liquid, and simultaneously affects grasp stability. Spilled liquid also poses safety risks in domestic and manufacturing settings, motivating a coupled model of the liquid and solid state.
AI.method: The authors use a water-filled sponge as the first RMI example. The dynamics engine is implicit incompressible porous flow coupled with smoothed particle hydrodynamics (SPH). Robotic manipulation is enabled by Coulomb contact memory, hybrid velocity and force regulation, and a stability gate for lifting. The resulting environment links robot commands to changes in the coupled liquid-solid state. An action-conditioned world model predicts state evolution under candidate commands, and a temporal UNet generates actions using either Diffusion Policy or rectified flow matching.
AI.result: The world model reduces retained-water prediction error by more than 60% versus the baseline. Selecting the best action sequence from policy proposals using the world model further reduces the predicted terminal water error by about half.
AI.conclusion: Modelling the coupled liquid and solid state allows the robot to better predict how its actions affect both the porous object and the liquid held inside, supporting more reliable multiphase manipulation.

title: AtomEgo: Exploring Ego-Robot Integration for Embodied Foundation Model Pretraining
summary: Embodied foundation models are constrained by the limited scale and diversity of robot demonstrations, motivating the use of large-scale egocentric human interaction data. However, how to effectively incorporate such data into embodied-model pre-training remains unclear because of substantial embodiment and action-space gaps between humans and robots. We present AtomEgo, a systematic study of ego--robot co-training supported by a curated corpus of approximately 2,659 hours and a scalable data processing pipeline. Across vision--language--action and world--action model architectures, we investigate three representative paradigms: joint co-training with domain-specific action heads, progressive ego-to-robot transfer through embodiment alignment, and joint video--action modeling. We evaluate these paradigms through multi-task real-robot experiments and language-conditioned cross-embodiment representation analysis. Our results reveal a simple principle: Data Scale * Alignment Quality --> Capability Gain; egocentric data can improve generalization, but their value depends on how effectively they are aligned and utilized. This principle can provide practical guidance for scalable ego--robot pre-training.

AI.tldr: AtomEgo systematically studies egocentric human data for robot pre-training, showing that the benefit of ego data follows "Data Scale × Alignment Quality → Capability Gain," with value hinging on effective embodiment alignment.
AI.motivation: Embodied foundation models are bottlenecked by the limited scale and diversity of robot demonstrations, prompting interest in large-scale egocentric human interaction data. However, substantial embodiment and action-space gaps between humans and robots make it unclear how to effectively integrate such data into pre-training.
AI.method: The authors build a curated corpus of approximately 2,659 hours of egocentric data plus a scalable processing pipeline, and study ego–robot co-training across vision–language–action and world–action architectures. They investigate three paradigms: (1) joint co-training with domain-specific action heads, (2) progressive ego-to-robot transfer via embodiment alignment, and (3) joint video–action modeling. Evaluation uses multi-task real-robot experiments and language-conditioned cross-embodiment representation analysis.
AI.result: Egocentric data can improve generalization, but the magnitude of the gain is determined not by data volume alone. The results support a simple principle: Data Scale × Alignment Quality → Capability Gain, indicating that the usefulness of ego data depends on how well it is aligned and utilized across embodiments and action spaces.
AI.conclusion: The study provides practical guidance for scalable ego–robot pre-training, highlighting embodiment alignment quality as a first-order factor that modulates the value of large-scale egocentric data.

title: 2nd Place Solution to the HANDS 2026 Workshop Challenge-Dexterous Grasp Motion Track: Single-Shot Trajectory Warping for Grasp Motion Generation
summary: This report describes our 2nd place solution to the HANDS 2026 workshop challenge (Dexterous Grasp Motion track) in conjunction with ECCV 2026. In this challenge, we address grasp motion generation for the 12-DoF LinkerHand O6, aiming to produce physically plausible reach-and-lift trajectories for unseen objects from randomized initial hand poses in simulation. This task is particularly challenging because each grasp requires a per-step policy to make approximately $70$ twelve-dimensional decisions, with errors accumulating over time, while test objects and physical dynamics may differ from those encountered during training. To address these challenges, we propose editing a single successful GraspM3 demonstration instead of generating the motion step by step: a policy observes the object once and outputs a 12-D warp of the demonstration, which is then replayed open-loop. Moreover, we train the warp policy with one-step PPO over all $4{,}824$ training objects in parallel. As a result, our method achieved success rates of $94.61\%$ on the easy track, the highest of all submissions, and $57.18\%$ on the hard track of the private test set.

AI.tldr: A 2nd-place HANDS 2026 challenge solution replaces per-step grasp motion generation with a one-shot 12-D warp of a single successful demonstration, replayed open-loop and trained via parallel one-step PPO, reaching 94.61% (easy) and 57.18% (hard) success on the private test set.
AI.motivation: Grasp motion generation for the 12-DoF LinkerHand O6 requires producing physically plausible reach-and-lift trajectories for unseen objects under randomized initial hand poses. Per-step policies must make roughly 70 twelve-dimensional decisions per grasp, so errors compound over time, and test objects and dynamics may differ from training. This motivates avoiding step-by-step generation in favor of a more robust, demonstration-anchored formulation.
AI.method: Instead of generating motion step by step, the method edits a single successful GraspM3 demonstration: a policy observes the object once and outputs a 12-D warp of the demonstration, which is then replayed open-loop. The warp policy is trained with one-step PPO over all 4,824 training objects in parallel.
AI.result: The approach achieved 94.61% success on the easy track—the highest among all submissions—and 57.18% on the hard track of the private test set.
AI.conclusion: Reframing dexterous grasp motion generation as a one-shot demonstration-warp prediction problem, rather than closed-loop per-step control, yields strong generalization and top-tier challenge performance.

title: Learning Distance-Conditioned Object Transport for Humanoid Loco-Manipulation from a Single Motion Clip
summary: Motion tracking can reproduce humanoid loco-manipulation from a single retargeted motion clip, but a policy trained on a fixed reference primarily reproduces its demonstrated transport outcome. Although the source trajectory visits intermediate object displacements, transport termination is demonstrated only at its endpoint. We identify this mismatch as the termination-versus-passage gap: intermediate displacements are observed as passage states rather than termination-complete outcomes. We introduce Distance-Conditioned Reference Recomposition (DCRR), which relocates the demonstrated termination segment to intermediate transport states. A frozen tracking teacher replays the recomposed references under closed-loop dynamics, and the retained trajectories are relabeled by their achieved object placements and distilled into a reference-free policy. This procedure constructs distance-conditioned supervision from the interaction behavior encoded in the source motion. Across Carry, Kick-Push, Crouch-Push, and Drag, DCRR-BC produces command-dependent transport with an overall normalized distance mean absolute error (MAE) of 0.15, compared with 0.28 for source-only behavior cloning. RL fine-tuning further improves the command response and execution robustness in the training simulator and under sim-to-sim transfer. Finally, hardware experiments demonstrate transport-distance modulation across all four interaction modes.

AI.tldr: The paper identifies a "termination-versus-passage gap" in motion-tracking-based humanoid loco-manipulation, where intermediate object displacements are only passage states, not demonstrated termination outcomes. It proposes Distance-Conditioned Reference Recomposition (DCRR), which relocates the termination segment to intermediate transport states, replays the recomposed references via a frozen tracking teacher, relabels retained trajectories by achieved placement, and distills a reference-free distance-conditioned policy. DCRR-BC achieves 0.15 normalized distance MAE versus 0.28 for source-only BC across four interaction modes, with RL fine-tuning and hardware validation.
AI.motivation: A policy trained on a single fixed reference motion clip mainly reproduces that clip's demonstrated transport outcome, since transport termination is only demonstrated at the endpoint even though the trajectory passes through intermediate object displacements. The authors formalize this mismatch as the termination-versus-passage gap: intermediate displacements appear as passage states rather than termination-complete outcomes, limiting the controllability of the resulting policy.
AI.method: Distance-Conditioned Reference Recomposition (DCRR): the demonstrated termination segment is relocated to intermediate transport states, producing recomposed references. A frozen tracking teacher replays these recomposed references under closed-loop dynamics; retained trajectories are relabeled by their achieved object placements and distilled into a reference-free policy. This yields distance-conditioned supervision derived from the interaction behavior encoded in the source motion. RL fine-tuning is applied on top of the distilled policy.
AI.result: Across Carry, Kick-Push, Crouch-Push, and Drag, DCRR-BC produces command-dependent transport with an overall normalized distance MAE of 0.15, versus 0.28 for source-only behavior cloning. RL fine-tuning improves command response and execution robustness in the training simulator and under sim-to-sim transfer, and hardware experiments demonstrate transport-distance modulation across all four interaction modes.
AI.conclusion: DCRR converts a single retargeted motion clip into distance-conditioned loco-manipulation supervision, enabling command-dependent transport distance control that surpasses source-only behavior cloning, with gains from RL fine-tuning and demonstrated transfer to hardware across all four interaction modes.

title: Potential-Field Action Representation for Reinforcement Learning in Contact-Rich Manipulation
summary: Model-free reinforcement learning can acquire contact-rich robotic manipulation skills through trial-and-error interaction, but it often requires the policy to learn both task strategy and low-level motion generation. In this setting, the action representation is critical because it determines how policy outputs are converted into robot motion, shaping both exploration and physical execution. Direct Cartesian command interfaces require the policy to generate motion at every decision step, coupling task-level adaptation with continuous low-level control and increasing the learning burden. We propose PA-RL, a reinforcement-learning framework that uses artificial potential fields as the action representation. Instead of commanding motion directly, the policy adapts the parameters of an energy-like potential field, which generates a state-dependent guidance direction executed through a Cartesian impedance controller. We evaluate PA-RL on peg-in-hole insertion, a representative contact-rich task with nonlinear dynamics and discontinuous contact transitions. In simulation, PA-RL is compared with Cartesian velocity, Cartesian pose, and variable-impedance action spaces using the same RL algorithm. PA-RL is the only method to reach a 100% evaluation success rate within the allotted training time, while the best baseline reaches 92.6%. It also reduces joint-torque variation by 55.4% and Cartesian acceleration variation by 70.8% relative to the best baseline, without explicit motion-quality penalties in the reward. The simulation-trained policy further completes 9/9 real-robot insertions without fine-tuning, demonstrating the deployment feasibility of the learned potential-field interface.

AI.tldr: PA-RL uses artificial potential fields as the action representation for model-free RL, letting the policy adapt field parameters rather than command motion directly. On peg-in-hole insertion it reaches 100% simulation success (vs. 92.6% best baseline), improves motion quality, and transfers to 9/9 real-robot insertions without fine-tuning.
AI.motivation: Model-free RL for contact-rich manipulation requires learning both task strategy and low-level motion generation. Direct Cartesian command interfaces force the policy to produce motion at every decision step, coupling task-level adaptation with continuous low-level control and increasing the learning burden. The action representation is therefore critical, as it shapes exploration and physical execution.
AI.method: PA-RL is an RL framework that uses artificial potential fields as the action representation. Instead of commanding motion directly, the policy adapts the parameters of an energy-like potential field, which generates a state-dependent guidance direction executed through a Cartesian impedance controller. Evaluation is on peg-in-hole insertion, a contact-rich task with nonlinear dynamics and discontinuous contact transitions.
AI.result: In simulation, PA-RL is compared with Cartesian velocity, Cartesian pose, and variable-impedance action spaces under the same RL algorithm. PA-RL is the only method reaching 100% evaluation success within the allotted training time, while the best baseline reaches 92.6%. It reduces joint-torque variation by 55.4% and Cartesian acceleration variation by 70.8% relative to the best baseline, without explicit motion-quality reward penalties. The simulation-trained policy completes 9/9 real-robot insertions without fine-tuning.
AI.conclusion: Using potential-field parameters as the action representation decouples task-level adaptation from low-level motion generation, improving learning efficiency, success rate, and motion quality, and enabling zero-shot sim-to-real deployment for contact-rich manipulation.

title: Adaptive Rollout Truncation Based on Epistemic Uncertainty for Efficient Offline World Model Training
comment: 8 pages, 12 figures. Accepted at the IEEE/RSJ IROS 2026 Workshop "Rethinking Uncertainty for Modern Robotics Paradigms"
summary:
Accurate neural world models are central to model-based robotics, where they enable robots to predict future states from previously observed trajectories. Multi-step autoregressive training improves long-horizon prediction, but fixed rollout horizons also increase computational cost and can amplify early training errors when the model is still inaccurate. Existing training schemes typically use the same rollout length throughout optimization, independent of the model's current predictive reliability.
  We propose an epistemic uncertainty-driven adaptive rollout strategy for offline world model training following an auto-curriculum training scheme. Instead of always unrolling to a fixed horizon, the model terminates autoregressive rollouts once epistemic uncertainty exceeds a threshold calibrated from a warm-up phase. We study two uncertainty estimators: a five-head ensemble with a shared recurrent backbone and Monte Carlo Dropout. A two-stage warm-up procedure stabilizes uncertainty estimates before we enable adaptive truncation.
  Experiments on ANYmal-D and ANT show that ensemble-based adaptive truncation matches or improves the prediction accuracy of fixed-horizon training and the RWM-U baseline while requiring substantially fewer cumulative rollout steps. Training a world model on ANYmal-D following the presented approach reaches comparable final performance with the baselines with roughly 72% less rollout computation. These results indicate that epistemic uncertainty is useful not only for downstream policy regularization, but also for making world model training itself more compute-efficient.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes an epistemic uncertainty-driven adaptive rollout strategy for offline world model training, truncating autoregressive rollouts once calibrated uncertainty exceeds a threshold, achieving comparable accuracy with ~72% less rollout computation on ANYmal-D.
AI.motivation: Multi-step autoregressive training improves long-horizon prediction in neural world models, but fixed rollout horizons raise computational cost and amplify early training errors when the model is still inaccurate. Existing schemes use the same rollout length throughout optimization, ignoring the model's current predictive reliability.
AI.method: An auto-curriculum training scheme where rollouts terminate once epistemic uncertainty exceeds a threshold calibrated during warm-up. Two uncertainty estimators are studied: a five-head ensemble with a shared recurrent backbone, and Monte Carlo Dropout. A two-stage warm-up procedure stabilizes uncertainty estimates before adaptive truncation is enabled.
AI.result: On ANYmal-D and ANT, ensemble-based adaptive truncation matches or improves prediction accuracy of fixed-horizon training and the RWM-U baseline while requiring substantially fewer cumulative rollout steps. On ANYmal-D, comparable final performance is reached with roughly 72% less rollout computation.
AI.conclusion: Epistemic uncertainty is useful not only for downstream policy regularization but also for making world model training itself more compute-efficient.

title: SynthDemo-RL: Breaking the Zero-Reward Barrier in VLA Adaptation with LLM-Guided Synthetic Demonstrations
summary: Fine-tuning Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models commonly relies on human teleoperation demonstrations, while reinforcement learning (RL) with sparse binary rewards faces an exploration challenge when successful trajectories are rarely sampled. We propose SynthDemo-RL, a teacher-student framework in which an automated teacher converts simulator-privileged state into successful manipulation trajectories, a VLA student is distilled from them by supervised fine-tuning (SFT), and PPO with binary task-success rewards refines the student. We study reward coverage, the fraction of tasks for which at least one success is observed under the fixed evaluation protocol, as a complement to the average success rate. On LIBERO-PRO, a public benchmark of perturbed LIBERO tasks for which no demonstrations exist, 27 of 57 scored tasks are at exactly 0% success for a pi_0.5 policy fine-tuned on the original LIBERO tasks. Direct PPO from this policy, under the same PPO recipe and the same RL compute as SynthDemo-RL's refinement stage, rescues 10 of these 27 tasks and leaves 17 at 0%. SynthDemo-RL, with 50 synthesized trajectories per task and no new human demonstrations, rescues all 27 and reaches average success rates of 97.8% and 97.1% on the Position and Task axes of LIBERO-PRO, respectively. On standard LIBERO, the same pipeline reaches 96.0% with no human demonstrations, within 1.7 points of pi_0.5 trained on 50 human demonstrations per task. We further validate the pipeline on RoboTwin 2.0 and verify that trajectories from a policy trained in a MuJoCo twin execute open-loop on a physical robot.

AI.tldr: SynthDemo-RL is a teacher-student framework that synthesizes privileged-state manipulation trajectories to distill a VLA student via SFT, then refines it with PPO under sparse binary rewards, rescuing all previously unsolvable tasks on LIBERO-PRO without human demonstrations.
AI.motivation: Fine-tuning VLA models typically requires human teleoperation demonstrations, while RL with sparse binary rewards struggles with exploration when successful trajectories are rarely sampled. Existing policies fine-tuned on original tasks can score exactly 0% on perturbed tasks where no demonstrations exist, leaving direct PPO unable to rescue many of them.
AI.method: A teacher-student framework: (1) an automated teacher converts simulator-privileged state into successful manipulation trajectories; (2) a VLA student is distilled from these trajectories via supervised fine-tuning (SFT); (3) PPO with binary task-success rewards refines the student using the same recipe and RL compute as the direct-PPO baseline. Reward coverage, the fraction of tasks with at least one observed success under a fixed evaluation protocol, is introduced as a complement metric.
AI.result: On LIBERO-PRO, direct PPO from a pi_0.5 policy rescues 10 of 27 zero-success tasks, leaving 17 at 0%. SynthDemo-RL, using 50 synthesized trajectories per task and no new human demonstrations, rescues all 27 tasks, reaching 97.8% and 97.1% average success on the Position and Task axes. On standard LIBERO it reaches 96.0% with no human demonstrations, within 1.7 points of pi_0.5 trained on 50 human demonstrations per task. Validated on RoboTwin 2.0, with trajectories from a MuJoCo twin executing open-loop on a physical robot.
AI.conclusion: Synthesized privileged-state demonstrations combined with sparse-reward RL provide an effective, demonstration-free path to fine-tuning VLA models, achieving full reward coverage on perturbed tasks and near-parity with human-demonstration baselines, with sim-to-real transfer confirmed.

title: FORTE: Task-Adaptive Force Capability Optimization for Mobile Manipulators
summary: Effective physical interaction control in robotic manipulation requires not only kinematically feasible motion but also sufficient force-interaction capability. Existing redundancy resolution methods often ignore task-specific force demands or maximize the force capability indiscriminately, sacrificing dexterity when large force margins are unnecessary. We propose a task-oriented force capability optimization framework for redundant mobile manipulators. A Vision-Language Model (VLM) infers object physical properties from an RGB image and a task description, generating a desired task-force sequence that captures gravitational and inertial demands. We then define a task-oriented force capability metric as the signed distance between a task-force uncertainty ball and the dynamic residual force polytope (RFP), quantifying compatibility between task demands and the robot's remaining actuation capacity. This metric is incorporated, alongside manipulability, joint-limit avoidance, trajectory smoothness, and base-oscillation suppression, into a whole-body multi-objective trajectory-optimization problem. Experiments on a mobile manipulator performing lifting and single-point-holding tasks under varying payload conditions demonstrate that the proposed method provides sufficient force capability for heavy loads while preserving high manipulability for light loads. This yields a task-adaptive balance that fixed capability-maximizing baselines (RFP inscribed radius, RFP cone) and manipulability-only optimization fail to achieve. The core implementation is publicly available at https://github.com/yeying256/FORTE.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a task-oriented force capability optimization framework for redundant mobile manipulators, using a VLM to infer task-force demands from an image and task description, then optimizing whole-body trajectories under a signed-distance force-capability metric.
AI.motivation: Robotic physical interaction control needs both kinematically feasible motion and sufficient force-interaction capability. Existing redundancy resolution methods either ignore task-specific force demands or indiscriminately maximize force capability, sacrificing dexterity when large force margins are unnecessary.
AI.method: A Vision-Language Model infers object physical properties from an RGB image and task description, producing a desired task-force sequence reflecting gravitational and inertial demands. A task-oriented force capability metric is defined as the signed distance between a task-force uncertainty ball and the dynamic residual force polytope (RFP), measuring compatibility between task demands and remaining actuation capacity. This metric is integrated with manipulability, joint-limit avoidance, trajectory smoothness, and base-oscillation suppression into a whole-body multi-objective trajectory-optimization problem.
AI.result: Experiments on a mobile manipulator performing lifting and single-point-holding tasks under varying payloads show that the method provides sufficient force capability for heavy loads while preserving high manipulability for light loads, achieving a task-adaptive balance that fixed capability-maximizing baselines (RFP inscribed radius, RFP cone) and manipulability-only optimization fail to achieve.
AI.conclusion: Task-oriented force capability optimization enables an adaptive balance between force capability and dexterity for redundant mobile manipulators, outperforming fixed capability-maximizing and manipulability-only baselines. The core implementation is publicly available at https://github.com/yeying256/FORTE.

title: Outcome-Conditioned End-Effector Geometry Across Vision-Language-Action Policies
comment: 8 pages, 3 figures, 7 tables, 23 references. Submitted to ICRA 2027
summary: Vision-language-action (VLA) policies solve the same manipulation task through different action interfaces, but task success alone does not establish whether their physical executions agree. We study cross-policy end-effector geometry in 15,000 closed-loop LIBERO rollouts from four policies. The primary clean-condition analysis forms 3,600 configuration-matched, and therefore dependent, policy pairs. Both-success pairs have a median normalized dynamic time warping distance of 0.0120 m versus 0.0380 m when exactly one policy succeeds. This ordering holds in every task, every policy pair, and nine sampling and band-limited representations; however, the ratio varies severalfold across representations, so we report the direction rather than a fixed multiple. Both-failure pairs are more separated again but rest on thin, uneven support, so we report them as exploratory. Within successful executions, partner replacements separate more across tasks than across initial states. A matched baseline still reveals measurable, heterogeneous residual policy differences, so a low cross-policy distance does not imply interchangeability. Successful executions sit about as far from same-task demonstrations as those demonstrations sit from each other, compatible with task-associated geometry without separating training-data overlap from task constraints. A common 72-action window preserves the ordering but reduces its magnitude; endpoint and duration adjustment likewise leaves a positive mixed-outcome coefficient relative to both-success pairs, though its magnitude is specification-dependent. Under composite visual stress, policy rankings and pair composition change together.

AI.tldr: Across 15,000 LIBERO rollouts from four VLA policies, cross-policy end-effector trajectories are markedly closer when both policies succeed than when only one succeeds, an ordering robust across tasks, policy pairs, and representations.
AI.motivation: Task success is the standard metric for VLA policies, but it does not reveal whether different policies solve the same manipulation task through physically similar executions. The paper asks whether cross-policy execution geometry carries signal beyond binary success.
AI.method: Closed-loop LIBERO rollouts (15,000) from four VLA policies. The primary clean-condition analysis yields 3,600 configuration-matched (hence dependent) policy pairs. End-effector geometry is compared via normalized dynamic time warping (DTW) distance, with nine sampling and band-limited representations, plus a matched baseline, a 72-action window, endpoint/duration adjustments, and composite visual stress.
AI.result: Both-success pairs show median normalized DTW distance of 0.0120 m versus 0.0380 m for mixed-outcome (exactly one success) pairs. The ordering holds in every task, every policy pair, and all nine representations, though the ratio varies severalfold. Both-failure pairs separate more but rest on thin, uneven support (exploratory). Partner replacements separate more across tasks than across initial states. Residual, heterogeneous differences persist after matching; successful executions are about as far from same-task demonstrations as demonstrations are from each other. The 72-action window preserves the ordering but reduces magnitude; endpoint/duration adjustments keep a positive mixed-outcome coefficient. Under composite visual stress, policy rankings and pair composition shift jointly.
AI.conclusion: Cross-policy end-effector geometry tracks task success: low distance is associated with joint success, providing a geometric complement to binary success metrics. However, low distance does not imply interchangeability, and magnitude is representation- and specification-dependent, so only the direction of the effect is reported as robust.

title: DPed-VLN: A Benchmark for Socially Compliant Vision-and-Language Navigation in Dynamic Pedestrian Environments
summary: Vision-and-language navigation (VLN) has advanced rapidly in static indoor environments, but robots operating in human-populated spaces must ground language while responding to moving pedestrians and social-safety constraints. We present DPed-VLN, a Habitat 3.0 benchmark for dynamic-pedestrian VLN that couples 33,093 navigation episodes with paired global and prior-augmented instructions, ORCA-controlled humanoid pedestrians, socially constrained expert paths, and metrics that jointly assess navigation efficiency and social safety. DPed-VLN separates ordinary goal-oriented route guidance from prior-augmented instructions that expose dynamic-pedestrian cues for controlled analysis. To instantiate the benchmark, we introduce DPet (Dynamic Pedestrian-aware Network), a pedestrian-aware policy network trained with reinforcement learning and imitation learning. We further adapt representative state-of-the-art VLM-based navigation models, including NaVILA and StreamVLN, to DPed-VLN through LoRA fine-tuning. Experiments show that LoRA adaptation improves zero-shot VLM baselines in several success and safety metrics, especially reducing StreamVLN's collision rate. Among the evaluated methods, DPet-RL achieves the highest SR, SPL, and STL.

AI.tldr: DPed-VLN is a Habitat 3.0 benchmark for vision-and-language navigation among dynamic pedestrians, with 33,093 episodes, paired global/prior-augmented instructions, ORCA-controlled pedestrians, socially constrained expert paths, and joint efficiency/safety metrics; a pedestrian-aware network (DPet) and LoRA-adapted VLMs are evaluated, with DPet-RL leading on SR, SPL, and STL.
AI.motivation: VLN has progressed mainly in static indoor settings, yet real robots in human-populated spaces must ground language while responding to moving pedestrians and social-safety constraints. Existing benchmarks do not jointly capture dynamic pedestrians and social safety, limiting controlled analysis and evaluation.
AI.method: The authors build DPed-VLN on Habitat 3.0, coupling 33,093 navigation episodes with paired global and prior-augmented instructions, ORCA-controlled humanoid pedestrians, socially constrained expert paths, and metrics assessing both navigation efficiency and social safety. The benchmark separates ordinary goal-oriented guidance from prior-augmented instructions that expose dynamic-pedestrian cues. They introduce DPet, a pedestrian-aware policy network trained with reinforcement learning and imitation learning, and adapt VLM-based navigation models (NaVILA, StreamVLN) via LoRA fine-tuning.
AI.result: LoRA adaptation improves zero-shot VLM baselines on several success and safety metrics, notably reducing StreamVLN's collision rate. Among all evaluated methods, DPet-RL achieves the highest SR, SPL, and STL.
AI.conclusion: DPed-VLN provides a controlled benchmark for dynamic-pedestrian VLN with joint navigation and social-safety evaluation. Pedestrian-aware training (DPet-RL) outperforms LoRA-adapted VLM baselines, indicating the value of explicit pedestrian awareness under social constraints.

title: ForceTwin: Physics-informed Digital Twins for Robotic Manipulation from Instrumented Human Interaction
summary: Manipulating objects requires understanding not only their motion, but also the physical properties that determine it. For articulated objects, these include inertia, friction, and mechanisms such as springs or door closers, whose effects can vary with configuration and velocity. Such properties are not directly observable from appearance: visually identical doors may require very different effort to manipulate. Existing digital-twin pipelines recover primarily kinematics or assign static physical parameters from visual and language priors, which can yield physically implausible estimates. As a result, state-dependent mechanism dynamics remain unidentified and are not represented in standard asset formats. We present ForceTwin, a system for identifying physics-informed digital twins of articulated objects from instrumented human interaction. A person probes an object using a handheld force-sensing gripper, providing synchronized poses and interaction forces from which we estimate the articulation, parametric dynamics including inertia, Coulomb friction, viscous damping, and a structured neural residual capturing state-dependent mechanism forces. ForceTwin nearly halves the inertial-parameter error of a VLM prior. As a feedforward dynamics model for impedance control on a Spot and a Franka FR3, ForceTwin achieves 87% goal completion across nine object-embodiment pairs, compared with 60% using VLM-prior and 57% using kinematics-only twins, with the largest gains on objects whose strong mechanisms cause both baselines to stall. We further use the identified twins to train whole-body door-traversal policies and deploy them in the real world. Project Page: https://timengelbracht.github.io/forcetwin-website/

AI.tldr: ForceTwin identifies physics-informed digital twins of articulated objects from instrumented human interaction, estimating articulation plus parametric dynamics (inertia, Coulomb friction, viscous damping) and a structured neural residual for state-dependent mechanism forces, enabling better impedance control and door-traversal policies.
AI.motivation: Manipulating articulated objects requires understanding physical properties (inertia, friction, springs, door closers) that vary with configuration and velocity, yet these are not observable from appearance, and visually identical doors may need very different effort. Existing digital-twin pipelines recover mainly kinematics or assign static physical parameters from visual and language priors, yielding physically implausible estimates; state-dependent mechanism dynamics remain unidentified and are absent from standard asset formats.
AI.method: A person probes an object with a handheld force-sensing gripper, yielding synchronized poses and interaction forces. From these, ForceTwin estimates the articulation, parametric dynamics (inertia, Coulomb friction, viscous damping), and a structured neural residual that captures state-dependent mechanism forces.
AI.result: ForceTwin nearly halves the inertial-parameter error of a VLM prior. As a feedforward dynamics model for impedance control on a Spot and a Franka FR3, it achieves 87% goal completion across nine object-embodiment pairs, versus 60% for VLM-prior and 57% for kinematics-only twins, with the largest gains on objects whose strong mechanisms cause both baselines to stall. The identified twins are further used to train whole-body door-traversal policies deployed in the real world.
AI.conclusion: ForceTwin provides a practical route to physics-informed digital twins of articulated objects from instrumented human interaction, improving dynamics estimation and downstream control/policy learning over vision- and kinematics-only baselines, and enabling real-world deployment of whole-body door-traversal policies.

title: When Should a Failing Robot Ask? Initiating Corrective Human-Robot Dialogue from Audited Sensor Evidence
comment: Accepted at the IROS 2026 Workshop on Human-Robot Dialogue
summary: A robot that fails at a task faces the first decision in corrective dialogue: act on its own diagnosis, consult another onboard sensor, or interrupt a person. Choosing well requires knowing how much the robot's sensors reveal about the cause and how reliable the robot's own diagnosis is. We build a simulated benchmark in which every failure's true cause is known, because we injected it, and measure what each sensor reveals, with explicit checks against data leakage. Some failures are diagnosable from camera images; others only from the robot's force data (0.99 from force data, no image method above 0.55). We then test six open vision-language models. Their behavior tracks the surface of the prompt, not the evidence: moving the refusal option from last to first in the answer list collapses refusal rates from 78-100% to 0-6% in three of the six swept model-and-family pairs. Accuracy from frames stays at or below a majority-class baseline under every prompt variant, with or without worked examples, and stated confidence carries no information about correctness. Handing the same models the force data as ten lines of text produces the first above-baseline diagnoses, in four of the six models: much of the failure reflects missing sensor data, not missing ability. We pose the choice as a three-action decision problem, act, consult your own sensors, or ask a human, whose optimal policy follows from measured accuracy. The models do not follow it, and their ask rates ignore a fourfold change in question cost. One question to a human still lifts them from that baseline to roughly the answerer's own reliability (0.70-0.81 when they ask). The decision to ask should be tied to measured accuracy and stated costs, not to the model's confidence.

AI.tldr: A simulated failure-diagnosis benchmark with known injected causes shows that vision-language models diagnose from camera frames at or below majority-class baseline, are highly prompt-sensitive in refusal behavior, and ignore question cost—yet still recover to roughly human-answerer reliability (0.70-0.81) when allowed to ask one question. Corrective-dialogue decisions should be tied to measured sensor accuracy and stated costs, not model confidence.
AI.motivation: A failing robot must decide among acting on its own diagnosis, consulting another onboard sensor, or interrupting a human. Making this choice well requires knowing what each sensor reveals about the failure cause and how reliable the robot's own diagnosis is, but current vision-language models provide neither calibrated accuracy nor cost-sensitive asking behavior.
AI.method: Build a simulated benchmark where each failure's true cause is known by injection, and measure per-sensor diagnostic informativeness with explicit data-leakage checks. Evaluate six open vision-language models under multiple prompt variants (option ordering, worked examples) on frame-based diagnosis, confidence statements, and refusal/ask rates. Provide force data as ten lines of text to isolate the effect of missing sensor data. Formalize the setting as a three-action decision problem (act, consult own sensors, ask a human) whose optimal policy follows from measured accuracy, and test compliance including a fourfold change in question cost.
AI.result: Some failures are diagnosable only from force data (0.99 from force data, no image method above 0.55). Model behavior tracks prompt surface rather than evidence: moving the refusal option from last to first collapses refusal rates from 78-100% to 0-6% in three of six swept model-and-family pairs. Frame-based accuracy stays at or below a majority-class baseline across all prompt variants, with or without worked examples, and stated confidence carries no information about correctness. Providing force data as text yields the first above-baseline diagnoses in four of six models, indicating much of the failure is missing sensor data rather than missing ability. Models do not follow the optimal three-action policy, and their ask rates ignore a fourfold change in question cost. One question to a human still lifts them from baseline to roughly the answerer's reliability (0.70-0.81 when they ask).
AI.conclusion: Corrective-dialogue asking should be governed by measured sensor accuracy and stated costs rather than the model's stated confidence. Much observed model failure stems from absent sensor modalities (e.g., force data), and a single human question can substantially recover performance, but principled, cost-sensitive decision policies must be imposed externally because current models do not exhibit them.

title: Skel-WAM: A Hand-Skeleton-Conditioned World Action Model for Human-to-Robot Manipulation Transfer
summary: Robot demonstrations are expensive to collect and often provide limited distributional coverage of task variations. Human videos offer a low-cost source of complementary manipulation experience, but learning from them requires bridging embodiment gaps in visual appearance and action spaces. We introduce Skel-WAM, a world action model that bridges these differences through a unified hand-skeleton motion interface. The key insight is to align human and robot motion through a common hand topology, combining skeleton overlays that ground motion in the scene with structured 2.5-D keypoints that encode explicit hand kinematics. Video and Keypoint Experts jointly learn visual and skeletal dynamics through a Mixture-of-Transformers, while a separate robot-trained Action Expert maps these predictions to executable controls. This separation enables human and robot demonstrations to directly supervise shared dynamics without requiring robot action labels for human videos. Across four real-world bimanual tasks and seven simulated tasks, Skel-WAM achieves average success rates of 79.86% and 63.29%, surpassing the strongest baseline by 22.22 and 8.28 percentage points, respectively. Human-robot cotraining more than doubles real-world success on task variations absent from robot training data, from 38.89% to 86.11%. These results demonstrate that a shared skeletal interface enables joint learning across human and robot data and expands robot task coverage through complementary human demonstrations.

AI.tldr: Skel-WAM is a world action model that bridges human-robot embodiment gaps via a unified hand-skeleton motion interface, enabling cotraining from human videos and robot demonstrations without robot action labels for human data.
AI.motivation: Robot demonstrations are costly and cover limited task variations, while human videos are cheap complementary experience but suffer from visual and action-space embodiment gaps.
AI.method: Align human and robot motion through a common hand topology using skeleton overlays grounded in the scene plus structured 2.5-D keypoints encoding hand kinematics. Video and Keypoint Experts learn visual and skeletal dynamics via a Mixture-of-Transformers; a separate robot-trained Action Expert maps predictions to executable controls.
AI.result: Average success rates of 79.86% (4 real-world bimanual tasks) and 63.29% (7 simulated tasks), exceeding the strongest baseline by 22.22 and 8.28 percentage points. Human-robot cotraining raises real-world success on unseen task variations from 38.89% to 86.11%.
AI.conclusion: A shared skeletal interface enables joint learning across human and robot data and expands robot task coverage through complementary human demonstrations.

title: SABER: Learning Attention-based Semantic Affordance for Legged Locomotion
summary: Perceptive legged locomotion has advanced rapidly by integrating terrain geometry into learned policies, yet the integration of terrain meaning remains sparse: a pipe, a patch of grass, or a fragile box may be geometrically traversable while being inappropriate for contact. In industrial environments, where legged robots increasingly operate, a single misplaced step can damage fragile equipment, destabilize the robot, or endanger the site. To address this, we introduce SABER, a planner-free reinforcement-learning policy that jointly reasons about terrain geometry and semantic contact permission. The policy consumes a unified terrain-affordance map, where each cell encodes local 3D geometry and a semantic contact cost. We augment cross-attention with a learned, signed semantic bias: an additive term on the attention logits, gated by the contact cost, that reweights flagged cells by their distance from the nearest foot. A hazard therefore reshapes attention where it can still affect the next foothold, and its influence fades where it cannot. The resulting policy selects footholds on permitted support and keeps the leg clear of forbidden regions throughout the swing phase. We perform a systematic ablation that isolates the contribution of each architectural component; removing the semantic bias alone increases forbidden contacts by 55% while velocity tracking is unchanged. We validate the policy on a Unitree B2, demonstrating sim-to-real semantic contact selection across indoor and outdoor environments and four semantic obstacle classes.

AI.tldr: SABER is a planner-free RL policy for legged locomotion that jointly reasons about terrain geometry and semantic contact permission via a unified terrain-affordance map and a signed semantic bias in cross-attention, enabling semantic contact selection on a Unitree B2.
AI.motivation: Perceptive legged locomotion has integrated terrain geometry but largely ignores terrain meaning: objects such as a pipe, grass patch, or fragile box may be geometrically traversable yet inappropriate for contact. In industrial settings, a single misplaced step can damage fragile equipment, destabilize the robot, or endanger the site, so contact permission must be reasoned about alongside geometry.
AI.method: The authors propose SABER, a planner-free reinforcement-learning policy that consumes a unified terrain-affordance map where each cell encodes local 3D geometry and a semantic contact cost. They augment cross-attention with a learned signed semantic bias: an additive term on attention logits, gated by contact cost, that reweights flagged cells by distance to the nearest foot. This makes hazards reshape attention where they can affect the next foothold and fade where they cannot, yielding footholds on permitted support while keeping the leg clear of forbidden regions during swing.
AI.result: A systematic ablation isolates each architectural component; removing the semantic bias alone increases forbidden contacts by 55% while velocity tracking is unchanged. The policy is validated on a Unitree B2, demonstrating sim-to-real semantic contact selection across indoor and outdoor environments and four semantic obstacle classes.
AI.conclusion: Jointly encoding geometry and semantic contact permission within a single affordance representation, and modulating attention by a distance-gated semantic bias, enables effective semantic contact selection without a planner, transferring to real hardware.

title: Tilt as a Certified Resource: Preserving Motor Wrench-Rate Authority on Articulated Multirotors
comment: This work has been submitted to the IEEE for possible publication
summary: Fully-actuated multirotor aerial vehicles must not only track nominal wrenches but retain the "readiness" to modulate them rapidly under disturbances. Classical effort-minimizing allocators ignore this dynamic limit, whereas maximizing readiness leads to topologically disconnected optimal sheets demanding physically impossible actuator rates. Enforcing a readiness safety floor on fixed-geometry symmetric platforms further encounters a zero-sum degeneracy: motor-speed redistribution cannot improve authority without conceding wrench tracking. This paper uses active morphology to break the degeneracy, treating servo tilt as a geometric resource supplying authority-recovery directions unavailable to static rotors. We construct a configuration-dependent, motor-only readiness certificate - the log-volume of the reachable wrench-rate set - that explicitly excludes servo capacity, preventing a "ghost capacity fallacy" in which the certificate would falsely credit slow mechanical kinematic limits instead of collapsing accurately at motor saturation. The certificate is enforced as a Control Barrier Function (CBF) within a Unified Physical-Command Quadratic Program acting on motor torques and servo setpoints. Closed-loop simulations of an articulated octorotor under severe gust disturbances show classical allocators diverging and uncertified articulated allocators violating the safety floor, while the proposed CBF filter bounds the system state and preserves vehicle authority.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces active morphology (servo tilt) and a motor-only readiness certificate, enforced via a Control Barrier Function in a unified quadratic program, to preserve dynamic wrench-modulation authority in fully-actuated multirotors under disturbances.
AI.motivation: Fully-actuated multirotors must not only track nominal wrenches but retain "readiness" to modulate them rapidly under disturbances. Classical effort-minimizing allocators ignore this dynamic limit, while maximizing readiness produces topologically disconnected optimal sheets requiring impossible actuator rates. On fixed-geometry symmetric platforms, enforcing a readiness safety floor suffers a zero-sum degeneracy: motor-speed redistribution cannot improve authority without conceding wrench tracking.
AI.method: Active morphology is used to break the degeneracy, treating servo tilt as a geometric resource providing authority-recovery directions unavailable to static rotors. The authors construct a configuration-dependent, motor-only readiness certificate - the log-volume of the reachable wrench-rate set - that excludes servo capacity to avoid a "ghost capacity fallacy." This certificate is enforced as a Control Barrier Function within a Unified Physical-Command Quadratic Program acting on motor torques and servo setpoints.
AI.result: Closed-loop simulations of an articulated octorotor under severe gust disturbances show classical allocators diverging and uncertified articulated allocators violating the safety floor, whereas the proposed CBF filter bounds the system state and preserves vehicle authority.
AI.conclusion: Using active morphology with a motor-only readiness certificate enforced as a CBF in a unified QP preserves vehicle authority and bounding system state, overcoming classical allocator divergence and the zero-sum degeneracy of fixed-geometry platforms.

title: A High-Payload Wall-Climbing Robot Using Passive Bistable Suction Cups
comment: 2026 IEEE International Conference on Robotics & Automation (ICRA)
summary: Wall-climbing robots capable of scaling vertical surfaces could help automate hazardous or labor intensive tasks such as window washing, inspection, maintenance, and construction. Active adhesion methods achieve higher payload capacities, but require power to maintain their grip. Passive adhesion devices such as suction cups are an attractive option for such robots because they do not require power to maintain their grip, but they are limited by their payload capacity. This work presents a novel high-payload wall-climbing robot that utilizes passive bistable suction cups to generate adhesion without needing to be pushed into the wall. The robot features a track-based system that automatically engages and disengages bistable suction cups to achieve locomotion on smooth surfaces. The robot is able to achieve vertical wall climbing on glass, wood, metal, and painted surfaces, sideways and upside-down climbing, and is able to tow a payload of 7.940 kg (with a payload-to-weight ratio of 2.25).

AI.tldr: A track-based wall-climbing robot uses passive bistable suction cups for power-free adhesion, achieving vertical, sideways, and upside-down climbing with a payload-to-weight ratio of 2.25.
AI.motivation: Active adhesion methods offer high payload capacity but need continuous power to maintain grip, while passive devices like suction cups save power but suffer from limited payload. The work aims to combine the benefits of passive adhesion with high payload capacity for wall-climbing robots performing hazardous or labor-intensive tasks.
AI.method: The robot employs passive bistable suction cups that generate adhesion without being pushed into the wall, integrated with a track-based locomotion system that automatically engages and disengages the cups for movement on smooth surfaces.
AI.result: The robot achieves vertical climbing on glass, wood, metal, and painted surfaces, can climb sideways and upside-down, and tows a payload of 7.940 kg with a payload-to-weight ratio of 2.25.
AI.conclusion: The proposed design demonstrates that passive bistable suction cups combined with a track-based engagement mechanism enable high-payload wall climbing without continuous power for adhesion, validating the approach across multiple surface types and orientations.

title: CounterPlay: Counterfactual Post-Training for Self-Play Driving Policies
summary: Self-play in high-throughput simulators yields driving policies with robust closed-loop performance, but improvement per unit of simulation diminishes as training scales. Policies learn to handle common situations early, while further rollouts repeatedly encounter unresolved failures. Post-training offers an opportunity to target these failures, but existing methods primarily evaluate alternative actions or continuations at visited states, although successful recovery may require changing driving style earlier. We propose CounterPlay, a counterfactual self-play post-training approach that backtracks from failed tasks and retries them under alternate driving styles. CounterPlay rests on three key components. First, failure-driven backtracking uses the policy's value estimates to select an earlier stored state from which to retry the task. Second, reward conditioning enables a single policy to retry the task from this state using candidate styles ranging from cautious to aggressive. Third, CounterPlay retains task-completing retries only if no other vehicle incurs a new or earlier collision or off-road event relative to the factual branch. Retries that pass verification with fresh randomness are then distilled into the policy under its deployment condition. On BehaviorBench, CounterPlay achieves state-of-the-art scores on both the Interactive and Random splits across all eight traffic regimes using 1B post-training transitions, which is just 1% of the anchor's 100B self-play training budget. Improvements over the anchor hold across all three evaluated driving styles. CounterPlay resolves a substantial fraction of the anchor's timeout cases on BehaviorBench and achieves a balance between task completion and safety that neither continued self-play nor adopting a more aggressive driving style attains.

AI.tldr: CounterPlay is a counterfactual self-play post-training method that backtracks from failed driving tasks and retries them under alternate driving styles, achieving state-of-the-art BehaviorBench results with only 1% of the anchor's training budget.
AI.motivation: Self-play in high-throughput simulators yields robust closed-loop driving policies, but returns diminish as training scales: policies master common situations early while further rollouts keep hitting unresolved failures. Post-training could target these failures, yet existing methods only evaluate alternative actions or continuations at visited states, whereas successful recovery may require changing driving style earlier.
AI.method: CounterPlay has three components: (1) failure-driven backtracking uses the policy's value estimates to pick an earlier stored state from which to retry the task; (2) reward conditioning lets a single policy retry from that state with candidate styles from cautious to aggressive; (3) verification retains task-completing retries only if no other vehicle incurs a new or earlier collision or off-road event versus the factual branch. Verified retries with fresh randomness are distilled into the policy under its deployment condition.
AI.result: On BehaviorBench, CounterPlay achieves state-of-the-art scores on both Interactive and Random splits across all eight traffic regimes using 1B post-training transitions, just 1% of the anchor's 100B self-play budget. Gains over the anchor hold across all three evaluated driving styles. It resolves a substantial fraction of the anchor's timeout cases and attains a task completion/safety balance neither continued self-play nor a more aggressive style achieves.
AI.conclusion: Counterfactual self-play post-training that backtracks from failures and retries under alternate driving styles is a highly sample-efficient way to improve closed-loop driving policies, fixing residual failures while preserving a favorable safety-completion trade-off.

title: Towards Fine-Grained Object Manipulation: SAM3-Guided Visuomotor Policy with Persistent Memory Learning and Focused Visual Conditioning
comment: 8 pages, 7 figures. Submitted to IEEE ICRA 2027
summary: Fine-grained object (FO) manipulation requires robots to distinguish a specified FO from visually similar objects and execute actions reliably despite scene distractors. However, scene-level visual conditioning lacks explicit object selection, while category-level guidance cannot reliably distinguish FOs within the same category. We present a SAM3-guided visuomotor framework that addresses these challenges through persistent object memory and focused visual conditioning. First, we introduce FO Memory-driven SAM3 (FOM-SAM3), which learns reusable FO memory tokens from limited multi-view registration images while keeping SAM3 fully frozen. Through one-vs-rest learning, these tokens encode persistent memories for localizing target FOs and rejecting similar alternatives, which can be stored in a memory bank. Second, we propose Focused Spatial-Appearance Encoding (FSAE), which combines in-FO local appearance features with explicit bounding-box coordinates to condition action policies including Diffusion Policy (DP) and Action Chunking with Transformers (ACT). The effectiveness of the proposed FOM-SAM3 was validated on the FO-30 dataset comprising 30 physical objects across four coarse categories. Across three real-robot FO manipulation tasks, our FOM-SAM3-guided policies demonstrated robustness against distractors, discrimination ability among similar FOs, and extendibility to new FOs.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a SAM3-guided visuomotor framework with persistent object memory (FOM-SAM3) and Focused Spatial-Appearance Encoding (FSAE) to enable fine-grained object manipulation by reliably localizing target objects among visually similar distractors.
AI.motivation: Fine-grained object manipulation requires robots to distinguish a specified FO from visually similar objects and act reliably amid scene distractors. Existing approaches fall short: scene-level visual conditioning lacks explicit object selection, while category-level guidance cannot reliably distinguish FOs within the same category.
AI.method: The framework has two components. (1) FOM-SAM3 learns reusable FO memory tokens from limited multi-view registration images while keeping SAM3 fully frozen; via one-vs-rest learning, these tokens encode persistent memories for localizing target FOs and rejecting similar alternatives, storable in a memory bank. (2) FSAE combines in-FO local appearance features with explicit bounding-box coordinates to condition action policies, including Diffusion Policy (DP) and Action Chunking with Transformers (ACT).
AI.result: FOM-SAM3 was validated on the FO-30 dataset, comprising 30 physical objects across four coarse categories. Across three real-robot FO manipulation tasks, the FOM-SAM3-guided policies demonstrated robustness against distractors, discrimination among similar FOs, and extendibility to new FOs.
AI.conclusion: Combining persistent object memory with focused visual conditioning enables reliable fine-grained object manipulation, achieving distractor robustness, fine-grained discrimination, and generalization to novel objects.

title: RAYA: Learning Where and When to Intervene for Robot Recovery
summary: A robot can predict failure and still be unable to prevent it. By the time a safety mechanism reacts, the nominal plan may already have spent the control authority that recovery requires, and fixed task priorities may block whatever response remains. Our key insight is that both aspects are decided inside the controller. Recoverability must inform actions while they are chosen rather than veto them afterward, and task objectives must be adapted as recoverability shrinks. Building on this, we present RAYA, a hybrid learned-analytic framework that places a learned finite-horizon recoverability margin inside an optimal controller with hard constraints and pairs it with a bounded learned scheduler that shifts task weights to facilitate recovery. Across 7,200 simulation episodes per controller spanning quadrotor and autonomous-vehicle benchmarks, RAYA not only improves survival rates, but also transfers the learned components zero-shot to unseen trajectories, disturbances, plant shifts, and friction layouts. We developed an embedded realization of RAYA and deployed it on-board a 35g Crazyflie quadrotor. Across 40 combined hardware flights under wind with either aerodynamic mismatch or an unmodeled 40% motor-command loss, each of three baselines fails in all trials, while RAYA completes 10/10 six-cycle missions. Project Website: https://raya-control.github.io/.

AI.tldr: RAYA is a hybrid learned-analytic control framework that embeds a learned finite-horizon recoverability margin inside an optimal constrained controller and pairs it with a bounded learned scheduler that shifts task weights to preserve recovery capacity, improving survival and enabling zero-shot transfer and on-board deployment.
AI.motivation: A robot may anticipate failure yet still be unable to prevent it: by the time a safety mechanism reacts, the nominal plan has often already depleted the control authority needed for recovery, and fixed task priorities may obstruct any remaining response. The paper argues both problems originate inside the controller, so recoverability must shape action selection rather than veto actions afterward, and task objectives must adapt as recoverability shrinks.
AI.method: RAYA is a hybrid learned-analytic framework. It places a learned finite-horizon recoverability margin inside an optimal controller with hard constraints, so that recoverability informs actions while they are chosen, and combines it with a bounded learned scheduler that shifts task weights to facilitate recovery. The system was also realized as an embedded implementation deployed on-board a 35g Crazyflie quadrotor.
AI.result: Across 7,200 simulation episodes per controller on quadrotor and autonomous-vehicle benchmarks, RAYA improves survival rates and transfers its learned components zero-shot to unseen trajectories, disturbances, plant shifts, and friction layouts. In 40 combined hardware flights under wind with either aerodynamic mismatch or an unmodeled 40% motor-command loss, each of three baselines fails in all trials, whereas RAYA completes 10/10 six-cycle missions.
AI.conclusion: Embedding learned recoverability awareness within a constrained optimal controller and adapting task priorities through a bounded learned scheduler yields safer control that generalizes zero-shot and works on resource-constrained hardware, outperforming baselines in both simulation and real-world flight.

title: NeuRIO: A Streaming Neural Estimator for Zero-Shot Sim-to-Real Multi-Robot Relative Inertial Odometry
summary: We present NeuRIO, a streaming neural estimator for anchor-free 6-DoF relative inertial odometry using only identified inter-robot bearings, ranges, and IMU measurements. NeuRIO canonicalizes measurements into gravity-aligned coordinates, represents robots as nodes and mutual observations as factors, and uses attention for spatial reasoning and GRUs for temporal modeling. As a graph network, NeuRIO applies shared node-wise and factor-wise operators throughout the network, enabling it to handle different team sizes and time-varying observation graphs. NeuRIO is trained on a simulator that couples various motion patterns, device-level sensor characteristics, and diverse, realistic modeled, and temporally persistent sensor corruptions. In this way, NeuRIO achieves zero-shot sim-to-real transfer. Across $24$ real-world sequences, NeuRIO achieves $14.1\,\mathrm{cm}$ position RMSE and $3.9^\circ$ rotation RMSE. More importantly, NeuRIO demonstrates strong computational scalability, maintaining an update cost below $20\,\mathrm{ms}$ with up to $400$ robots in simulation, while optimization-based methods exceed $20\,\mathrm{ms}$ at only $24$ robots. Moreover, even trained on limited team sizes, NeuRIO transfers directly to unseen larger teams without architectural or parameter changes.

AI.tldr: NeuRIO is a streaming graph-based neural estimator for anchor-free 6-DoF relative inertial odometry from inter-robot bearing, range, and IMU measurements, achieving zero-shot sim-to-real transfer and high scalability.
AI.motivation: Multi-robot relative odometry from onboard sensing is challenging due to unknown anchors, gravity alignment, time-varying observation graphs, and sensor corruptions. Optimization-based methods do not scale well with team size and are slow, motivating a learned, scalable estimator that transfers from simulation to real robots.
AI.method: NeuRIO canonicalizes measurements into gravity-aligned coordinates, models robots as nodes and mutual observations as factors in a graph network with shared node-wise and factor-wise operators, uses attention for spatial reasoning and GRUs for temporal modeling. It is trained on a simulator coupling motion patterns, device-level sensor characteristics, and realistic temporally persistent sensor corruptions to enable zero-shot sim-to-real transfer.
AI.result: Across 24 real-world sequences, NeuRIO achieves 14.1 cm position RMSE and 3.9° rotation RMSE. It maintains an update cost below 20 ms with up to 400 robots in simulation, whereas optimization-based methods exceed 20 ms at only 24 robots. It also transfers directly to unseen larger teams without architectural or parameter changes.
AI.conclusion: NeuRIO provides accurate, anchor-free 6-DoF relative inertial odometry with strong computational scalability and zero-shot sim-to-real generalization, outperforming optimization-based methods in scalability and transferring to larger unseen teams.

title: AgenticSwarm: Semantic Perception and Adaptive Task Allocation for Heterogeneous Multi-UAV Missions
summary: Multi UAV missions in complex environments require the system to understand both the surrounding scene and the intent of a human operator while maintaining feasible task allocation as mission conditions change. This paper presents AgenticSwarm, an agentic framework for semantic perception and adaptive task allocation in heterogeneous multi UAV missions. An agent interprets aerial imagery and natural language instructions to construct a grounded mission representation that links perceived objects and regions with task requirements, capability constraints, and mission dependencies. This information augments a constrained task allocation process in which obstacle aware path feasibility, energy consumption, and protected return home requirements are incorporated before assignment. During execution, changes such as UAV failure, battery degradation, or task modification trigger residual mission reconstruction from the current system state, while completed work and reconnaissance progress are retained. AgenticSwarm is evaluated across five diverse Gazebo environments and an indoor real test environment, demonstrating its ability to connect semantic reasoning with constrained allocation and adaptive multi UAV mission execution. Compared with a Grounding DINO+SAM~2.1 perception baseline, the SAM3-based pipeline improves class-aware recall by 25.2 percentage points (pp) and semantic label accuracy by 29.5 pp. Ablating residual mission replanning increases mean repeated work from 0% to 61.7% and post-event recovery time by 58.6%, highlighting the contribution of adaptive replanning to mission execution.

AI.tldr: AgenticSwarm is an agentic framework that unifies semantic perception with constrained, adaptive task allocation for heterogeneous multi-UAV missions, using residual mission reconstruction to handle dynamic failures, and it outperforms a Grounding DINO+SAM 2.1 baseline on recall and label accuracy.
AI.motivation: Multi-UAV missions in complex environments demand simultaneous understanding of the scene and human operator intent, while preserving feasible task allocation as mission conditions change. Existing approaches struggle to connect high-level semantic reasoning with physically constrained allocation under dynamic events such as UAV failure, battery degradation, or task modification.
AI.method: An agent interprets aerial imagery and natural language instructions to build a grounded mission representation linking perceived objects/regions to task requirements, capability constraints, and mission dependencies. This representation augments a constrained task allocation process that incorporates obstacle-aware path feasibility, energy consumption, and protected return-home requirements before assignment. During execution, mission changes trigger residual mission reconstruction from the current system state while retaining completed work and reconnaissance progress. A SAM3-based perception pipeline is used for semantic grounding.
AI.result: Evaluated across five diverse Gazebo environments and an indoor real test environment. The SAM3-based pipeline improves class-aware recall by 25.2 percentage points and semantic label accuracy by 29.5 pp over a Grounding DINO+SAM 2.1 baseline. Ablating residual mission replanning raises mean repeated work from 0% to 61.7% and increases post-event recovery time by 58.6%.
AI.conclusion: AgenticSwarm successfully connects semantic reasoning with constrained allocation and adaptive multi-UAV mission execution. The results highlight the contribution of residual mission replanning to mission execution efficiency and confirm the value of grounded mission representations for dynamic, heterogeneous multi-UAV operations.

title: A Novel Path-Tracking Algorithm for Automated Tractor-Trailer Forward and Backward Maneuvers
summary: Fully autonomous tractor--trailer systems are increasingly deployed in logistics, agriculture, and industrial environments, where precise and robust path-tracking capabilities are essential. However, the articulation between the tractor and the trailer introduces additional nonlinearities and significantly complicates lateral and longitudinal control, particularly during reversing maneuvers. This paper introduces a novel path-tracking algorithm specifically designed for articulated vehicles with a single trailer. The proposed method combines a lateral control law applied at the trailer level with a short-horizon predictive adjustment of the tractor steering angle, ensuring stable convergence toward the desired path in both forward and backward motion. The approach is geometry-based and requires no per-vehicle calibration or training. Simulation studies in a high-fidelity physics simulator demonstrate the ability of the controller to match or outperform classical and state-of-the-art methods in terms of accuracy, stability, and robustness to disturbances.

AI.tldr: A geometry-based path-tracking algorithm for tractor-trailer (single trailer) systems that applies lateral control at the trailer level with short-horizon predictive adjustment of the tractor steering angle, achieving stable convergence in forward and reverse motion without per-vehicle calibration or training.
AI.motivation: Fully autonomous tractor-trailer systems are increasingly deployed in logistics, agriculture, and industrial environments requiring precise, robust path tracking.
