The articulation joint introduces additional nonlinearities that complicate lateral and longitudinal control, especially during reversing maneuvers.
AI.method: The method combines a lateral control law applied at the trailer level with a short-horizon predictive adjustment of the tractor steering angle to ensure stable convergence to the desired path in both forward and backward motion. It is geometry-based and requires no per-vehicle calibration or training.
AI.result: High-fidelity physics simulator studies show the controller matches or outperforms classical and state-of-the-art methods in accuracy, stability, and robustness to disturbances.
AI.conclusion: The proposed trailer-level lateral control with predictive steering adjustment provides a practical, calibration-free solution for robust path tracking of articulated vehicles, effective in both forward and reverse maneuvers.

title: ZeroTouch: Tactile-Supervised Visual Contact Estimation for Contact-Rich Manipulation
summary: Reliable robotic grasping benefits from estimating the evolving physical interaction and selecting a grasp-dependent compression target. Tactile sensors provide direct interaction measurements but require dedicated hardware at deployment. We introduce ZeroTouch, a tactile-supervised framework that predicts dense contact deformation, the instantaneous six-axis wrench, and a grasp-dependent desired compression target from wrist RGB observations, gripper state, and local gravity direction. Tactile measurements are used only as privileged supervision during training and are not required at deployment. On the full validation set, the complete architecture reduces normal-force MAE from 2.017 N for a state-only baseline to 0.531 N. In physical evaluation with 20 trials per condition, ZeroTouch achieves 95% success on an unseen object, 80% in a seen-object/unseen-grasp condition, and 90% under a content/load shift. Under the same evaluation protocol, OpenVLA achieves 25%, 40%, and 55%, while SmolVLA achieves 10%, 25%, and 35%, respectively.

AI.tldr: ZeroTouch predicts dense contact deformation, six-axis wrench, and a grasp-dependent compression target from wrist RGB and gripper state, using tactile only as privileged training supervision. It cuts normal-force MAE to 0.531 N and achieves 80-95% physical grasp success versus 10-55% for OpenVLA and SmolVLA.
AI.motivation: Reliable robotic grasping depends on estimating evolving physical interaction and choosing a grasp-dependent compression target. Tactile sensors give direct interaction measurements but require dedicated hardware at deployment, motivating a tactile-free inference approach.
AI.method: ZeroTouch is a tactile-supervised framework that predicts dense contact deformation, instantaneous six-axis wrench, and a grasp-dependent desired compression target from wrist RGB observations, gripper state, and local gravity direction. Tactile measurements serve only as privileged supervision during training and are absent at deployment.
AI.result: On the full validation set, the complete architecture reduces normal-force MAE from 2.017 N (state-only baseline) to 0.531 N. In physical evaluation (20 trials per condition), ZeroTouch reaches 95% success on an unseen object, 80% on seen-object/unseen-grasp, and 90% under content/load shift; OpenVLA reaches 25/40/55% and SmolVLA 10/25/35%.
AI.conclusion: Tactile privileged supervision enables accurate contact/wrench estimation and compression-target prediction from non-tactile signals, yielding substantially higher and more robust grasping success than VLA baselines across unseen objects, grasps, and load shifts.

title: Visual Proactivity: Enhancing Human-Robot Collaboration Through Intent Communication
comment: Accepted for publication at the 2026 IEEE International Conference on Robotics and Automation (ICRA)
summary: As robots transition from performing repetitive tasks to collaborating with humans, understanding human intent becomes crucial to effective interaction. Anticipation enables robots to predict human actions, while proactivity allows them to take initiative and guide human behavior toward optimal outcomes. Although research has largely focused on how robots infer and respond to human intentions, less attention has been paid to how robots communicate their own intent. This paper introduces visual proactivity, a novel, simple yet effective approach that enables robots to communicate their intentions through visual feedback, influencing human behavior and enhancing transparency and fluency. We develop and evaluate proactive robotic behaviors in a human-to-robot handover scenario, where a user study validates human perception of reactive, anticipatory, and proactive behaviors. The results demonstrate that effective visual proactivity fosters better alignment and coordination, paving the way for more intuitive human-robot collaboration.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces "visual proactivity," a simple yet effective method for robots to communicate their own intentions via visual feedback, and validates it in a human-to-robot handover study.
AI.motivation: As robots shift from repetitive tasks to human collaboration, understanding human intent is key. Prior work focuses on robots inferring and reacting to human intent, but how robots communicate their own intent is under-explored, limiting transparency and fluency.
AI.method: The authors propose visual proactivity, letting robots convey intentions through visual feedback to influence human behavior. They design and evaluate proactive robotic behaviors in a human-to-robot handover scenario, using a user study to assess human perception of reactive, anticipatory, and proactive behaviors.
AI.result: The user study validates human perception of the three behavior types and shows that effective visual proactivity fosters better alignment and coordination between human and robot.
AI.conclusion: Visual proactivity enhances transparency and fluency in human-robot interaction, paving the way for more intuitive collaboration; robot-to-human intent communication merits further attention.

title: When Should Robots Intervene? Balancing Engagement and Intrusiveness in Human-Robot Interaction
comment: Accepted for publication at the 35th IEEE International Conference on Robot and Human Interactive Communication (RO-MAN 2026)
summary: Designing effective Human-Robot Interaction in task-oriented settings requires carefully balancing user engagement with socially acceptable levels of robot intrusiveness. In this paper, we examine how different robot intervention strategies shape user experience, interaction dynamics, perceived intrusiveness, and sense of support. We compare two approaches: a continuous engagement-seeking robot strategy, and a context-aware strategy that selectively intervenes based on the user's state and task context. Both approaches rely on multimodal behavioral cues, including body orientation and attentional signals, to guide robot actions. We evaluate these strategies in a user study with 32 participants performing a task in a simulated hospital environment. Our findings show that higher interaction frequency does not necessarily lead to better engagement. Instead, we observe a systematic trade-off between perceived support and intrusiveness, influenced by factors such as physical proximity and user effort. These results provide empirical evidence that effective engagement in HRI depends on adaptive, context-sensitive intervention policies.

AI.tldr: The paper compares a continuous engagement-seeking robot strategy against a context-aware, selective intervention strategy in a task-oriented HRI setting, finding that higher interaction frequency does not improve engagement and that support versus intrusiveness follows a systematic trade-off.
AI.motivation: Task-oriented Human-Robot Interaction requires balancing user engagement against socially acceptable robot intrusiveness, yet it is unclear how different robot intervention strategies affect user experience, interaction dynamics, perceived intrusiveness, and sense of support.
AI.method: Two robot intervention strategies are compared: a continuous engagement-seeking strategy and a context-aware strategy that selectively intervenes based on the user's state and task context. Both use multimodal behavioral cues, including body orientation and attentional signals. Evaluation is conducted via a user study with 32 participants performing a task in a simulated hospital environment.
AI.result: Higher interaction frequency does not necessarily yield better engagement. A systematic trade-off is observed between perceived support and intrusiveness, influenced by factors such as physical proximity and user effort.
AI.conclusion: Effective engagement in HRI depends on adaptive, context-sensitive intervention policies; the findings provide empirical evidence supporting this design principle.

title: Sandwich-Residuals: Parameter-Efficient Test-time Adaptation of World Models
summary: Latent world models enable planning by predicting the effects of actions in a learned representation space, but their predictions can become unreliable when test-time conditions differ from training. Existing test-time adaptation methods address this by updating parts of the pretrained model, often modifying millions of parameters and requiring a choice of which internal components to adapt. We introduce Sandwich-Residuals, a lightweight alternative that keeps the pretrained world model frozen and learns only small residual corrections around the predictor. The residuals are optimized online using the model's self-supervised prediction error and require no rewards, labels, or source-domain data. Across 21 conditions on the AdaJEPA benchmark, our method achieves $1.3\times$ the success rate of the frozen model while retaining 95% of the performance of the strongest AdaJEPA variant and adapting 97-99% fewer parameters. Under compound shifts, this advantage increases to $1.9\times$ the success rate of the frozen model, while remaining comparable to internal block adaptation. We further demonstrate the same adaptation principle on a DINO-WM model for 3-D manipulation. These results suggest that effective test-time adaptation of world models does not necessarily require modifying their pretrained internal weights.

AI.tldr: Sandwich-Residuals adapts frozen latent world models at test time by learning only small residual corrections around the predictor, achieving large gains in success rate while updating 97-99% fewer parameters.
AI.motivation: Latent world models enable planning via action-effect prediction in learned representation space, but their predictions become unreliable under test-time distribution shifts. Existing test-time adaptation methods update millions of pretrained parameters and require selecting which internal components to adapt, which is costly and design-heavy.
AI.method: Sandwich-Residuals keeps the pretrained world model frozen and learns only small residual corrections around the predictor. These residuals are optimized online using the model's self-supervised prediction error, requiring no rewards, labels, or source-domain data.
AI.result: Across 21 conditions on the AdaJEPA benchmark, the method reaches 1.3x the success rate of the frozen model while retaining 95% of the strongest AdaJEPA variant's performance and adapting 97-99% fewer parameters. Under compound shifts, it achieves 1.9x the frozen model's success rate, comparable to internal block adaptation. The principle also transfers to a DINO-WM model for 3-D manipulation.
AI.conclusion: Effective test-time adaptation of world models does not necessarily require modifying pretrained internal weights; lightweight residual corrections around the predictor can match stronger adaptation variants with far fewer adapted parameters.

title: Understanding Engagement and Intrusiveness in Assistive Human-Robot Interaction Using Individual Traits
comment: Accepted for publication at the 35th IEEE International Conference on Robot and Human Interactive Communication (RO-MAN 2026)
summary: Robot assistance is particularly crucial in unfamiliar tasks, where users must understand task requirements while coordinating with the robot. Previous research offers mixed evidence on the role of robot proxemics in user engagement: some studies suggest closer proximity enhances interaction, while others report it can feel intrusive. In this work, we argue that perceptions of intrusiveness depend not only on proxemics but also on the frequency of robot interventions, and are strongly influenced by individual traits such as personality and demographics. We conducted an experiment with 32 participants who interacted with two assistive robots that provided similar task support but differed in their intervention strategies. Results indicate that overall engagement remains stable across conditions, yet affective responses and perceived intrusiveness vary significantly with personality traits. Moreover, personality shapes interaction dynamics differently depending on the robot's behavior. These findings emphasize that effective human-robot interaction should account for individual differences, tailoring robot behavior to maintain engagement while respecting each user's unique affective and behavioral profile.

AI.tldr: Perceived intrusiveness in robot assistance depends on intervention frequency and individual traits (personality, demographics), not proxemics alone; engagement stays stable but affective responses vary by personality.
AI.motivation: Robot assistance is critical in unfamiliar tasks where users must grasp task requirements while coordinating with a robot. Prior work gives mixed evidence on robot proxemics: closer proximity sometimes enhances interaction, sometimes feels intrusive, leaving unclear what actually drives user engagement and perceived intrusiveness.
AI.method: The authors hypothesize that intrusiveness perceptions depend not only on proxemics but also on robot intervention frequency, and are strongly shaped by individual traits such as personality and demographics. They ran an experiment with 32 participants interacting with two assistive robots that delivered comparable task support but differed in intervention strategy.
AI.result: Overall engagement remained stable across conditions. However, affective responses and perceived intrusiveness varied significantly with personality traits, and personality shaped interaction dynamics differently depending on the robot's behavior.
AI.conclusion: Effective human-robot interaction should account for individual differences, tailoring robot behavior to sustain engagement while respecting each user's affective and behavioral profile.

title: PSR: Predictive Sensorimotor Representation Learning for Contact-Rich Manipulation
summary: Contact-rich manipulation requires policies to generate precise actions by reasoning over contact forces, robot configurations, and interaction histories beyond visual observations. Existing methods passively condition on force feedback rather than actively predicting future contact dynamics, limiting their ability to generate high-precision actions. To address this problem, we introduce Predictive Sensorimotor Representation (PSR) learning, a framework that learns a hierarchy of predictive representations from multimodal sensorimotor signals and integrates them into the action stream of a visuomotor policy. Specifically, during a pretraining stage, a multimodal Transformer is trained to learn a hierarchy of predictive representations by jointly forecasting future interaction dynamics. The learned hierarchy subsequently augments the action stream, enabling the resulting policy to exploit contact-relevant cues at multiple depths. We further instantiate PSR within a Vision-Language-Action (VLA) model, resulting in PSR-VLA, and evaluate it on six real-world contact-rich manipulation tasks. Experimental results show that PSR-VLA achieves 91.7% overall success, improving over $π_{0.5}$, ForceVLA-$π_{0.5}$, and ForceVLA2-$π_{0.5}$ by 30.0, 22.5, and 19.2 percentage points, respectively. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed PSR for force-aware, contact-rich manipulation. Videos of the tasks and stability tests are available at https://psr-vla.pages.dev/.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes Predictive Sensorimotor Representation (PSR) learning, a framework that learns hierarchical predictive representations from multimodal sensorimotor signals and injects them into a visuomotor policy's action stream, yielding PSR-VLA that substantially outperforms existing force-aware baselines on real-world contact-rich manipulation tasks.
AI.motivation: Contact-rich manipulation requires reasoning over contact forces, robot configurations, and interaction histories beyond vision. Existing methods passively condition on force feedback instead of actively predicting future contact dynamics, which limits their ability to generate high-precision actions.
AI.method: PSR learns a hierarchy of predictive representations from multimodal sensorimotor signals. In a pretraining stage, a multimodal Transformer is trained to jointly forecast future interaction dynamics, producing representations at multiple depths. These learned representations are then integrated into the action stream of a visuomotor policy, augmenting it with contact-relevant cues. PSR is instantiated within a Vision-Language-Action (VLA) model to form PSR-VLA.
AI.result: Evaluated on six real-world contact-rich manipulation tasks, PSR-VLA achieves 91.7% overall success, outperforming π0.5, ForceVLA-π0.5, and ForceVLA2-π0.5 by 30.0, 22.5, and 19.2 percentage points, respectively.
AI.conclusion: The proposed PSR framework is effective for force-aware, contact-rich manipulation, demonstrating that actively predicting future contact dynamics and integrating hierarchical predictive representations into the action stream improves policy precision.

title: CRISP: Contact-Rich Robotic Simulation Platform with Extensive Geometries and Contact Solvers
summary: We present CRISP (Contact-RIch Simulation Platform), a high-fidelity physics engine tailored for complex multi-contact simulations such as tight-tolerance robotic manipulation. Achieving high physical fidelity in robotic simulation requires both expressive modeling of geometry and contact interactions, as well as accurate numerical resolution via robust collision detection and contact solvers. However, existing simulators often either rely on limited support for geometric representations and simplified modeling of contact interactions, or employ numerical resolution methods whose accuracy or robustness is inherently constrained. Accordingly, we develop a new simulator that supports diverse geometric representations with accurate optimization-based collision detection, and combines contact modeling with robust augmented Lagrangian-based contact solvers. This integration enables efficient and consistent detection of contact information across complex geometries while accurately resolving multi-contact constraints without problematic relaxations, which is essential for simulating contact-intensive and sharp interactions. We validate the physical fidelity of our simulator against state-of-the-art platforms and further demonstrate its capabilities through complex robotic manipulation scenarios. CRISP is publicly available at https://github.com/INRoL/crisp.

AI.tldr: CRISP is a high-fidelity physics engine for complex multi-contact simulation, integrating diverse geometric representations, optimization-based collision detection, and augmented Lagrangian contact solvers; it outperforms state-of-the-art platforms in physical fidelity and handles contact-intensive robotic manipulation scenarios.
AI.motivation: High physical fidelity in robotic simulation requires both expressive geometry/contact modeling and accurate numerical resolution via robust collision detection and contact solvers. Existing simulators fall short: they either support limited geometric representations with simplified contact modeling, or use numerical methods whose accuracy/robustness is inherently constrained. This gap hinders simulation of tight-tolerance, contact-intensive robotic manipulation.
AI.method: CRISP combines (1) support for diverse geometric representations with accurate optimization-based collision detection, and (2) contact modeling coupled with robust augmented Lagrangian-based contact solvers. This integration enables efficient, consistent detection of contact information across complex geometries while accurately resolving multi-contact constraints without problematic relaxations.
AI.result: The simulator's physical fidelity is validated against state-of-the-art platforms, and its capabilities are further demonstrated through complex robotic manipulation scenarios. CRISP is publicly released at https://github.com/INRoL/crisp.
AI.conclusion: CRISP delivers high-fidelity multi-contact simulation by uniting expressive geometry, optimization-based collision detection, and robust augmented Lagrangian contact solvers, resolving multi-contact constraints without relaxations—making it well suited to contact-intensive, sharp interactions in robotic manipulation.

title: Scaling Vision-Language Reward Learning for Robot Manipulation in Parallel Simulation
summary: Vision-language models (VLMs) can replace human annotators in preference-based reward learning, but sequential API requests and single-environment data collection make training slow and costly. We present RAPID (Reward learning with Adaptive Parallel Image Diversity), a system that couples GPU-parallel rollout with data-aware policy updates, single-request preference labeling, automatic reward stabilization, and representative image sampling. We evaluate these components on five Franka Panda manipulation tasks in IsaacLab. Parallel rollout and adaptive updates provide the first substantial reduction in training time: under matched two-stage prompting, mean runtime falls from 9.18 to 3.13 hours. With all RAPID components enabled, training completes in 1.15 hours using 896 rather than 19,840 API calls per run, and aggregate final success rises from 86.3\% to 98.7\%. This represents an 8.0$\times$ end-to-end speedup and a 95.5\% reduction in API usage. An offline evaluation with Gemma~3 12B and GPT-4.1 mini demonstrates that single-request prompting reduces labeling latency and cost across both models. Code is available at: https://github.com/rapid-vlm/rapid-vlm-rl.

AI.tldr: RAPID, a system coupling GPU-parallel rollout with data-aware policy updates, single-request preference labeling, automatic reward stabilization, and representative image sampling, achieves an 8.0x end-to-end speedup and 95.5% reduction in VLM API usage for preference-based reward learning, raising final task success from 86.3% to 98.7%.
AI.motivation: Using vision-language models (VLMs) as replacements for human annotators in preference-based reward learning is attractive, but sequential API requests and single-environment data collection make training slow and costly, limiting practical applicability.
AI.method: RAPID combines four components: (1) GPU-parallel rollout with data-aware policy updates, (2) single-request preference labeling instead of sequential API queries, (3) automatic reward stabilization, and (4) representative image sampling. It is evaluated on five Franka Panda manipulation tasks in IsaacLab, with an offline labeling study using Gemma 3 12B and GPT-4.1 mini.
AI.result: Under matched two-stage prompting, parallel rollout and adaptive updates cut mean runtime from 9.18 to 3.13 hours. With all components, training completes in 1.15 hours using 896 instead of 19,840 API calls per run, and aggregate final success rises from 86.3% to 98.7% (8.0x speedup, 95.5% fewer API calls). Offline evaluation shows single-request prompting reduces labeling latency and cost for both Gemma 3 12B and GPT-4.1 mini.
AI.conclusion: RAPID substantially improves both the efficiency and effectiveness of VLM-based preference reward learning for robotic manipulation, demonstrating that parallelized rollout, batched single-request labeling, and representative sampling jointly enable large runtime and API-cost reductions while improving task success.

title: TRACE: Coverage Path Planning for Unknown Environments Using Hierarchical Coverage Tree
summary: This paper presents a novel online coverage path planning (CPP) algorithm, called TRACE, for real-time coverage of unknown environments. TRACE is built upon a hierarchical coverage tree that provides a global representation of the evolving connectivity of the uncovered space. As the environment is incrementally revealed and covered, newly discovered obstacles and covered cells may fragment the remaining uncovered space into disconnected regions. TRACE recursively expands the corresponding tree nodes to explicitly represent these regions and organize them for subsequent coverage planning. Based on the updated tree, an incremental global tour is maintained to guide the coverage process. TRACE locally refines only the affected portions while preserving the visiting order of unchanged regions, thereby reducing the computational burden of global replanning and maintaining a consistent coverage progression. Guided by the global tour, a local planner generates back-and-forth coverage paths and switches to global-tour-aware planning to efficiently complete the target regions. Theoretical analysis establishes the computational complexity and complete coverage property of TRACE, and derives an approximation bound for the incremental global tour refinement. The performance of TRACE is evaluated through extensive high-fidelity simulations and real-robot experiments using a mobile robot. Comparative evaluations against six existing CPP methods demonstrate significant improvements in coverage time, path length, overlap ratio, and number of turns.

AI.tldr: TRACE is a novel online coverage path planning algorithm for real-time coverage of unknown environments, using a hierarchical coverage tree and incremental global tour refinement to achieve efficient, complete coverage with reduced replanning cost.
AI.motivation: Online coverage of unknown environments is challenging because newly discovered obstacles and covered cells can fragment the remaining uncovered space into disconnected regions, requiring repeated global replanning that is computationally expensive and disrupts coverage progression.
AI.method: TRACE builds a hierarchical coverage tree representing the evolving connectivity of uncovered space. It recursively expands tree nodes to represent newly formed disconnected regions. An incremental global tour guides coverage, with local refinement limited to affected portions while preserving the visiting order of unchanged regions. A local planner generates back-and-forth coverage paths and switches to global-tour-aware planning to complete target regions.
AI.result: Theoretical analysis establishes the computational complexity, complete coverage property, and an approximation bound for incremental global tour refinement. Extensive high-fidelity simulations and real-robot experiments show significant improvements over six existing CPP methods in coverage time, path length, overlap ratio, and number of turns.
AI.conclusion: TRACE provides an effective hierarchical, incremental approach to online coverage path planning, achieving complete coverage with lower computational burden and superior performance compared to existing methods.

title: Compact but Moving: Intervention-Relevant Geometry in Recurrent World Models
summary: Learned world models may have compact interventions even when their recurrent state is high-dimensional, but it is unclear what happens to such a correction after it enters the model. We study this question in a controlled recurrent world model where prior work identified a checkpoint-specific rank-4 interface for one-shot counterfactual velocity interventions. The correction rapidly leaves this fixed entry subspace during autonomous rollout. Nevertheless, a low-rank image obtained by transporting the entry directions through the factual recurrent Jacobian chain continues to capture most of the nonlinear correction. Restarts using the tangent-predicted correction preserve substantial counterfactual future function. This transport/function pattern recurs across independently trained structured-GRU models and a parameter-matched LSTM initialized with a privileged compact correction. We further characterize a finite-horizon future-response operator over the full recurrent carrier. Patching shifts its leading future-sensitive directions toward the matched native-counterfactual organization, and the local operator accurately ranks finite perturbation effects over the registered direction panels at the patched and native-counterfactual basepoints. A separate full-amplitude assay finds substantial factual-endpoint tangent residuals and supports response reconfiguration in two of three checkpoints. Together, these results show that compact intervention structure can persist as a moving, state-dependent local geometry embedded in high-dimensional recurrent dynamics, without implying a fixed or dynamically closed low-dimensional state.

AI.tldr: A fixed low-rank (rank-4) counterfactual velocity intervention in a learned recurrent world model does not stay in its entry subspace during rollout, yet its image transported through the factual recurrent Jacobian chain still captures most of the nonlinear correction; this transport/function pattern replicates across models and reveals a moving, state-dependent local geometry.
AI.motivation: Learned world models can exhibit compact interventions despite high-dimensional recurrent state, but it is unclear what happens to such a correction once it enters the model and the rollout unfolds. The paper asks whether compact intervention structure persists, dissolves, or re-forms within high-dimensional recurrent dynamics.
AI.method: The authors use a controlled recurrent world model in which prior work identified a checkpoint-specific rank-4 interface for one-shot counterfactual velocity interventions. They track how the correction leaves the fixed entry subspace during autonomous rollout, then transport entry directions through the factual recurrent Jacobian chain to obtain a low-rank image. They test whether this tangent-predicted correction preserves counterfactual future function via restarts, replicate across independently trained structured-GRU models and a parameter-matched LSTM seeded with a privileged compact correction, and characterize a finite-horizon future-response operator over the full recurrent carrier. They also run patching experiments and a full-amplitude assay to examine response reconfiguration.
AI.result: The correction rapidly leaves the fixed rank-4 entry subspace during rollout, but the Jacobian-transported low-rank image still captures most of the nonlinear correction, and restarts using it preserve substantial counterfactual future function. The transport/function pattern recurs across structured-GRU models and a parameter-matched LSTM. The finite-horizon future-response operator's leading future-sensitive directions shift toward the matched native-counterfactual organization under patching, and the local operator accurately ranks finite perturbation effects over registered direction panels at patched and native-counterfactual basepoints. A full-amplitude assay finds substantial factual-endpoint tangent residuals and supports response reconfiguration in two of three checkpoints.
AI.conclusion: Compact intervention structure can persist as a moving, state-dependent local geometry embedded in high-dimensional recurrent dynamics, without implying a fixed or dynamically closed low-dimensional state.

title: From Pretraining to Proficiency: Real-World Subtask RL for Long-Horizon Manipulation with Minimal Human Intervention
summary: A pretrained robot foundation policy may execute most of a long-horizon task yet repeatedly fail at a few critical subtasks. Collecting additional full-task demonstrations for supervised fine-tuning (SFT) requires operators to repeat behaviors the policy already performs well. Reinforcement learning (RL) fine-tuning offers a promising path to bridge this gap, but existing approaches struggle to solve long-horizon tasks using only sparse rewards. We present PARTS (Policy Adaptation with RL on Targeted Subtasks), a real-world subtask RL framework that concentrates practice at these bottlenecks while allowing training rollouts to proceed with minimal human intervention. The frozen pretrained policy supplies nominal actions throughout execution, while agent-generated selectors and success verifiers activate residual corrections and provide local outcome rewards. These rewards support learning from successful subtasks even when complete-task successes are scarce. Training combines online RL with success-reweighted retraining, and each retrained residual policy is redeployed to collect further experience. Humans identify bottlenecks during setup and perform physical resets when needed. On bimanual YAM and single-arm Franka tasks, PARTS improves complete-task success from 32% to 61% and from 50% to 95%, respectively, using tens of minutes of real-world RL rollouts per task on average. Compared with existing real-world RL fine-tuning methods, PARTS raises full-task success by more than 25% under the same robot-rollout budget while requiring less human involvement.

AI.tldr: PARTS is a real-world subtask RL framework that adapts a frozen pretrained policy by adding learned residual corrections with selector/verifier modules, concentrating practice on bottleneck subtasks to improve long-horizon task success under sparse rewards.
AI.motivation: Pretrained robot foundation policies often execute most of a long-horizon task yet repeatedly fail at a few critical subtasks. Full-task SFT demonstrations force operators to repeat behaviors the policy already handles well, and existing RL fine-tuning methods struggle on long-horizon tasks with only sparse rewards.
AI.method: PARTS freezes the pretrained policy to supply nominal actions across execution, while agent-generated selectors and success verifiers activate residual corrections and provide local outcome rewards per subtask. These local rewards enable learning from successful subtasks even when full-task successes are rare. Training alternates online RL with success-reweighted retraining, and each retrained residual policy is redeployed to gather further experience. Humans identify bottlenecks at setup and perform physical resets when required.
AI.result: On bimanual YAM and single-arm Franka tasks, PARTS raises complete-task success from 32% to 61% and from 50% to 95%, respectively, using tens of minutes of real-world RL rollouts per task on average. Under the same robot-rollout budget, it improves full-task success by more than 25% over existing real-world RL fine-tuning methods while requiring less human involvement.
AI.conclusion: Targeted subtask RL with local reward shaping and residual adaptation is an efficient, low-supervision path to fixing bottlenecks in pretrained robot policies, outperforming full-task RL fine-tuning on long-horizon sparse-reward tasks.

title: AcousticDiffusion: Semantically Conditioned Audio-Guided Diffusion Policy for Search-and-Rescue Assistance
summary: Navigating toward human callers is an important capability for rescue robots operating where visual contact is degraded or occluded. We present AcousticDiffusion, a semantically conditioned, audio-guided diffusion policy for human-directed navigation. A frozen pretrained audio recognizer processes 10.24 s windows, with speech gating and distress-aware prioritization converting recognition outputs into source-level navigation roles. Microphone-array direction-of-arrival measurements are recursively integrated into a robot-centric Bayesian bird's-eye-view belief field. Ego-motion compensation aligns successive observations, progressively constraining source position while preserving bearing-induced range uncertainty. The semantic belief, recent acoustic observations, audio features, and robot state condition a diffusion model that generates waypoint trajectories. On a synthetic-navigation validation set using recorded audio, AcousticDiffusion achieves a mean end-point bearing error of 11.20 degrees, with 91.78% of trajectories aligned within 30 degrees of the caller. Distractor rejection ranges from 89.20% to 98.99%, and the policy favors a HELP-designated caller over a competing speaker in 91.07% of windows. Deployed online on a ZSL-1 quadruped without additional retraining, it achieves a mean bearing error of 64.9 degrees, compared with 98.2 degrees for A* and 90.4 degrees for RRT, with a mean planner compute time of 6.07 ms. Despite imperfect acoustic localization, the reported mean final source distance is reduced from 3.96 m for the classical planners using ODAS-derived (Open embedded Audition System) guidance to 2.48 m, a 37.4% improvement. These results demonstrate the framework's ability to translate uncertain acoustic observations into closer approaches to human callers.

AI.tldr: AcousticDiffusion is a semantically conditioned, audio-guided diffusion policy that enables rescue robots to navigate toward human callers under degraded visual conditions by fusing speech recognition and microphone-array direction-of-arrival into a Bayesian belief field that conditions waypoint generation.
AI.motivation: Rescue robots often operate where visual contact with human callers is degraded or occluded, making acoustic guidance essential. Existing classical planners (e.g., A*, RRT) relying on ODAS-derived guidance perform poorly under imperfect acoustic localization, so a policy is needed to translate uncertain acoustic observations into effective human-directed navigation.
AI.method: A frozen pretrained audio recognizer processes 10.24 s windows with speech gating and distress-aware prioritization to assign source-level navigation roles (e.g., HELP). Microphone-array direction-of-arrival measurements are recursively integrated into a robot-centric Bayesian bird's-eye-view belief field, with ego-motion compensation aligning successive observations to constrain position while preserving bearing-induced range uncertainty. The semantic belief, recent acoustic observations, audio features, and robot state condition a diffusion model that generates waypoint trajectories.
AI.result: On a synthetic-navigation validation set with recorded audio: 11.20° mean end-point bearing error, 91.78% of trajectories within 30° of the caller, distractor rejection of 89.20%–98.99%, and 91.07% preference for a HELP-designated caller over a competing speaker. Deployed online on a ZSL-1 quadruped without retraining: 64.9° mean bearing error vs. 98.2° (A*) and 90.4° (RRT), with 6.07 ms mean planner compute. Mean final source distance dropped from 3.96 m (classical planners with ODAS guidance) to 2.48 m, a 37.4% improvement.
AI.conclusion: Despite imperfect acoustic localization, the framework successfully converts uncertain acoustic observations into closer approaches to human callers, outperforming classical planners in bearing accuracy and final distance while running efficiently enough for online deployment.

title: Contact-Rich Motion Planning via GPU-Parallel Mode Evaluation
summary: Contact-rich motion planning (CRMP) is essential for robotic manipulation and locomotion, yet remains computationally challenging due to combinatorial contact decisions. Existing methods typically avoid broad evaluation of contact-mode sequences through search heuristics or optimization reformulations. We revisit broad evaluation in light of modern GPU hardware and introduce Contact-Mode Expansion with parallel Trajectory optimization (CoMET), which combines GPU-parallel trajectory evaluation with greedy contact-mode expansion. On planar pushing benchmarks, CoMET is competitive with optimization-based, sampling, and tree-search baselines in solution quality and planning time, matching the full-enumeration reference on nearly all instances with fewer evaluations and shorter planning times. Ablations suggest that much of the performance gain comes from the high-throughput trajectory evaluator. In bimanual nonprehensile manipulation, GPU-friendly local mode expansion achieves higher planning success than the tested adaptive tree search as the mode space grows. These results demonstrate that broad explicit mode evaluation provides a simple yet effective alternative for CRMP.

AI.tldr: CoMET combines GPU-parallel trajectory evaluation with greedy contact-mode expansion, showing that broad explicit contact-mode evaluation is simple and effective for contact-rich motion planning.
AI.motivation: Contact-rich motion planning (CRMP) is important for robotic manipulation and locomotion but computationally hard due to combinatorial contact decisions. Existing methods avoid broad evaluation of contact-mode sequences via search heuristics or optimization reformulations.
AI.method: The authors revisit broad evaluation using modern GPU hardware and propose CoMET (Contact-Mode Expansion with parallel Trajectory optimization), which couples a GPU-parallel trajectory evaluator with greedy contact-mode expansion.
AI.result: On planar pushing benchmarks, CoMET is competitive with optimization-based, sampling, and tree-search baselines in solution quality and planning time, matching full-enumeration reference on nearly all instances with fewer evaluations and shorter planning times. Ablations attribute much of the gain to the high-throughput trajectory evaluator. In bimanual nonprehensile manipulation, GPU-friendly local mode expansion yields higher planning success than the tested adaptive tree search as the mode space grows.
AI.conclusion: Broad explicit contact-mode evaluation offers a simple yet effective alternative for contact-rich motion planning.

title: A Sim-to-Real Integration Pipeline for Training and Deployment of Chunk-Based VLA Manipulation Policies
comment: Accepted at IROS 2026 Workshop on Sim2Real and Classical Control: From Rigorous Theory to Data-Driven Robotics
summary: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have become a prominent paradigm for mapping multimodal inputs, including semantic instructions, visual observations of the scene, and proprioceptive observations, to robot actions. Most state-of-the-art models predict actions in the end-effector pose space as sequences of action chunks. Training and evaluating these models requires large-scale collections of real-world demonstrations, pairing robot actions with the corresponding visual and proprioceptive observations. Collecting such data on real hardware typically relies on human teleoperation, making the process costly, time-consuming, and difficult to scale. We present an open-source sim-to-real experimental protocol that addresses this bottleneck: expert trajectories generated in simulation are replayed open-loop on a real Franka FR3 setup, where the corresponding real visual and proprioceptive observations are recorded and converted into a format compatible with VLA training. The same deployment stack is then reused, in closed-loop, to evaluate a trained policy on that setup, so that data collection and evaluation share an identical hardware configuration. Because each real recording is paired with the simulated trajectory that produced it, the protocol also yields a direct measurement of the sim-to-real gap. We release the collected datasets on Hugging Face together with the pipeline source code https://gitlab.isir.upmc.fr/kappel/sim2real_public_chunk_control.

AI.tldr: The paper presents an open-source sim-to-real protocol that reuses simulated expert trajectories to collect real VLA training data on a Franka FR3, eliminating costly teleoperation and enabling direct measurement of the sim-to-real gap.
AI.motivation: Collecting real-world demonstrations for training and evaluating Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models typically requires human teleoperation on real hardware, which is costly, time-consuming, and hard to scale. This data bottleneck limits progress in the field.
AI.method: Expert trajectories are generated in simulation and replayed open-loop on a real Franka FR3 setup, where the corresponding real visual and proprioceptive observations are recorded and converted into a VLA-compatible format. The same deployment stack is reused in closed-loop to evaluate trained policies on the identical hardware configuration. As each real recording is paired with its generating simulated trajectory, the protocol directly measures the sim-to-real gap.
AI.result: The protocol yields datasets of real visual and proprioceptive observations paired with simulated trajectories, provides a direct measurement of the sim-to-real gap, and enables policy evaluation under the same hardware configuration. Datasets are released on Hugging Face alongside the pipeline source code.
AI.conclusion: An open-source sim-to-real experimental protocol addresses the data collection bottleneck for VLA models by sharing an identical hardware configuration for both data collection and evaluation, while also quantifying the sim-to-real gap.

title: LunaDrive: A Delay-Compensated High-Voltage GaN FET-Based Motor Driver for Dynamic Robots with Flat BLDC Motors
comment: Accepted at IROS2026, website - https://woodrobo.github.io/lunadrive/ , YouTube - https://youtu.be/iD8vzvis_5w
summary: The performance improvement of high-power flat BLDC motors has accelerated the development of dynamic robots. However, many commercially available servo motors assume operating voltages of 48 V or lower, which limits the maximum rotational speed. Dynamic robots require rapid energy generation, so this voltage constraint restricts motion performance. Therefore, driving motors beyond the rated voltage is desirable to increase the instantaneous maximum speed. On the other hand, semiconductor devices used in motor drivers have a trade-off between voltage rating and current capacity. Conventional drivers using Si MOSFETs have difficulty achieving both high-voltage and high-current operation. Although GaN FETs are promising, compact drivers that can be mounted on the rear side of flat BLDC motors remain limited. In this study, a motor driver for high-power flat BLDC motors using GaN FETs is developed. The effect of delay compensation in the high-speed region beyond the rated operating range is also investigated. In the experiments, under 96 V operation, a continuous current of 30 A was achieved with a heat sink attached. A peak current of 80 A and a maximum electrical frequency of 3110 Hz were confirmed. A high-speed load lifting experiment driven by a LiPo battery 24S (100 V) was also conducted, demonstrating applicability to dynamic robot operation.

AI.tldr: A compact GaN FET-based motor driver for high-power flat BLDC motors is developed to enable overvoltage operation, achieving 96 V/30 A continuous, 80 A peak, and 3110 Hz max electrical frequency, with delay compensation extending high-speed performance.
AI.motivation: Dynamic robots demand rapid energy generation and high instantaneous speed, but commercial servo motors are typically limited to 48 V or lower, capping maximum rotational speed. Driving motors beyond rated voltage is desirable, yet Si MOSFET drivers cannot simultaneously achieve high voltage and high current. GaN FETs are promising, but compact drivers mountable on the rear side of flat BLDC motors remain scarce.
AI.method: A motor driver for high-power flat BLDC motors using GaN FETs is developed, designed compactly for rear-side mounting. The study also investigates delay compensation to improve performance in the high-speed region beyond the rated operating range.
AI.result: Under 96 V operation with a heat sink, a continuous current of 30 A was achieved. A peak current of 80 A and a maximum electrical frequency of 3110 Hz were confirmed. A high-speed load lifting experiment powered by a 24S LiPo battery (100 V) was also conducted.
AI.conclusion: The GaN FET-based driver enables high-voltage, high-current operation beyond conventional limits, and delay compensation supports high-speed operation, demonstrating applicability to dynamic robot operation.

title: PopNavShift: Stress-Testing Social Navigation under Behavioral Population Shift
summary: Social-navigation algorithms are often evaluated under a fixed pedestrian-behavior distribution, despite substantial variation in pedestrian responses to robots across individuals and social contexts. We introduce PopNavShift, a matched simulation framework for stress-testing social-navigation strategies under pedestrian population shifts. PopNavShift constructs population-conditioned pedestrian motion profiles by prompting Gemini 3.7 Flash with 600 synthetic persona records from MatrAIx Persona 1M and deterministically mapping the responses into bounded motion parameters. It then compares three representative navigation strategies, reactive avoidance, early yielding, and reciprocal collision avoidance, across eight population conditions and 7,488 matched robot runs. In a matched intervention on the same 202 personas, changing only time pressure reverses 8.6% of controller rankings based on robot travel time, but 22.4% based on mean pedestrian delay and 23.9% based on worst-decile delay. Across population conditions, this sensitivity is greater for pedestrian burden than for robot travel time and increases in spatially constrained settings; the same qualitative pattern persists under a second pedestrian dynamics model. These findings support evaluating navigation strategies across behavioral populations using both robot performance and pedestrian burden.

AI.tldr: PopNavShift is a matched simulation framework that stress-tests social-navigation strategies under pedestrian population shifts, showing that controller rankings are far more sensitive to pedestrian burden metrics than to robot travel time.
AI.motivation: Social-navigation algorithms are usually evaluated under a fixed pedestrian-behavior distribution, ignoring substantial variation in how individuals and social contexts affect pedestrian responses to robots. This risks overstating the robustness of a chosen strategy.
AI.method: PopNavShift builds population-conditioned pedestrian motion profiles by prompting Gemini 3.7 Flash with 600 synthetic persona records from MatrAIx Persona 1M and deterministically mapping responses into bounded motion parameters. It compares three strategies—reactive avoidance, early yielding, and reciprocal collision avoidance—across eight population conditions and 7,488 matched robot runs, plus a matched intervention on the same 202 personas varying only time pressure, and validation under a second pedestrian dynamics model.
AI.result: In the matched intervention, changing only time pressure reverses 8.6% of controller rankings by robot travel time, but 22.4% by mean pedestrian delay and 23.9% by worst-decile delay. Sensitivity is greater for pedestrian burden than for robot travel time and increases in spatially constrained settings; the same qualitative pattern persists under a second pedestrian dynamics model.
AI.conclusion: Navigation strategies should be evaluated across behavioral populations using both robot performance and pedestrian burden, since rankings and robustness conclusions depend heavily on the population distribution and the chosen metric.

title: VIRGA: Virtual-Agent-Intermediated Riemannian Geometry for Active-Sensing Air-Ground Coordination
summary: Air-ground autonomy becomes harder when the unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) must remain observable by a gimbal light detection and ranging (LiDAR) mounted on the unmanned ground vehicle (UGV). The platforms must avoid dynamic obstacles while coordinating heterogeneous motion, limited sensing, and changing task initiative within one closed loop. This paper presents VIRGA, a neural geometric coordination framework that turns dual-LiDAR observations into bounded source-specific Riemannian fields and couples them through a virtual agent with reciprocal elastic feedback. Platform-aware execution maps convert the shared coordination reference into feasible UAV, UGV, and gimbal commands while enforcing active-observation safeguards. Evaluation against three complementary baselines reveals distinct limitations. An adapted Ray-RMP controller provides the fastest Riemannian response but produces insufficient clearance in the coupled air-ground task. A dense analytical Riemannian field improves geometric avoidance, yet its high evaluation cost prevents stable field-of-view maintenance. An adapted ColAG controller achieves the lowest latency but still incurs safety and observability violations. VIRGA completes all paired warehouse conditions safely, while a long-range cave stress test without retraining demonstrates sustained coordination in irregular and confined geometry. Ablations confirm contributions from online geometric evaluation, virtual-agent mediation, and reciprocal feedback.

AI.tldr: VIRGA is a neural geometric coordination framework that couples dual-LiDAR observations into a virtual-agent-mediated Riemannian field for observable, collision-free UAV-UGV-gimbal coordination.
AI.motivation: Air-ground autonomy becomes harder when the UAV must remain observable by a gimbal LiDAR on the UGV. The platforms must avoid dynamic obstacles while coordinating heterogeneous motion, limited sensing, and changing task initiative within one closed loop, which existing approaches do not jointly address.
AI.method: VIRGA turns dual-LiDAR observations into bounded source-specific Riemannian fields and couples them through a virtual agent with reciprocal elastic feedback. Platform-aware execution maps convert the shared coordination reference into feasible UAV, UGV, and gimbal commands while enforcing active-observation safeguards.
AI.result: Against three baselines, Ray-RMP is fastest but has insufficient clearance; the dense analytical Riemannian field improves avoidance but is too costly to maintain the field of view; ColAG has lowest latency but violates safety and observability. VIRGA completes all paired warehouse conditions safely and sustains coordination in a long-range cave stress test without retraining. Ablations confirm the contributions of online geometric evaluation, virtual-agent mediation, and reciprocal feedback.
AI.conclusion: VIRGA achieves safe, observable air-ground coordination in coupled tasks and generalizes to irregular, confined geometry without retraining, with ablations validating its key components.

title: CommitFlow: Semantic Commitment Verification and Local Correction for Long-Horizon Robot Manipulation VLA Execution
comment: 8 pages, 7 figures. Submitted to the IEEE International Conference on Robotics and Automation (ICRA) 2027
summary: Although vision-language-action (VLA) policies have advanced rapidly, long-horizon execution may still progress to the next task stage before the required physical effect has been established. We call this a mismatch between semantic commitments, physical conditions that a stage must establish or maintain, and the actual physical state. Because an action command alone cannot confirm such a condition, local deviations can propagate and cause task failure. To address this problem, we present CommitFlow, a closed-loop execution framework that combines commitment monitoring with local correction while keeping the base policy frozen. CommitFlow integrates three components. A Semantic Commitment Monitor (SCM) compares stage requirements against current state evidence and holds back dependent actions when a required condition is unmet or violated. BoundaryFlow then generates a local correction conditioned on the current state and base action, and Relation and Gain Calibration (RGC) selects the smallest correction strength that satisfies the relevant constraints. Across the ten common RoboTwin 2.0 benchmark tasks, CommitFlow achieves a mean success rate of 75.9 percent, improving on the base policy pi0.5 by 22.7 percent. Cross-policy experiments show consistent gains, pointing toward reliable long-horizon robot execution.

AI.tldr: CommitFlow is a closed-loop execution framework that adds commitment monitoring and local correction to a frozen VLA policy, achieving 75.9% mean success on ten RoboTwin 2.0 tasks (+22.7% over pi0.5).
AI.motivation: Long-horizon VLA policies may advance to the next task stage before the required physical effect is established. This creates a mismatch between semantic commitments (physical conditions a stage must establish or maintain) and the actual physical state. Since a single action command cannot confirm such a condition, local deviations propagate and cause task failure.
AI.method: CommitFlow keeps the base policy frozen and integrates three components. A Semantic Commitment Monitor (SCM) compares stage requirements against current state evidence and holds back dependent actions when a required condition is unmet or violated. BoundaryFlow generates a local correction conditioned on the current state and base action. Relation and Gain Calibration (RGC) selects the smallest correction strength that satisfies the relevant constraints.
AI.result: Across ten common RoboTwin 2.0 benchmark tasks, CommitFlow achieves a mean success rate of 75.9%, improving on the base policy pi0.5 by 22.7%. Cross-policy experiments show consistent gains.
AI.conclusion: CommitFlow provides reliable long-horizon robot execution by combining commitment monitoring with local correction while keeping the base policy frozen.

title: MAAP: Multi-Agent Active Perception for Collaborative Manipulation
summary: Multi-agent manipulation naturally produces multiple task-driven viewpoints: every arm carries a wrist camera and moves through the scene while acting. Yet these observations are typically underutilized, and active perception in manipulation is still often treated as requiring a dedicated sensing agent. We introduce MAAP (Multi-Agent Active Perception), in which every arm is dual-purpose: it executes manipulation actions and, through the wrist camera it carries, simultaneously serves as a moving viewpoint for the team. We pair this with RAIL (Role-Aware Imitation Learning), a controller that predicts each arm's current role alongside its action chunk and conditions action generation on it, representing role-dependent actions within one network. Across four simulated tasks, widening the perception regime lifts average success from 56.5% with a fixed camera to 62.5% with one active wrist view and 70.0% with all of them, while MAAP+RAIL reaches 79.2%. RAIL's additional gain is concentrated on the three-arm Microwave task, where success rises from 47% to 82% on identical multi-wrist inputs. On a dual-arm platform, MAAP+RAIL succeeds in 14 of 20 placement trials compared with 0 of 20 for fixed-view ACT. Collaborative manipulation can thus serve as an active perception mechanism in its own right.

AI.tldr: MAAP enables every robotic arm to serve as both manipulator and moving viewpoint via its wrist camera, and RAIL (Role-Aware Imitation Learning) predicts each arm's role to condition action generation, lifting average success on four simulated tasks to 79.2% and achieving 14/20 placement trials on a dual-arm platform versus 0/20 for fixed-view ACT.
AI.motivation: Multi-agent manipulation naturally generates task-driven viewpoints because each arm carries a wrist camera and moves through the scene while acting, yet these observations are typically underutilized; active perception in manipulation is still often treated as requiring a dedicated sensing agent rather than leveraging the manipulators themselves.
AI.method: The authors introduce MAAP (Multi-Agent Active Perception), where each arm is dual-purpose—executing manipulation actions while simultaneously acting as a moving viewpoint through its wrist camera—and pair it with RAIL (Role-Aware Imitation Learning), a controller that predicts each arm's current role alongside its action chunk and conditions action generation on that role, thereby representing role-dependent actions within a single network.
AI.result: Across four simulated tasks, widening the perception regime raised average success from 56.5% with a fixed camera to 62.5% with one active wrist view and 70.0% with all wrist views; MAAP+RAIL reached 79.2%. RAIL's additional benefit concentrated on the three-arm Microwave task, where success rose from 47% to 82% on identical multi-wrist inputs. On a dual-arm platform, MAAP+RAIL succeeded in 14 of 20 placement trials versus 0 of 20 for fixed-view ACT.
AI.conclusion: Collaborative manipulation can itself function as an active perception mechanism, without requiring a dedicated sensing agent, since arm-mounted wrist cameras provide task-driven viewpoints that improve policy success when properly exploited through role-aware control.

title: GALA: Geometry-Aware Latent Action Modeling for Vision-Language-Action Model Pretraining across Embodiments
summary: Learning large-scale vision-language-action (VLA) models from multi-embodiment datasets remains challenging due to heterogeneous action spaces across end effectors. Although latent action models (LAMs) can learn embodiment-agnostic action representations from diverse video data, existing image-based LAMs often fail to capture fine-grained end-effector articulation, particularly finger-level geometric changes in human and dexterous robot hands. To address this limitation, we propose GALA, a Geometry-Aware Latent-Action modeling framework that augments image-based latent actions with 3D end-effector geometric motion. However, naively incorporating point clouds yields fine-grained action representations with limited shared semantics, hindering cross-embodiment pretraining. To address this issue, we introduce the Unified End-effector Motion Representation (UEMR), which preserves fine-grained motion information while improving the cross-embodiment generalizability of latent actions. Building upon UEMR, GALA combines visual latent actions that capture scene-level dynamics with geometric latent actions that capture shared fine-grained end-effector articulation, providing effective supervision for VLA pretraining from multi-embodiment data, including action-free ego-centric human videos. Experiments on fine-grained motion probing, cross-embodiment retrieval, and downstream VLA evaluation demonstrate GALA's effectiveness in modeling generalizable fine-grained motions across embodiments, achieving 68.3% RoboCasa-GR1 success rate and 75.5% real-world success rate. Code, appendix, and demos are available at https://puzhenyuan.github.io/GALA-website/.

AI.tldr: GALA is a Geometry-Aware Latent-Action modeling framework that augments image-based latent actions with 3D end-effector geometric motion via a Unified End-effector Motion Representation (UEMR), enabling generalizable fine-grained motion modeling and VLA pretraining across embodiments.
AI.motivation: Learning large-scale VLA models from multi-embodiment datasets is challenging due to heterogeneous action spaces across end effectors. Existing image-based latent action models (LAMs) can learn embodiment-agnostic representations from diverse video but fail to capture fine-grained end-effector articulation, especially finger-level geometric changes in human and dexterous robot hands.
AI.method: The authors propose GALA, which augments image-based latent actions with 3D end-effector geometric motion. To avoid the limited shared semantics of naively using point clouds, they introduce the Unified End-effector Motion Representation (UEMR), preserving fine-grained motion while improving cross-embodiment generalizability. GALA then combines visual latent actions capturing scene-level dynamics with geometric latent actions capturing shared fine-grained articulation, supervising VLA pretraining from multi-embodiment data including action-free ego-centric human videos.
AI.result: Experiments on fine-grained motion probing, cross-embodiment retrieval, and downstream VLA evaluation show GALA effectively models generalizable fine-grained motions across embodiments, achieving a 68.3% RoboCasa-GR1 success rate and 75.5% real-world success rate.
AI.conclusion: GALA demonstrates that integrating geometry-aware latent actions with image-based latent actions enables generalizable fine-grained motion representation and effective multi-embodiment VLA pretraining. Code, appendix, and demos are available at https://puzhenyuan.github.io/GALA-website/.

title: CARF: Contrastive Attraction-Repulsion of Failure-Guided Flow Matching
summary: Robot demonstration collection often produces imperfect or failed trajectories in addition to successful demonstrations. Existing methods typically exploit failed trajectories by identifying segments that still make progress toward task completion, but largely overlook \textit{failure-critical behaviors} that directly lead to task failure. Here we argue that these two types of segments provide fundamentally asymmetric supervision: progressive segments should be imitated, whereas failure-critical segments should be explicitly avoided. Based on this observation, we propose CARF, a Contrastive Attraction-Repulsion of Failure-guided framework for learning from imperfect robot data. CARF introduces a progress-based importance scorer, trained solely on successful expert demonstrations and its perturbation results, to estimate step-wise contributions toward task completion and identify informative regions in failed trajectories. These scores guide a unified flow-matching objective that attracts the policy toward progressive behaviors and repels it from failure-critical ones, while excluding ambiguous segments. This enables more comprehensive utilization of imperfect data and avoids unreliable supervision from ambiguous failure segments. Extensive experiments in simulation and the real world demonstrate consistent improvements over competing baselines across diverse failure scenarios, with ablations further validating the effectiveness of the proposed scoring and attraction-repulsion mechanisms. Our website is https://zhao-sq.github.io/carf/#.

AI.tldr: CARF is a framework for learning robot policies from imperfect demonstrations by asymmetrically treating progressive segments (imitate) and failure-critical segments (avoid), guided by a progress-based importance scorer trained only on successful data.
AI.motivation: Robot demonstration collection often yields failed or imperfect trajectories. Prior methods extract only progressive segments from failures and overlook failure-critical behaviors that directly cause task failure, wasting informative supervision.
AI.method: CARF uses a progress-based importance scorer, trained solely on successful expert demonstrations and their perturbations, to estimate step-wise task progress and identify informative regions in failed trajectories. These scores drive a unified flow-matching objective that attracts the policy toward progressive behaviors, repels it from failure-critical ones, and excludes ambiguous segments.
AI.result: Extensive simulation and real-world experiments show consistent improvements over baselines across diverse failure scenarios; ablations validate the effectiveness of the proposed scoring and attraction-repulsion mechanisms.
AI.conclusion: Treating progressive and failure-critical segments as asymmetric supervision (imitation vs. avoidance) enables more comprehensive use of imperfect data and avoids unreliable supervision from ambiguous failure segments, yielding a more effective robot learning framework.

title: SkelWAM: A Skeleton-Guided World-Action Model for Zero-Shot Cross-Embodiment Manipulation
summary: Reusing manipulation experience across robot embodiments is important for scaling robot learning and reducing repeated task-specific data collection. However, changes in embodiment alter visual appearance, action dimensionality and semantics, and the whole-body configurations that can realize the same tool pose. We present SkelWAM, a skeleton-guided world-action model that couples perception and control through one explicit geometric representation for single-source cross-embodiment manipulation. Arm centerline geometry, tool-center-point (TCP) pose, and parallel-jaw commands form a shared 25-D state. The same definition underlies canonical third-person and wrist observations and future whole-body action targets. Trained with predictive visual supervision, a video-action mixture of transformers predicts canonical skeleton action chunks, which embodiment-specific constrained decoders convert into joint or continuum-robot controls. This formulation requires no one-to-one joint correspondence and uses no target-task demonstrations or target policy updates. We introduce LIBERO-Cross10, a source-only cross-embodiment transfer benchmark covering ten tasks and ten target embodiments across four morphological groups. On this benchmark, Franka-trained SkelWAM achieves 43.3% success over 1,000 episodes, exceeding the best-performing evaluated baseline by 36.2 percentage points. We further deploy a JAKA mini2-trained policy on the Feagine A03 continuum robot for three tabletop manipulation tasks, illustrating the approach's potential for real-world cross-embodiment manipulation. Project page: http://www.liukepku.com/skelwam/index.html

AI.tldr: SkelWAM is a skeleton-guided world-action model that uses a shared 25-D geometric state (arm centerline, TCP pose, parallel-jaw commands) to enable single-source cross-embodiment manipulation without target demonstrations or policy updates.
AI.motivation: Reusing manipulation experience across robot embodiments is key for scaling robot learning and reducing repeated task-specific data collection, but embodiment changes alter visual appearance, action dimensionality/semantics, and whole-body configurations that realize the same tool pose.
AI.method: SkelWAM couples perception and control through one explicit geometric representation. Arm centerline geometry, TCP pose, and parallel-jaw commands form a shared 25-D state used for canonical third-person and wrist observations and future whole-body action targets. Trained with predictive visual supervision, a video-action mixture of transformers predicts canonical skeleton action chunks, which embodiment-specific constrained decoders convert into joint or continuum-robot controls—requiring no one-to-one joint correspondence, target-task demonstrations, or target policy updates.
AI.result: On the new LIBERO-Cross10 source-only benchmark (ten tasks, ten target embodiments, four morphological groups), a Franka-trained SkelWAM achieves 43.3% success over 1,000 episodes, exceeding the best evaluated baseline by 36.2 percentage points. A JAKA mini2-trained policy deployed on the Feagine A03 continuum robot succeeds on three tabletop tasks.
AI.conclusion: Leveraging a shared skeleton-based geometric state enables effective source-only cross-embodiment transfer across diverse morphologies, including continuum robots, demonstrating practical potential for real-world cross-embodiment manipulation.

title: Gripper-Aware Automatic Dense Packing of Irregular Objects
summary: Automatic dense packing is widely desired in warehouse operations but remains a fundamental challenge in robotic manipulation. Existing work on irregular-object packing largely targets simulation with idealized contact, treating the object as an isolated rigid body. The gripper often enters as a discrete, post-hoc feasibility check, if considered at all, and the perception and contact drift accumulated during execution are not addressed. We present a closed-loop pipeline that integrates perception, gripper-aware placement optimization, and force-guided execution on a real manipulator. The optimizer represents the object together with the gripper as a single composite body of hierarchical sphere trees. It searches over five degrees of freedom on a GPU within a CMA-ES framework, with the vertical coordinate grounded analytically against the current heightmap. During execution, a force-monitored vertical descent stops on first contact. A post-release consolidation push then closes the residual lateral clearance that gripper-aware planning leaves behind. The container is re-perceived between placements so that drift does not accumulate. We validate the system on a Franka Emika Panda robot packing a 3D-printed set of flat, curved, and concave objects, and a YCB object subset. An ablation study isolates the contribution of gripper-aware optimization, the consolidation push, and mesh-derived geometry to end-to-end success, achieved density, and computational cost. We further benchmark against the heightmap-minimization method as a baseline representative of prior irregular-object packing work.

AI.tldr: A closed-loop robotic dense-packing pipeline integrating perception, gripper-aware placement optimization, and force-guided execution, validated on a real Franka Panda manipulator.
AI.motivation: Automatic dense packing is highly desired in warehouse operations but remains a fundamental challenge. Prior irregular-object packing work mostly targets simulation with idealized contact, treats objects as isolated rigid bodies, handles the gripper only as a discrete post-hoc feasibility check (if at all), and ignores perception and contact drift accumulated during execution.
AI.method: The optimizer represents the object and gripper as a single composite body of hierarchical sphere trees and searches over five degrees of freedom on a GPU within a CMA-ES framework, with the vertical coordinate grounded analytically against the current heightmap. During execution, a force-monitored vertical descent stops on first contact, and a post-release consolidation push closes residual lateral clearance left by gripper-aware planning. The container is re-perceived between placements to prevent drift accumulation.
AI.result: Validated on a Franka Emika Panda robot packing a 3D-printed set of flat, curved, and concave objects, plus a YCB object subset. An ablation study isolates the contributions of gripper-aware optimization, the consolidation push, and mesh-derived geometry to end-to-end success, achieved density, and computational cost. Benchmarked against a heightmap-minimization method as a baseline representative of prior work.
AI.conclusion: The integrated closed-loop system addresses idealized-contact, isolated-rigid-body, post-hoc-gripper, and drift-accumulation limitations of prior work, offering a practical real-manipulator solution for dense irregular-object packing whose key components are individually quantified via ablation.

title: Duty Factor Predicts Robust Constrained Quadrupedal Locomotion Across Gait Types
summary: Quadrupedal robots are increasingly deployed in environments where locomotion must remain robust to disturbances and constrained terrain. Gait type, such as walking or trotting, is commonly used to characterize quadrupedal locomotion. However, gait type does not uniquely define locomotion, as parameters such as duty factor, speed, and stance width can vary within a single gait type. In this work, we investigate the relationship between these gait parameters using three distinct quadrupedal locomotion control approaches. First, using whole body trajectory optimization with LQR feedback, we show that duty factor is a stronger predictor of local error convergence than nominal gait type. Second, we investigate duty factor selection with a learned locomotion controller, suggesting how duty factor may serve as a low-dimensional parameter for adapting locomotion robustness in narrow-terrain environments. Finally, we show that these trends persist under a centroidal model predictive control framework and validate them through narrow-terrain experiments on a physical quadruped. These results show that duty factor provides a simple and effective basis for understanding and selecting robust quadrupedal locomotion across gait types and control architectures.

AI.tldr: This work shows that duty factor, rather than nominal gait type, is a stronger predictor of quadrupedal locomotion robustness and can serve as a low-dimensional parameter for adapting locomotion across control architectures.
AI.motivation: Quadrupedal robots must maintain robust locomotion under disturbances and constrained terrain. Gait type (e.g., walking or trotting) is commonly used to characterize locomotion, but it does not uniquely define it since parameters like duty factor, speed, and stance width vary within a single gait type. The authors therefore investigate how these gait parameters relate to locomotion robustness.
AI.method: The authors examine the relationship between gait parameters using three distinct quadrupedal locomotion control approaches: (1) whole-body trajectory optimization with LQR feedback, (2) a learned locomotion controller, and (3) a centroidal model predictive control framework. They also validate the trends through narrow-terrain experiments on a physical quadruped.
AI.result: Duty factor is a stronger predictor of local error convergence than nominal gait type. With the learned controller, duty factor appears to serve as a low-dimensional parameter for adapting locomotion robustness in narrow-terrain environments. These trends persist under the centroidal MPC framework and are validated experimentally on a physical quadruped.
AI.conclusion: Duty factor provides a simple and effective basis for understanding and selecting robust quadrupedal locomotion across gait types and control architectures.

title: LIMBO: Learning and Internalizing Model-Free Barrier Objectives for Agile and Safe Whole-Body Control
summary: Safe whole-body control requires coordinating collision avoidance and balance under high-dimensional, nonlinear dynamics--making safety certificates difficult to design and reuse across behaviors. We present LIMBO, a framework for synthesizing a state-action control barrier function and distilling its safety structure into a task policy. LIMBO learns the safety certificate from black-box transitions and a state-based failure specification over residual actions around a frozen base controller, making Q-CBF synthesis tractable in the full control dimension while placing the certificate in the task policy's control space. During synthesis, the learned safety value drives risk-guided sampling near the estimated boundary of recoverability; during task learning, it serves as a teacher that provides action-level safety feedback, yielding a robust task policy and alleviating the need for an online safety filter at deployment. We demonstrate LIMBO on a 29-degree-of-freedom humanoid performing dodgeball avoidance and locomotion beneath low obstacles. Beyond scaling learned Q-CBFs to whole-body control, we show that risk-guided boundary sampling provides a theoretically grounded way to explore the edge of recoverability. Under the same safety specification, ceteris paribus, varying the sampling concentration produces strategies ranging from crouching to a novel backward-leaning limbo maneuver. In both settings, the learned policies transfer to hardware without online safety filtering, showing that learned safety synthesis scales to agile whole-body control.
