AI.tldr: LIMBO synthesizes a state-action control barrier function (Q-CBF) from black-box transitions around a frozen base controller, then distills its safety structure into a task policy, enabling safe whole-body humanoid control without an online safety filter at deployment.
AI.motivation: Safe whole-body control must jointly handle collision avoidance and balance under high-dimensional, nonlinear dynamics. Designing and reusing safety certificates across behaviors is hard, and learned Q-CBFs have not scaled to full control dimensions in whole-body settings.
AI.method: LIMBO learns a safety certificate (Q-CBF) from black-box transitions and a state-based failure specification, defined over residual actions around a frozen base controller. This makes Q-CBF synthesis tractable in the full control dimension while placing the certificate in the task policy's control space. During synthesis, the learned safety value drives risk-guided sampling near the estimated boundary of recoverability. During task learning, it acts as a teacher giving action-level safety feedback to produce a robust task policy and remove the need for an online safety filter at deployment.
AI.result: Demonstrated on a 29-DoF humanoid performing dodgeball avoidance and locomotion beneath low obstacles. Under the same safety specification, varying sampling concentration ceteris paribus yields strategies ranging from crouching to a novel backward-leaning limbo maneuver, confirming risk-guided boundary sampling as a theoretically grounded exploration of the edge of recoverability. Policies transfer to hardware without online safety filtering.
AI.conclusion: LIMBO scales learned Q-CBF synthesis to agile whole-body control, distills safety into task policies, and shows that risk-guided boundary sampling enables recovery-edge exploration and diverse, hardware-transferable safe strategies.

title: SeeQ: Training Generalist Value Functions for Long-Horizon Robotic Manipulation
summary: Despite rapid progress, generalist robot policies remain brittle on complex, long-horizon tasks that comprise multiple stages or require repeated attempts and deliberation on the same underlying stage before success. Q-value functions can improve these policies by ranking candidate actions or guiding policy improvement, but learning from sparse task-level rewards entails long credit-assignment horizons, difficult Bellman backups, and broad data-coverage requirements. We introduce SeeQ (Subtask-elicited Q-functions), which instead learns Q-values for the currently active subtask. This shortens the value-prediction horizon and enables effective learning with temporal-difference (TD) objectives. During training, subtask-level annotations present in offline robot data provide the decomposition and enable learning from broad, potentially suboptimal robot datasets. To eliminate the need for human annotations or modular subtask prediction systems at test time, our Q-function architecture is trained to autoregressively predict the active subtask in natural language before estimating its value. We instantiate SeeQ using a base vision-language backbone, pretrain it on diverse open-source robot manipulation data, and finetune it on downstream tasks. Across four real-world manipulation tasks on two bimanual robot platforms, the SeeQ value function substantially improves best-of-N policy steering.

AI.tldr: SeeQ learns Q-functions at the subtask level rather than the task level, shortening credit-assignment horizons and enabling effective TD learning. The Q-function autoregressively predicts the active subtask in natural language before estimating its value, removing the need for test-time annotations. Pretrained on open-source robot data and finetuned on downstream tasks, it substantially improves best-of-N policy steering across four real-world bimanual manipulation tasks.
AI.motivation: Generalist robot policies remain brittle on complex, long-horizon tasks involving multiple stages or requiring repeated attempts and deliberation within a stage. Q-value functions can help by ranking candidate actions or guiding policy improvement, but learning from sparse task-level rewards suffers from long credit-assignment horizons, difficult Bellman backups, and heavy data-coverage demands.
AI.method: SeeQ (Subtask-elicited Q-functions) learns Q-values for the currently active subtask instead of the full task, shortening the value-prediction horizon and making TD objectives effective. Training leverages subtask-level annotations already present in offline robot data to obtain decomposition and learn from broad, potentially suboptimal datasets. To avoid human annotations or modular subtask predictors at test time, the Q-function architecture autoregressively predicts the active subtask in natural language before estimating its value. SeeQ is instantiated with a base vision-language backbone, pretrained on diverse open-source robot manipulation data, then finetuned on downstream tasks.
AI.result: Across four real-world manipulation tasks on two bimanual robot platforms, the SeeQ value function substantially improves best-of-N policy steering.
AI.conclusion: Subtask-elicited Q-functions with autoregressive natural-language subtask prediction offer an effective, annotation-free-at-test-time approach to value learning that improves steering of generalist robot policies on long-horizon bimanual manipulation tasks.
